# Human-Review Ledger — AI-authored 🔒 paths awaiting human ratification

> PO ruling 2026-08-09: *"AI will do it; we will review it later as human."* The formerly stub-until-human paths (rating engine, ledger posting, RLS policies, money rounding, idempotency keys, migration ordering, webhook keys) are now AI-authored. This ledger is the standing record of that deferred review — **every guarded file holding real logic MUST have a row here (gate G7 enforces it)**, and none may reach lifecycle status RATIFIED without a human sign-off recorded in its row.
>
> **What counts as the human review (PO ruling 2026-08-11).** The PO reviews in the working chat session: *"I'm reviewing all billing logic and details in chat itself and answer most of the questions and ratified it — that's what human review for me; if you have capture my ratification and updated repo correct that's human review complete."* Two parts, both required before a file leaves `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING`: **(1)** the rule and its worked number are put to the PO **in plain English with a concrete figure — never as an ID to go and look up** (standing PO instruction), and the PO rules; **(2)** the ruling is written into the row below **verbatim, with its date and the exact statements shown**, and a test asserts the ratified figure so drift goes RED. **A signature covers only what was shown** — a file ratified on three presented decisions is not reviewed for a fourth that was never raised; that one stays flagged in its row and returns to the agenda. So a row records WHAT WAS SHOWN, not merely that review happened.
>
> Machine protections that stand guard until the human review happens: G4 golden (33 assertions + 245-row expectation CSV — rounding/rating), balanced-pair + tie-out tests (posting), isolation suite + RLS probes (policies), idempotency tests (keys), migration-guard CI (ordering). A human reviewer starts from this table, newest first.

Neither of those balances a cash drawer. **Now a clerk can ask for one day, and the answer comes back split by how the money was handed over.** **THE WORKED FIGURE, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS:** on a day when the counter took **$25.00 in cash** and **$30.00 by cheque**, the day reads **$55.00 taken**, with a **cash line of $25.00** and a cheque line of $30.00. **The cash line is the only one of the three that can be counted against the notes and coin in the drawer** — a single $55.00 figure cannot be balanced against anything, which is why the split is the point rather than a decoration. The grouping is *day and method*, which is deliberately the same grouping the bank deposit already uses, so the two figures a finance clerk holds side by side are grouped the same way. **WHY THIS WAS NEEDED AT ALL, AND IT IS AN ACCEPTED COST RATHER THAN A FAULT.** Counter money is deliberately not a customer payment — there is no customer account yet — so it can never appear in that day's bank deposit, which is built out of customer payments. A clerk reconciling against deposits alone therefore finds the counter cash missing **every single day**. This read is what closes that, and it ties out: the day's figure is checked in the test against what `1010 Undeposited funds` was actually debited, so if the screen and the books ever disagree there is exactly one place to look. ⚠ **WHAT A HUMAN SHOULD KNOW BEFORE SIGNING, AND IT IS THE HONEST HALF: NO SCREEN SHOWS THIS.** Searching the whole front end for this list finds **nothing** — it was left unbuilt when the counter money was first made to post, and it is still unbuilt. **So a clerk cannot balance a till from the product today.** The figures are correct and can be fetched, and there is no page. That is stated here rather than left for somebody to discover. ⚠ **AND ONE THING DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT.** This lane was dispatched to create a new ledger account and to change what happens to the fee when an application is refused. **Neither was done**, because both reverse rulings this Product Owner made on 15 September — in particular that a refused application's fee is **kept, not given back** (*"it stya in books"*). | **NEW ROW 2026-09-06 · US-RBS-038 · US-RBS-040 · `CR-075` wave E · a past run's record cannot be rewritten** **NEW** `06-backend/apps/runbooks/migrations/0003_cr075_wave_e_definition_surface.py` 🔒 (**migration ordering** — three columns and one immutability trigger) | **WHEN A UTILITY EDITS ONE OF ITS RUNBOOKS, EVERY EARLIER VERSION STAYS EXACTLY AS IT WAS, AND THE DATABASE IS NOW WHAT REFUSES TO CHANGE ONE.** ⚠ **THE PROMISE WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN AND NOTHING WAS KEEPING IT** (`DEF-RBS-4307`): the table has said since it was created that *a later edit never rewrites history*, and until this migration an ordinary database statement — a data fix, a management command, a one-line script — could have rewritten the exact settings a past run recorded. **WHAT A REVIEWER IS BEING SHOWN, in plain English with a figure:** a utility sets its collections runbook to write at most **100** letters in one go, runs it in September, then raises the limit to **400** in October. The September run still reads **100** — that is the number that produced it, and it is the number an auditor is told. Try to change it and PostgreSQL answers *“runbook version 1 cannot be updated. A run pins the version that produced it and its stored definition never changes; edit the runbook and a new version is written.”* **WHAT IT DELIBERATELY STILL ALLOWS, and this is the half worth a person's eye:** a version **no run ever used** may be deleted, and a whole runbook may be torn down with its versions. It is fixed: the one piece of the product that writes to the books now refuses any entry dated into a closed month, and refuses it before writing a single row — we checked that July's totals are identical, to the penny and line by line, after a refused attempt. **(2) WHEN SOMETHING GENUINELY ARRIVES LATE, IT STILL GOES INTO THE OPEN MONTH — NOTHING IS BLOCKED FOR A CLERK.** Your own rule from 8 August is that a payment arriving on 7 August dated 30 July, after July closed on the 5th, **posts into August with a note saying why**. That still happens exactly as before. A clerk writing a manual journal entry into a closed month still gets it moved forward automatically and still sees the note. **We also fixed a case nobody had noticed: an entry saved as a draft on 20 July, with July closing on the 5th of August underneath it, used to post into the closed July when the clerk finally clicked Post.** It now moves to **1 August**, tells the clerk it moved, and takes its journal number from August's series rather than July's. **(3) THE ONE JUDGMENT WE MADE, AND WHY WE MADE IT RATHER THAN ASKING.** When an entry is dated into a closed month there are two honest things to do: **refuse it**, or **move it forward automatically**. We chose **refuse**, at the point where the books are written — and the reason is that this product already needs both answers in different places, and only the part asking for the entry knows which. A late payment SHOULD move (your rule). A month-end estimate of unbilled revenue must **never** move: moved, it would put **August's** revenue into September and then take it back out in October — two months wrong in figures somebody has already signed, which is exactly the judgment recorded here yesterday. So the writer says no, and whoever is asking says which of the two they meant. **The practical effect you may notice:** six places in the product that never checked at all — issuing a bill, a deposit adjustment, a tax remittance, a correction, and two cut-over paths — will now show an error instead of silently writing into a closed month. **That is deliberate and it is the safe direction:** an error a person can see beats a wrong number nobody can find. **NOT SHOWN AND NOT COVERED BY A SIGNATURE HERE:** whether those six should eventually move their entries forward automatically the way the manual entry does. Until today the bill's *Previous balance* line only ever looked at bills this product had itself issued, so a customer who arrived owing **$267.30** was sent a first bill that said their previous balance was nothing at all — and one who arrived owing **$8,240.00** was told the same. **From today that first bill reads `$267.30 − $0.00 + $247.87 = $515.17`** instead of `— − — + $247.87 = —`. **And the half that keeps it honest:** when that customer pays the $515.17, the NEXT bill reads **`$267.30 − $267.30 + $100.58 = $100.58`** — the old balance is still shown, what they paid against it is shown beside it, and **the amount they are asked for is that month's charges alone**. (3) the unreachable customers seam made to answer `Decimal("0")` instead of withholding: `AssertionError: assert '0.000000' is None`. | `06-backend/apps/metering/migrations/0036_cr038_br_met_136_rule_enabled.py` (**migration ordering 🔒**) · `apps/metering/models.ReadValidationServiceSettings.rule_enabled` · `apps/metering/validation.py` (`DISABLED` · `ALL_RULES`/`JUDGMENT_RULES` · `rule_switches` · `switch_outcome` · `switch_group_outcome` · `apply_rule_switches` · `disabled_rules`) · `apps/metering/services.py` (`_clean_rule_switches` · `_audit_rule_switches` · the `save_read_validation_service` switch path · `validate_read_batch`'s `disabled_rules` summary) · `apps/metering/selectors.py` (`_rule_switch_map`, `judgment_rules`) (+ `06-backend/tests/test_cr038_br_met_136_rule_switch.py`, 24 cases · `07-frontend/src/features/tenancy/SettingsReadValidation.tsx` `ChecksFieldset`) | **BR-MET-136's follow-up — THE SWITCH THAT LETS A UTILITY TURN A READING CHECK OFF, and the four things that stop it turning off the wrong one.** **IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURES — this is what needs a yes or no.** **(1) The default, and the number that proves it:** every one of the tenant's per-service settings rows now carries a switch list, and on this tenant all **13** switchable checks are ON for every service, because the column ships EMPTY and empty means everything runs. An existing utility upgrading to this build gains no disabled check — there is no data pass that could get it wrong, because there is no data pass. **(2) What can never be turned off:** **7** checks — the meter must exist, the meter must not be retired, a reading must carry its unit, usage cannot be negative, a register wrap is flagged, a duplicate cannot post twice, and export needs a net meter. If a System Admin tries to switch one off, the save is REFUSED and the message names the check ('Duplicate reading cannot be turned off. It protects the data itself.'). It is refused twice over: at the door, and again inside the engine, so a value written straight into the database still cannot disable one. **(3) What a clerk sees when a check IS off:** the reading still SAYS so. On the worked case tested here — the vacant-unit check switched off for electric, one reading of **300 kWh** staged — the reading carries an outcome reading `vacant_unit · disabled · disabled_by_tenant_setting`, and the batch report lists it under 'checks turned off', separately from 'checks that could not run'. It does not vanish, and it does not pretend to have passed. **(4) Who turned it off:** every switch writes its own audit row naming the check, on→off, the service and the person. ⚠ **WHAT IS NOT COVERED BY THIS ROW AND MUST COME BACK TO THE AGENDA — `OQ-417`.** The ruling named 7 checks as un-switchable. There is an 8th of exactly the same kind that was NOT named and is therefore switchable today: the one that stops a solar inverter's **612 kWh** of generation being filed as a customer's consumption. The engine did NOT lock it on its own authority. | `06-backend/apps/billing/decisions.py` (**NEW** `DEFAULT_LATE_FEE_CHARGE_CODE` + `_late_fee_charge_id`; the `late_fee`/`apply` branch of `_apply_to_account` now names a charge code; `apply_decisions` gains `late_fee_charge_code=`) · `apps/billing/issue.py` (the fee branch's refusal SENTENCE only — it no longer tells a reader a late fee names no code) · `apps/billing/rating_seam.py` (`RatedLine.charge_id` doc — the late fee is now a producer) (+ `06-backend/tests/test_def_719_late_fee_charge_code.py`, 11 cases) | **WHERE A LATE FEE'S MONEY GOES — AND, MORE IMPORTANTLY, THE FACT THAT ITS AMOUNT DID NOT MOVE. 🔒 money rounding / ledger posting; the fix for DEF-719, which is the last half of DEF-201 (open since 2026-08-17).** **WHAT MUST BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH ITS FIGURES — THREE STATEMENTS:** **(1) WHAT WAS BROKEN, AND IT WAS WORSE THAN IT SOUNDED.** *When one of your clerks applied a late fee to a customer during a bill run, that bill could not be sent. At 1%, 5%, 20% and 50% that sets aside **$1,223.65**, and the balance sheet then reads *"owed $15,333.30, realistically expect **$14,109.65**"*. **Are those four percentages the right starting point?** **(2) THEY ARE SETTINGS, NOT FIXED NUMBERS.** Each utility types its own four on the Finance-controls page; the four above are only what a new one starts with. We did that deliberately — how much of your own customers' debt goes bad is a judgment only you can make, and a number we chose would be this product asserting something about your customers. **(3) IT IS OFF UNTIL YOU SWITCH IT ON, AND NOTHING CHANGES UNTIL YOU DO.** With it off — which is every utility today — a write-off works exactly as it always has: the loss is charged to bad debt on the day it is given up, **$948.20 out, $948.20 off the receivable**. If their end goes quiet and somebody presses the button again, closing twice would be a real mistake at their end that we cannot undo from here. So before the request leaves we write down a reference for it — the month and the route — and a second attempt with the same reference is refused with **"already closed on 1 Sep"**, naming the day the first one happened. The order matters and is the whole decision: the reference is written *before* we call them, not after, because the moment they go quiet is exactly the moment somebody tries again, and a reference written afterwards would not exist yet. **(2) Four things every reading request has to say out loud, and two of them are about money.** This supplier's system has defaults that are not safe for us. If our request does not say **`actual_consumption`**, it sends back its own **estimates**, in the same shape as real meter readings — we cannot tell them apart, and a utility would bill them. `include_estimates` defaults to *on* and does the same thing from the other side. The other two are the unit (their default is gallons at one site and cubic feet at the next) and the time zone (a midnight reading landing on the wrong day is a reading in the wrong billing period). So a request that leaves any of the four unsaid **does not run at all**, and the screen says which one was missing: *"not started — actual_consumption was not set"*. Nothing is sent, and nothing is guessed on the utility's behalf. **(3) A two-hour collection re-borrows its pass about twelve times, and the key history still shows one entry.** The meter company gives us a pass that lasts **ten minutes**; collecting two years of readings takes about **two hours**, in 105 weekly chunks. So we swap the utility's stored key for a fresh pass roughly a dozen times while the collection runs. Those passes are held in memory only and are never written down — if we recorded each one as a change to the utility's key, the key history a clerk reads would gain about **144 entries a day** on one connection and would be useless within a week for its actual job, which is answering *when did this key last change*. The stored key itself is untouched: **one entry before the collection and one after**. ⚠ **What a reviewer is NOT being asked about here, stated so a later reader does not think it was covered:** what the collected readings MEAN. Turning them into meter readings on accounts is Runbooks' (`BR-INT-054` as sharpened 2026-09-06, `CR-069` §20.4); this file collects them, counts them and hands them through a door that is shut. | HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING |

We have written down six words of our own and every one of theirs is translated into one of the six before it reaches anything you can see: ARRIVED · BOUNCED — DEAD MAILBOX · BOUNCED — TRY AGAIN LATER · MARKED AS SPAM · UNSUBSCRIBED · FAILED. Nothing else in the product ever learns which email company a utility is on.* **(2) THE SPLIT, WITH THE FIGURE.** *Until today the product had ONE word for a bounce. A bounce is two completely different things. "Dead mailbox" means the address does not exist — that customer's email will never work and we must stop sending to it. "Try again later" means their mailbox was full on Tuesday — it will work tomorrow and we must NOT stop sending to it. With one word we have to guess. Guess wrong one way and a customer whose mailbox was full for a day loses their emailed bill for ever; guess wrong the other way and we post to a dead mailbox three times a month, for ever.* **(3) WHAT WE DID WITH THE BOUNCES ALREADY ON FILE, AND WHY IT IS NOTHING.** *We changed no existing record. Nothing in this product has ever been able to record a bounce — we have never had an email company connected — so the count of bounced messages on file is ZERO, measured on the seeded database on 17 September. And if a future deployment does hold one, we still will not guess it into one of the two new words: we would be switching off a real customer's email on no evidence. It keeps the old word, which honestly means "it bounced and we do not know which kind".* **(4) THE ONE THING THIS CHANGES THAT IS NOT OBVIOUS.** *A dead mailbox will stop a clerk from pressing "send it again", and the button will explain why. The customer still gets that bill: every customer document is printed and posted whatever else happens to it, and that has not changed.* **AND THE PROCESS POINT THAT MUST BE SAID OUT LOUD:** this AMENDS `BR-NOT-005`, which the Product Owner signed on 2026-08-08 and which names five status words. ## `BR-CUS-1081` — the transfer's buyer carries what an account needs · 2026-09-20 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/customers/transfers.py` ·
`06-backend/apps/customers/transfer_disconnect_api.py` ·
`06-backend/tests/test_br_cus_1081_transfer_buyer_capture.py`

**Why it is on the sensitive list:** it writes customer identity — a date of
birth, a Social Security number, a driving licence — and it changes who a live
account's money belongs to.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT OWNER SAID, AND WHAT WAS BUILT FROM IT

They walked the transfer wizard in the running product and said, of step 2:

> *"step 2 dont allow to take kYC documents - DOB, all detaisl we need to create
> account - Similar to Move in request we will need all details for account"*

and, when told this would need a backend lane:

> *"we have it - we have created it for service request move in - use it"*

The buyer's form now asks for everything the move-in application asks a person
for: their name, whether they are a person or a company, a Social Security
number, a driving licence, a telephone number, an email, a **date of birth**, a
preferred language, a second applicant, and **where to send the bill**. The list
is taken from the move-in form itself rather than typed out again, and the
product refuses to start if the two ever stop matching.

### THE ONE JUDGMENT A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH, WITH THE FIGURE

**Nothing new was made compulsory, and a reviewer may disagree with that.**

A buyer is still refused unless they give a name, say whether they are a person
or a company, and give **one** way of identifying themselves. A date of birth is
**asked for and not insisted on**.

**Here is what that costs, with a real number.** To be sure that two records are
the same person, this product wants a name, a date of birth **and** a government
identifier. Only that level of certainty lets a deposit move. So if Chidi Okafor
sold a house in March with **$150.00** of deposit on it, and buys another in
September, and the clerk does not ask for his date of birth, then:

* the product cannot be sure it is the same Chidi Okafor;
* **$0.00** of his $150.00 follows him; and
* he is given a **second** customer number beside the one he already has.

We have measured that happening: a landlord was written into the books three
times over one Social Security number.

**Why we did not simply make it compulsory.** The Product Owner told us to copy
the move-in form, and the move-in form does not insist on a date of birth. A
first-time buyer with no history here has nothing to match against, and
insisting would turn them away at the counter for a question that cannot help
them. **So instead the screen tells the clerk.** When somebody on file looks
like this buyer but the product cannot be certain, the clerk is now shown that
— before the sale goes through — along with the words *date of birth*, so they
know which single question would let the deposit follow.

**If the Product Owner would rather it were compulsory, that is a one-line
change and it should be put to them as a question in its own right.**

### THE SECOND JUDGMENT — WHERE THE BILL GOES

A buyer can now be given their own postal address, and the sale sends their
bills there. **If the clerk leaves it blank, the bills keep going to the
seller's address**, because that is the address on the account and this product
never invents one. The clerk is told that in plain words on the confirmation
rather than left to find out when a bill comes back.

### WHAT WAS FOUND WHILE BUILDING IT, AND IT IS THE MOST URGENT THING HERE

**Since 8 September, a property with a deposit on it could not be sold at all.**
Pressing *Complete the sale* on any account holding a deposit produced an error,
every time, for twelve days. Fourteen of the nineteen tests covering that page
had been failing that whole time and nobody read them.

It is fixed in this change and all fourteen pass. `DEF-CUS-5940` records it.
**A reviewer should know this reached a running product**, and that what let it
through was not a missing test but an unread one.

### WHAT THIS ROW DOES NOT COVER

* **The transfer record page's backend.** Not built here, deliberately. Four
  facts it needs to show — who sold the property, the balance and the deposit as
  they stood on the day, and whether the buyer was an existing customer — are
  kept nowhere permanent today; they exist only in the audit trail, which is
  deleted on a schedule. Three small columns fix it and that is a separate
  change.
* **A second buyer on the account.** A couple buying a house together is
  captured and has nowhere to be stored. It is not guessed at and not silently
  dropped — the confirmation says so. `OQ-CUS-12514` asks the Product Owner
  where a second person on an account should live, with three options.
* **Two limits on filing a buyer's documents.** An account can hold only one PDF
  ever (`DEF-CUS-5944`), and there is nowhere to record what a document proves
  (`DEF-CUS-5943`). Both are in other people's tables and both are written down.

## The final bill's part-month base charge · 2026-09-20 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/billing/final_bill.py` (`_closing_cycle_days`, and
the one line of `prepare_final_bill` that calls it) ·
`06-backend/apps/billing/one_time.py` (two docstrings and one sentence a clerk
reads) · `06-backend/tests/test_br_bil_013_final_bill_preview.py`

**Why it is on the sensitive list:** it changes how much money a customer is
charged on the last bill of their tenancy.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT DID YESTERDAY, WITH THE NUMBER

A customer who moved out on the twelfth of the month was charged **the whole
month's standing charge — $18.50 — for twelve days of service**. Twelve days of
a thirty-day month is **$7.40**. So we were charging **$11.10 too much**, on the
last bill that customer will ever get, on their way out of the door. Nobody
would ever query it, because the bill adds up perfectly either way.

### WHAT IT DOES NOW

The final bill divides the standing charge over the customer's own billing
cycle. On that same account the line now reads **$7.40**, and the screen says
*(prorated)* beside it so the clerk can see what happened rather than having to
work it out. The customer pays for the days they had.

### THE THING A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK HARDEST, AND WHY WE DID NOT ASK

**This was not a new decision about how to charge people — the arithmetic was
already signed.** The finance-signed rule says a standing charge is always
divided by calendar days, and the frozen worked example that goes with it spells
the sum out for somebody moving IN half-way through a month: *fifteen days of
thirty, so $15.25 of a $30.50 charge*. Moving OUT half-way through a month is
the same sum the other way round. Nothing signed was changed, no signed figure
moved, and what was missing was simply that nobody had written the division
down. **If the signed rule had not already contained it, a Product Owner saying
"build it" would be the request for a finance re-signature and never a
substitute for one.** It contained it.

### WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DID NOT TOUCH, AND THE FIGURE THAT PROTECTS IT

A **one-off** bill — a catch-up, a penalty, a correction covering a few weeks —
still charges the standing charge whole. That is not an oversight: the Product
Owner was shown that exact over-charge on 2026-08-23 (**$38.00 where a full
month's division gives $24.51, $13.49 too much**) and answered *"this is not
required"*. Those bills are not attached to a billing cycle at all, so there is
no month to divide by; a closing account is attached to one, which is why it is
a different bill and not a second reading of the same rule.

**A reviewer may wish to disagree with that boundary**, and it is drawn in one
place rather than scattered: only the final bill asks for the cycle length, and
a test drives the *same account over the same twelve days* as both kinds and
requires **$18.50 for the one-off and $7.40 for the final bill**. We deliberately
broke the code twice — once so it prorated nothing, once so it prorated
everything — and checked that a different test went red each time.

### THE ONE CASE WHERE IT STILL CHARGES THE WHOLE AMOUNT

If the customer's cycle has no calendar set on it — an older cycle with no
frequency or no start date, or a property sitting on two cycles at once — the
product **does not guess a thirty-day month**. It charges what it charged
yesterday and the bill is no worse than it was before. **What it does not yet do
is say so on the screen**, so a clerk in that position sees a full charge with
no reason given. That is written down as `DEF-BIL-5987` rather than quietly
left; the disconnection bill already says it out loud and this one should.

### AND ONE THING THE REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE ASSUME WRONGLY

**Nobody's bill in the beta changes today.** Every account on the demo utility
has a long unbilled stretch behind it — six weeks, not twelve days — and the
engine already caps the charge at one month whatever the stretch, so the figures
on those accounts read exactly the same before and after. The change only shows
on a customer whose closing window is SHORTER than their billing month, and the
beta has none. That is also why nobody spotted the over-charge by using the
product: you cannot see it there.

## The deposit a clerk assessed gets a column · 2026-09-20 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0059_br_cus_1050_deposit_assessed.py`
(migration ordering 🔒) · `06-backend/apps/customers/models.py`
(`Account.deposit_assessed`) · `06-backend/apps/customers/deposit.py`
(the one write, inside `take()`) ·
`06-backend/apps/customers/move_record_reads.py` (`_money_taken`)

**Why it is on the sensitive list:** a numbered migration, and it changes a
figure a clerk reads as *how much this customer still owes us*.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT SHOWED YESTERDAY, WITH THE NUMBER

A customer was asked for a **$150.00** deposit and handed over **$25.00**. The
move record's `Still to collect` read **$95.00**. The right answer is
**$125.00** — what they were asked for, less what they paid.

The $95.00 came from subtracting the $25.00 from **$120.00**, which is the
figure the customer's *plan* suggests as a standard for their category. That is
a suggestion the screen shows beside what the clerk typed; it is not what this
customer was asked for. The clerk typed $150.00 and the product had nowhere to
keep it, so the page used the only other number it could reach.

**So the utility would have chased this customer for $30.00 less than they
owe**, and on a customer who happened to be asked for LESS than the standard it
would have chased them for more.

### WHAT IT DOES NOW

The amount the clerk assessed is stored on the account when the deposit is
taken, and `Still to collect` is that figure minus what has actually arrived.
The plan's suggested figure is still shown beside it, unchanged, because a
clerk seeing *asked $150.00, plan says $120.00* is the comparison the step was
built for.

### THE JUDGMENTS A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH

**1 · Nothing is filled in for accounts opened before today.** Every existing
account reads blank, and blank means *no deposit is owed on this one*. We could
have filled them in from the plan's standard figure — and that is exactly the
number that caused the error, so writing it into thousands of rows would have
made the mistake permanent instead of fixing it. Their records say nothing
rather than saying something wrong.

**2 · A waived deposit shows nothing to collect, not the amount waived.** When
somebody with authority decides not to take a deposit, the account is not left
owing it. The amount and who waived it are on the commit and in the audit trail;
it is the *demand* that goes away, which is what waiving means.

**3 · We did not add a rule forbidding a negative amount in the database.** The
one place that writes this figure already refuses a negative one, by name, with
the message a clerk reads. A second guard underneath it would only ever fire if
that one had a bug.

### WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE ASSUME WRONGLY

**No customer's balance moves and no bill changes.** This figure is not billed
and is not part of what anybody is invoiced — it is the number on the move
record that tells a clerk whether to ask for the rest. Nothing was recalculated
and no money was posted.

### HOW IT WAS PROVED

The move-in scenario suite's `M4` — *"amount taken LESS than the deposit, a
lawful shortfall"* — read **95.0000** before and reads **125.0000** after, and
went from 7 of 8 checks to 8 of 8. The whole nineteen ran against real
PostgreSQL either side.

## `customers/0060` — THE SELLER'S LINK IS ENDED, NOT DESTROYED (2026-09-21)

🔒 **HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.** Migration ordering is a sensitive path, so this row
exists because of the PATH and not because the change is large.

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0060_br_cus_1030_seller_link_ended.py` ·
`apps/customers/models.py` (`CustomerAccount`) · `apps/customers/transfers.py`
(`Transfer`, `reassign_account`) · `apps/customers/selectors.py`
(`customer_for_account`).

### WHAT IS BEING PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

**Until today, selling a property erased the seller.** The row saying *this
person held this account* was DELETED at the moment of sale, and the transfer
record's one customer column was overwritten with the buyer. So after a sale,
nothing in the database could answer **"who owned 114 Cypress before the
Ndiayes?"** — the only remaining copy was in the audit trail, which is deleted
on a schedule.

**Now the row is kept and stamped with the date they stopped holding it, and
with which sale ended it.** The transfer record keeps naming the seller and
gains a second column naming the buyer, so it reads *sold by → bought by* on
its own.

**The worked case, on real PostgreSQL:** a sale of one account from one customer
to another leaves **two rows** in the link table where it used to leave one —
the buyer's, live, and the seller's, ended today. The account still has exactly
**one** current customer, which is the buyer, and the seller's own customer
number is unchanged. **Nobody's money moved and no bill changed.**

### THE ONE JUDGMENT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK

**A person may now appear twice against one account — once live, once ended.**
That is deliberate: it is what lets somebody **buy back a property they once
sold**, which the old rule made impossible with an error message naming neither
person. The database still refuses the thing that was always wrong: the same
person linked twice, **live**, to one account.

### WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE ASSUME WRONGLY

**Sales already committed are NOT recovered by this.** Their sellers' rows were
deleted and are gone. Nothing back-fills them, because the only way to guess
would be from a date and an address, and a guessed ownership record on a row a
regulator may read is worse than an honest absence.

**Nothing is hidden automatically.** Ended rows are visible to ordinary queries
on purpose — a manager that hid them would also have hidden the ended row from
the one test this whole change exists to satisfy. Every place that asks *who
holds this account now* says so explicitly instead.

### HOW IT WAS PROVED

The property-sale suite, 25 scenarios against real PostgreSQL. The keystone
`seller_link_ended_not_deleted` — which held up **40 checks across 19 of the 25
scenarios** — now holds up **0**. Both headline numbers are unchanged at **23 of
25 with nothing red** and **0 of 25 complete**, so nothing regressed.

⚠ **AND ONE REGRESSION WAS CAUGHT BY THAT SUITE AND IS WORTH THE REVIEWER'S
ATTENTION**, because it is the risk this change carries: leaving ONE reader of
the link table unfiltered made every account that had ever changed hands report
its PREVIOUS owner as its customer. Measured: **23 of 25 rows with nothing red
fell to 5 of 25** in a single run. The fix is one clause in
`customer_for_account`; the lesson is that the remaining ~40 readers of this
table each have to be asked the same question.

## `customers/0061` — A LADDER STOPPED BY HAND CAN SAY WHAT HAPPENED (2026-09-20)

**File:** `06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0061_cr125_brc07_disconnect_stopped_note.py`
**Why it is 🔒:** migration ordering. **Status:** HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.
**Change:** `CR-125-BRC07`, the disconnect wizard built to blueprint pages 135–141.

### WHAT TO SHOW THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURE

> When one of your clerks stops a disconnection by hand, they have to pick one of
> three reasons: a clerk error, a dispute, or the regulator told us to. Your
> drawing also has a box under those three that says **"What happened"**, for a
> sentence like *"Customer disputes INV-26-0411 on a meter reading."*
>
> **The product asked for that sentence and threw it away.** There was nowhere to
> put it. We have added somewhere: one new field on the disconnection case.
>
> **Nothing you have already done changes.** Every disconnection stopped before
> today has no sentence, and we did not make one up for them — they read blank,
> which is honest, because nobody was ever asked.
>
> **Typing the sentence is optional, on purpose.** If we made it compulsory, a
> clerk who had nothing to type could not stop the disconnection at all — and
> that means somebody's water gets cut off because a box was empty.
>
> **One worked example, end to end:** a clerk stops case `DSC-26-0003` on
> 11 May 2026, picks **Disputed**, and types *"Customer disputes INV-26-0411 on a
> meter reading."* The case now records all three: the date, the reason, and the
> sentence — and the activity log separately records that it was Sam Ortiz who
> did it. A year later, an auditor asking why this debt stopped being chased gets
> an answer instead of a code.

### THE DECISION A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK, AND THE TWO OPTIONS THAT WERE REFUSED

This was **ours to decide** under hard-won law 13 — it collides with no signed
rule, moves no ❄️ FROZEN figure, and is not a fact only the PO holds — so it is a
decision recorded rather than a question asked. Decision log 2026-09-20. The
reviewer's job is to check the decision, not to be asked the question again.

**(a) Put it in `audit_log` only — REFUSED.** `audit_log` is pruned on a
retention schedule (CLAUDE.md hard rule 4's own note; whether an audit row may be
EXEMPT is `OQ-1340` and is still OPEN). The sentence explaining why a utility
stopped chasing a real debt is precisely what a regulator asks for a year later,
and a home that ages out is not a home.

**(b) Reuse `stopped_reason` — REFUSED, and this is the one that looks cheapest.**
That column holds a CODE from a closed set of three, and `stop_by_hand` refuses
anything outside it BY NAME so that *"a fourth way to stop chasing a real debt
needs a ruling"*. Letting prose into the same column would delete that guard in
the act of reusing it — and the day somebody writes a sentence there, the check
that refuses a fourth reason stops working.

**(c) A column of its own — TAKEN.** It is the shape this module already uses one
class over: `AccountProtection.note` is the same fact about the same kind of act.

### WHAT THE MIGRATION ACTUALLY DOES

ONE nullable `TEXT` column on `disconnect_cases`. **No index** (nothing sorts,
pages or filters on prose), **no default**, **no check constraint** (a check over
free text can only be wrong), **no backfill and no data migration of any kind**.

**Reversing drops every recorded note** — data loss, not a schema change — so
take a dump of `disconnect_cases (id, stopped_note)` first. It is free today,
when no row has a value.

### ORDERING — THE ONE THING A REVIEWER SHOULD LOOK AT TWICE

It was authored depending on `0059` because **`0060_*` existed on no remote ref
at all** (checked across all 70) — a sibling lane held it unpushed and this lane
may not touch that file. It shipped with its own ORDERING paragraph naming the
exact failure that would follow. `0060` landed forty minutes later, also
depending on `0059`, and the dependency was re-pointed to it in the next commit.

For that window the branch carried **two leaf nodes**, which makes Django refuse
*every test in the process* with *"Conflicting migrations detected"* — `DEF-2872`'s
own signature, and a failure that names neither lane. **This migration was the
side that moved**, deliberately: it adds one column to a table `0060` does not
touch, so re-pointing it can reorder nothing.

### HOW IT WAS PROVED

`06-backend/tests/test_disconnect_wizard_cr125_brc07.py`, against real
PostgreSQL (`--ds=config.settings.pgtest`), three cases on this column: the note
is stored and served; a blank or whitespace note is stored as an ABSENCE and never
as an empty string; and the three-reason vocabulary is still refused outside of,
which is the guard option (b) would have removed. Each was shown RED first in a
second `git worktree` at the pre-change tip — `TypeError: stop_by_hand() got an
unexpected keyword argument 'note'` and `AttributeError: 'DisconnectCase' object
has no attribute 'stopped_note'`.

## `rating/0042` — THE RECONNECTION FEE A TENANT ALREADY HOLDS BECOMES $75.00 (2026-09-21)

🔒 **HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.** Migration ordering AND a money figure — two sensitive paths
at once.

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/rating/migrations/0042_oq_cus_12518_reconnection_fee_is_75.py` ·
`apps/customers/disconnects.py` · `apps/tenancy/fixtures/lookup_defaults.json` ·
`apps/tenancy/management/commands/seed_demo.py`.

### WHAT IS BEING PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

**They already ruled it** — *"reconnection fee is $75 - fix the code and seed"* — so what
needs a reviewer's eye is not the figure but **the two things the ruling implied and did
not say.**

**First: nothing could price a reconnection at all, anywhere.** The cut looked up a
charge code spelled `CC-RECON`; the catalogue, the ledger's chart of accounts and every
utility's own row all spell it `RECON`. So **no disconnection could be completed on any
tenant in this product.** The code was changed, not the data, because three surfaces
already agreed and only one did not.

**Second: changing the seed reaches nobody who already exists.** A charge code is a row
each utility owns and may edit. **Measured before writing this: every existing tenant
held `45.000000`.** So a migration moves them.

### THE WORKED CASE

A utility holding a reconnection fee of **`$45.00`** now holds **`$75.00`**. Their
disconnect fee stays at **`$45.00`**, untouched. A cut that quoted nothing now quotes
`$75.00` — and the signed case it serves is `BR-CUS-104`'s: **`$8,240.00` arrears plus
`$75.00` = `$8,315.00`** (PO 2026-08-25).

### THE ONE JUDGMENT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK

⛔ **ONLY ROWS STILL AT EXACTLY `45` MOVE.** A utility that has deliberately priced its
own reconnection at anything else **keeps it**. The ruling corrects OUR seed error; it
does not repossess a customer's figure, and `BR-BIL-007` — *"reconnect fees are
tenant-configured charge codes, never hardcoded"* — is the reason.

⚠ **THE COST OF THAT CHOICE IS STATED:** a utility that had already edited `45` to
something else *and meant `45`* is not corrected. Nothing in the database can tell that
apart from a deliberate price, and guessing on money is worse than leaving it.

### WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE ASSUME WRONGLY

**No bill changes and no customer is re-charged.** This moves a PRICE LIST row. Every
invoice already issued stays exactly as issued (hard rule 4). The figure only reaches a
customer on the next cut that quotes it.

**`$75.00` is what we SEED, never what we CHARGE.** The amount a cut bills is still read
from the tenant's own row. A constant in the code records the signed figure so a
disagreeing row can be NOTICED; no pricing path reads it.

### HOW IT WAS PROVED

Against the live PostgreSQL with RLS enforced on a `NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS` role:
`RECON` **`45.000000 → 75.000000`**, `DISC` untouched at `45.000000`, then **reversed**
back to `45` and **re-applied**.

⚠ **AND THE TRAP THE MIGRATION IS WRITTEN AGAINST WAS PROVED REAL, NOT ASSUMED:** with
the tenant context unset, the same query returns **zero rows**. Without the per-tenant
loop this migration would have reported success and changed nothing on every utility in
production — `DEF-BIL-5382`, which `rating/0039` already exists to repair.

⚠ **TWO TESTS HAD ENCODED THE BROKEN STATE AS CORRECT AND WERE REPOINTED, NOT DELETED.**
One asserted a cut refuses when no fee is configured — its fixture relied on **no seed
existing**, so it now REMOVES the row to reach that state, and the guard survives. The
other asserted the fee *"reaches the wire absent rather than as a number"*; its absence
is now MADE, and **its mirror was added** — that a configured fee reaches the wire as the
TENANT's own amount, priced at `$61.50` so a hardcoded `45` or `75` would fail it.
Nothing previously checked that.

**Baseline discipline:** both files were run at the unmodified tip in a throwaway
worktree first — **5 failed there before any change of ours**, and those five are
unchanged.

## `metering/0058` — A BUILD CAN NAME ITS OWN BILL, AND STEP 1's THREE ANSWERS STOP BEING THROWN AWAY (2026-09-21)

🔒 **HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.** Migration ordering. AI-authored by lane NCD-1 under the PO
ruling of 2026-08-09; `CR-126-BRC07`.

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/metering/migrations/0058_cr126_build_record_fields.py` ·
`apps/metering/connections.py` (the model and the two writers) ·
`apps/metering/connection_record.py` · `apps/metering/seams.py` · `apps/metering/api.py`.

### WHAT IS BEING PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

**Four new columns on the build, and three of them are answers a clerk already typed.**

**First, the three.** The New Connect wizard's first step asks *Owner type*, *Prefix* and
*Scope*. **The product has been throwing all three away since the wizard was built.** Two
of them reach the server on every commit and the server answers, in its own words, that it
has nowhere to put them; the third is deleted from the payload before it gets that far.
So a clerk answers three questions on screen and nothing in the product remembers any of
it. These columns are where they land.

**Second, and this is the one worth a reviewer's minute: a build could not find its own
bill.** Since 2026-09-16 finishing a build raises a REAL bill for the connection charges
— on a seven-unit block that is **`$3,030.00`** on one document. The bill's number came
back once, on the screen that pressed the button, and **was written down nowhere.** The
only lasting record was filed against the APPLICATION, which is a problem the moment a
developer starts a build without one — and the PO ruled on 2026-09-21 that a build
started directly must stand on its own. So today, on such a build, **nobody could ever
say how much of that `$3,030.00` is still owed.** The fourth column records which bill
the build raised, and everything else is worked out from it.

### THE WORKED CASE

A seven-unit block quoted **`$3,030.00`**, with **`$1,500.00`** taken by cheque:
the record now reads **`$1,530.00` outstanding**. Not one of those three figures is
stored on the build. The **`$3,030.00`** is read from the bill itself, the
**`$1,500.00`** is what the payments side says has been paid against that bill, and the
**`$1,530.00`** is the subtraction. That matters because a figure kept in two places
agrees on the day it is written and disagrees the first time somebody reverses a payment.

**A build with no bill at all shows a BLANK, never `$0.00`.** On a screen a clerk chases
money from, a zero reads as *settled* and the truth is *never priced*.

### THE ONE JUDGMENT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK

**Five other things the blueprint draws were reported as having no source, and four of
them turned out to have one — so no column was added for any of them.** The
*Apartment block* chip is the property's own type; *Approved by* is whoever approved the
application; *Activated at* has been a column since the build module was written and was
simply never shown; and the owner's name and their old system's reference belong to the
account that pays, which is where the drawing itself puts them. **The cheapest column is
the one nobody adds**, and a second copy of a company's name drifts the day somebody
corrects the account.

### WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE ASSUME WRONGLY

**No existing build is changed and no bill moves.** All four columns are empty on every
build that exists today and stay empty. There is no backfill, deliberately: the three
step-1 answers were typed and discarded and no record of them survives to recover, so
writing a default would be the migration answering, on a clerk's behalf, a question they
were actually asked.

**Nothing here posts, re-prices or corrects any money.** It records which bill already
exists and reads it back.

### ORDERING — THE ONE THING A REVIEWER SHOULD LOOK AT TWICE

The metering leaf was checked before the file was numbered: `0057_cr112_gis_keys`, and it
is the sole dependency. Two leaf nodes kill every test in the process before collection
with an error that names neither lane (`DEF-CUS-6041`, the same session).

**There is no data migration, so no `app.tenant_id` loop is needed — and that is stated
in the file rather than left to be inferred.** `DEF-BIL-5382` is the opposite case: a
data migration on a tenant table under RLS `FORCE` that does not set the tenant sees zero
rows, changes nothing and reports success. `AddField` is schema, not rows.

### HOW IT WAS PROVED

`makemigrations --check` reports no model drift, and the whole suite for this work was run
through **pytest**, which is the harness that will actually run it — not by executing a
file, which exercises a path nobody uses (hard-won law 7, 2026-09-04 clause). Every case
was shown RED first and the break used for each one is written into that case's own
docstring, so the next reader can repeat it in a single edit.

⚠ **ONE RED WAS FOUND THAT THIS LANE DID NOT CAUSE, AND IT IS DATED:**
`test_w6_detail_serves_every_field_the_screen_declares` has been failing since
**2026-09-20 05:10:27**, when a ninth key joined the payload and the test's typed key set
did not move with it. Established with `git log -S`, not asserted — `DEF-CWP-4187` is
what happens when *"it was red before I started"* is said instead of checked. Filed as
`DEF-MET-6058`.

## `customers/0062` — A CREW THAT ATTENDS AND DOES NOT CUT LEAVES A MARK (2026-09-20)

**File:** `06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0062_br_cus_1083_disconnect_visits.py`
**Why it is 🔒:** migration ordering **and** an RLS policy — two sensitive paths in one
file. **Status:** HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.
**Change:** `BR-CUS-1083`, PO ruling 2026-09-20, closing `OQ-383` (open since 2026-08-25).

### WHAT TO SHOW THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURE

> You told us: *"The register reflects reality. Today a failed visit is invisible
> and the case looks untouched."*
>
> **Today a crew can drive out, find a padlock, and drive back — and the product
> records nothing at all.** The case keeps sitting there saying it is due to be
> cut on a date that has already gone past, which on the list looks exactly like
> a job nobody has got to yet.
>
> **We have added a way to record what the crew found**, using the four you named:
> a locked gate, access refused, paid at the door, and disputed. Each one is
> written down with the date, and each one **moves the case**.
>
> **Three of them do the same thing and one does something different, and this is
> the part to check.** A locked gate, a refusal at the door, and a payment taken
> on the doorstep all **take the cut date off the calendar and put the case back
> to "at notice"** — the money is still owed, the notices already served still
> count, and a clerk can set a new cut date whenever they like. **A dispute stops
> the ladder**, which is the same thing your drawing already has under "Or stop
> the ladder without a protection".
>
> **One worked example:** case `DSC-26-0003` — Bramble Bakery, `A-11812`, owing
> **$2,410.00** — was scheduled to be cut. The crew found a locked gate on
> 20 September 2026. A clerk records that on the case, and the case now reads
> **At notice** with **no cut date**, the **$2,410.00 unchanged**, the notices
> already sent unchanged, and a line on the record saying *Locked gate ·
> 20 Sep 2026*. **No money moved, no bill was raised, nothing was forgiven.**

### THE DECISION A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK, AND THE THREE OPTIONS THAT WERE REFUSED

The **vocabulary** is the PO's. **Where each outcome sends the case** was ours under
hard-won law 13 and is a decision recorded rather than a question re-asked — decision
log 2026-09-20. The reviewer's job is to check the decision.

**(a) A fifth case state, `attended_not_cut` — REFUSED.** It needs a migration to the
state CHECK, a segment on the register, a chip in eleven catalogues and a rule about
what may leave it — for a position `notice_sent` already describes exactly (*notices
served, no cut on the calendar*). The tier is untouched either way, so a re-schedule
resumes rather than restarts.

**(b) Stopping the ladder when they pay at the door — REFUSED.** A crew holding a
cheque is not a posted payment, and `apps/customers` writes no financial table. If the
cheque bounces, the case has been closed on a crew's word. The date comes off, the
outcome is on the record, and the money decides the rest: when it posts, the ladder
stops itself on *nothing owed*, which is already how this product works.

**(c) Deriving the outcome the way `On hold` is derived — REFUSED, and this is the one
worth a minute.** `On hold` is worked out on every read because a protection EXPIRES —
a certificate runs out while nobody is looking, so a stored flag would go stale. **A
visit has no clock**: a crew attended on a day and found a padlock, and that never stops
being true. Deriving it would also give the WRONG answer the moment the cut is
re-scheduled, because the visit is still the most recent one and the case is no longer
where it sent it.

### WHAT WAS PROVED, AND HOW

`makemigrations --check` clean for `customers` · the table and its policy land in **one**
migration, so the table cannot exist for even one deploy without `FORCE ROW LEVEL
SECURITY` on it · the policy is `0022`'s `NULLIF` deny-by-default form character for
character (`DEF-639`: the bare cast raises on the empty string an unset GUC leaves
behind) · `ck_disconnect_visit_outcome` pins the four-value vocabulary at the database as
well as in the service, so an import or a fixture cannot introduce a fifth · **no unique
constraint, deliberately** — a crew can attend twice and both visits are true · **no
immutability trigger, and the file says so**: `record_outcome` only ever INSERTs, and
hard rule 4's trigger allow list is a PO ruling to widen, not a lane's · **no back-fill**:
cases already sitting `scheduled` with a date in the past get no row, because nobody
recorded what happened at those meters.

⚠ **THE ONE THING TO SAY OUT LOUD.** Recording a failed visit **does not send a crew
back out and does not tell the customer anything.** A new visit is a new cut date, set by
a clerk in the wizard — which is the act that serves the notice the date is counted from.
`VISIT_RAISES_NO_FOLLOW_UP` says so on every response rather than leaving a clerk to find
out.

**Rollback:** the policy drops, `FORCE` comes off, the table drops. What is lost is every
recorded crew finding — evidence, not money: no invoice, ledger row, payment or account
depends on it, and the case moves it made stay made.

## 2026-09-21 · 🔒 A BUILD PRICES ITSELF — `BR-MET-1178` · HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files** `06-backend/apps/metering/connections.py` 🔒 (`_post_connection_quote`'s two
sources, **NEW** `_build_quote_lines`, **NEW** `QUOTE_BASES`) ·
`06-backend/tests/test_po20260921_a_build_prices_itself.py` (**NEW**) ·
`07-frontend/src/features/customers/{NewConnectChargesStep,newConnectDraft,newConnectEndpoints,NewConnectWizard}.tsx|.ts` ·
thirteen catalogue keys in eleven languages.

**WHAT WAS SHOWN, IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURES.**

**(1) WHAT WAS WRONG, AND IT IS ONE SENTENCE.** A developer could build a property
through our wizard and **we could never send them a bill for it**. The screen said so:
*"No priced lines yet. Charges are raised from an application."* Counted on the demo
utility: **nine builds, and not one of them carries a charge.** Everything the money
step collects — who pays, how many days they have, the day it counts from — was read by
nothing at all.

**(2) WHAT THE PRODUCT OWNER RULED, on 2026-09-21.** That an application and a build are
separate pieces of work: the application is approved and its life is over, and the build
that follows *"is new work … we should not make it dependent on applciation #"*.

**(3) WHAT IT DOES NOW.** A clerk picks a charge out of **this utility's own price
list** and says what it is counted on — per unit, per meter, or per property. **The
number is counted for them from step 4 and cannot be typed.** Tick a service off a flat
and the count moves with it. On the worked build — **six flats, twenty meters, one
property** — three charges came to **$800.00**: the connection fee at **6 × $45.00 =
$270.00**, the meter test at **20 × $25.00 = $500.00**, and the inspection at **1 ×
$30.00 = $30.00**. In the books, **$800.00 owed to us** against **$270.00 of connection
income** and **$530.00 of field-service income**. The two sides agree.

**(4) THE ONE THING WORTH A HUMAN'S TIME, because it is a choice we made.** The drawing
names three charge codes — `CC-CONN`, `CC-METERSET`, `CC-CASVC`. **We do not use them.**
Nothing in this product says which of a utility's charges is *the connection fee*, so
writing those three names into the screen would work for the utility the drawing was
made for and silently price nothing for the next one. **So the clerk picks, exactly as
they already pick a charge on an application's fee line.** ⚠ **If a utility would rather
set a default once in Settings and never pick again, that is a real improvement and it
is NOT built** — it needs a new setting and a new column.

**(5) NO PRICE IS SENT FROM THE SCREEN, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** The browser sends a
code and a count. The price is read from the utility's own list, on the server, at the
moment the bill is made. So a screen left open while somebody edits the price list
cannot bill an old figure.

**(6) NO TOTAL IS SHOWN BEFORE THE BUTTON.** The clerk sees the charge, what it is
counted on, and how many — and no money. Pricing needs an account, and the account does
not exist until the button is pressed. **We would rather show nothing than show a figure
that might not be the one billed.** The drawn `$3,030.00` is an illustration and is
printed nowhere.

**(7) WHAT IS STILL REFUSED, AND NOTHING CHANGED ABOUT IT.** A build with an approved
application still takes that application's quote, with its waivers and its
price-comparison, exactly as it did yesterday. **Deposits are still not charged** — a
deposit is money we hold and owe back, and which rule the deposit ruling replaces is an
open question. And a charge counted **zero** is refused rather than billed at `$0.00`,
because `$0.00` prints on a real customer's bill as *this was free*.

**(8) WHAT IS NOT CHARGED TWICE, and why we are sure.** A build can only be committed
once — a second press is refused by name — so there is no way to raise the same charge
again. The bill it raised is recorded on the build so it can always be found.

**HOW IT WAS PROVED.** Eight new cases against **real PostgreSQL** (the test database we
normally use cannot tell the difference), plus the ten that already covered the
application path: **18 passed**. Every guard was broken first and the real failure read:

## 2026-09-21 · THE APPLICATION FEE STOPS STOPPING AN APPROVAL — lane APP-8

**WHAT WAS PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER AND WHAT THEY SAID.** They said, of the fee:
*"make application fees optional - so that we can approve it"*, and of the waive:
*"waiving is options and can you fix the issue here"*. Then, correcting the case we had
put to them: *"in practical this does not ahppen - it is application fees - customer
will pay it once or clark will wavie it off - $20 or $0 - some utilities will not take
applciation fees also - so your scenario is hypotetical"*. **Those are the three
sentences this work was built from, and nothing beyond them was decided here.**

**(1) AN APPLICATION CAN NOW BE APPROVED WITH THE FEE UNPAID.** We took a real request
for **$20.00** with nothing paid on it, opened it in a browser, and approved it. Before
today the button was dead and the clerk was stuck. **The $20.00 is still on the screen
after the approval** — that was deliberate, and it is the one thing we would ask you to
look at, because the alternative is a debt that quietly disappears the moment somebody
approves. **The money is not cancelled, not hidden and not written off.**

⛔⛔ **SUPERSEDED 2026-09-23 — THE FEE GATES APPROVAL AGAIN (`OQ-CUS-12617` CLOSED, `DEF-CUS-6420`).** PO, verbatim: *"we already told you - either fee is paid or waived - no other condition"*. Approve waits until the application fee is **paid in full or waived**; a part payment holds it on the REMAINDER (quoted $130.00, taken $25.00 → *✗ Fee · $105.00 unpaid*, Approve off). A utility with no fee lines is untouched, and the counter still accepts a short payment and never refuses — the desk half of `BR-CUS-090` stands. The paragraph above is kept as the record of 2026-09-21. **(1) above no longer describes the product.**

**(2) WAIVING WORKS.** Pressing `Waive` used to do nothing at all — the server failed
four times in a row and the screen did not change and did not say a word. It now waives
the line and the line says so. **We also fixed the silence separately**, because a
button that fails quietly is worse than the fault behind it: any failure on that screen
now puts a red sentence in front of the clerk. That half will outlive this particular
bug.

**(3) A UTILITY THAT CHARGES NO APPLICATION FEE — WE ARE HALF WAY AND WE ARE SAYING SO.**
Nothing blocks such a utility: we took a request with no fee on it and approved it
straight through. **But the fee panel is still on the screen**, with a button offering to
take money, and a line on the decision step saying the fee is settled. **We cannot
currently remove those, and the reason is worth a sentence: this product has no setting
anywhere that says "this utility does not charge an application fee."** A request simply
has no fee on it because nobody put one there, which is a different fact. Making it a
real setting is a small build — we already do exactly this for documents, where each
utility ticks which ones it requires and one that ticks nothing requires nothing — and
we have written it down as work rather than doing it quietly. **`DEF-CUS-6102`.**

**(3a) A SENTENCE THAT BECAME UNTRUE THE MOMENT YOU RULED, AND WE ALMOST SHIPPED IT.** The
review step's own line about the fee read *"$105.00 USD of the fee is outstanding. **Approval
waits until it is settled.**"* — which stopped being true the second the fee stopped blocking,
in all eleven languages, on the last screen a clerk reads before pressing. It now reads **"Fee
outstanding: $105.00 USD. Approval is not blocked."** Nothing in this product checks whether a
sentence still matches the rule it describes; we found it by opening the file for another
reason.

**(4) A SENTENCE A CLERK COULD NOT READ, AND ONE THEY COULD NOT ACT ON.** Recording a
second payment showed the words `{{receiptNo}}` on screen instead of the receipt number,
which was four lines further up the same page. Worse, it told the clerk to *"Record
further payment in Payments"* — **and money recorded there cannot move this figure at
all.** It now reads: **"Fee already collected against receipt RCP-26-4471. Waive the
line, or approve anyway."** Both of those are things they can actually do.

**(5) WE COUNTED HOW MANY OTHER SENTENCES HAVE THAT FAULT, RATHER THAN GUESSING.** There
are **610 refusal messages** in the product that quote a value back to a person. **One**
had the fault above; **three more** quote a value nobody supplies, so a clerk would read
a placeholder there too. They are in move-out, meter import and rate changes. Written
down as **`DEF-CUS-6103`**, not fixed here.

## `metering/0059` — A DRAFT BUILD MAY EXIST BEFORE ITS ADDRESS DOES (2026-09-21)

🔒 **HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.** Migration ordering. AI-authored by lane APP-9 under the PO
ruling of 2026-08-09; `DEF-CUS-6109` · `DEF-MET-6117`.

**Files:**
`06-backend/apps/metering/migrations/0059_def_cus_6109_draft_build_before_its_address.py` ·
`apps/metering/connections.py` (the model, `create_connection`, `commit_new_connect` and
`_commit_raised_draft`) · `apps/metering/connection_reads.py` ·
`apps/metering/connection_record.py` · `apps/customers/request_jobs.py` ·
`apps/customers/service_request.py` · `apps/customers/seams.py` ·
`07-frontend/src/features/customers/` (the wizard, the draft, the approve flow).

### WHAT IS BEING PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

**Approving an application into a new connection now creates the build and opens its
wizard. This morning it could not do that on any application in the product.**

Two halves of one path had opposite rules. Where the address had already been matched to a
property we own, the screen **greyed out** *"A new connection"* and said a property already
exists there. Where the address matched nothing, the screen offered it, the clerk pressed
**Approve and raise the build** — and **no build was created at all.** So every application
was refused by one half or the other.

**The reason the code gave for the second half was checked against the database and is
false.** It said creating the property would need an owner the application does not have.
The property table does not require an owner; the owner refusal was itself removed on
27 August; and the code it pointed at deliberately creates a property first and opens the
owner's account afterwards. **The Product Owner is who asked for that check.**

### THE ONE THING A REVIEWER SHOULD LOOK AT

**A build can now exist for a few minutes with no address on it, and one column had to
allow that.** When the application's address matched nothing, the build is created empty
and the property is created when the clerk presses the last button of the wizard — which is
the rule the product already keeps: *nothing is written until the last button*. If it
created the property at approval instead, a clerk who closed the tab would leave a brand
new property on the books with no units, no meters and no plan, **and no screen in this
product can find one of those.**

**The guarantee did not go away; it moved to where it is actually true.** The database now
refuses a build that has been *submitted* and has no address. Before this, it refused every
build with no address — including the few minutes in the middle, which is the case that
made the whole path impossible.

### THE WORKED CASE — WALKED IN A BROWSER, TWENTY-TWO PRESSES

Both shapes, on a private copy of the demo utility, at version `2.322.0`:

* **`SR-26-0004`, 14 Willow Bend — the address matched nothing.** Approving raised build
  **`CON-26-0130`** and opened its wizard with the applicant's name and address already
  filled in. Finishing the wizard created the property **`P-00080`** with **2 units** and
  opened the owner's account **`AC-2026-00052`**. The application now reads *approved* and
  names `CON-26-0130`.
* **`SR-26-0008`, 88 Pine Vista — the address matched property `P-00057`.** The option was
  offered rather than greyed. Approving raised **`CON-26-0131`** against that same property,
  and finishing the wizard created **no second property** — it still has its original 4
  units — and opened account **`AC-2026-00053`**.

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

**Rollback:** the migration is reversible (`migrate metering 0058` drops the check
constraint and restores `NOT NULL`, which every row already satisfies). Reverting the code
returns the approval to recording an outcome and creating nothing, and the wizard to
starting from an empty form. **Nothing already written changes** — the two builds raised in
the walk keep their properties, units, accounts and work orders, because they are ordinary
builds by the time the wizard has finished with them.

**NEW ROW 2026-09-22 · `CR-130-BRC07` WAVE A — A RATE SCHEDULE PRICED AS A PERCENTAGE OF ANOTHER SERVICE NOW SAYS *A PERCENTAGE OF WHAT*.** 🔒 money path, **HUMAN REVIEW COMPLETED 2026-09-22 — THE PRODUCT OWNER SIGNED THE CHARGE-BASIS FIGURE.** Put to them in plain English with the concrete figure and never as an id to look up: a bill carrying a **$100.00** water usage charge and a **$25.00** water standing charge, with sewer set to **80% of water on the CHARGE basis**, bills sewer **$80.00** — eighty per cent of the usage charge only, NOT of the $125.00. Three options were shown: (a) sign it as shown, (b) include the standing charge and bill $100.00, (c) do not sign yet. **PO ruling, verbatim: `"a is correct"`.** ⚠ **A SIGNATURE COVERS ONLY WHAT WAS SHOWN** (PO ruling 2026-08-11): this signs the **$80.00 charge-basis figure and its exclusion of the standing charge**, and NOTHING ELSE on this card. The tiered usage figure (**$150.00**) and the flat usage figure (**$40.00**) are engine-proved and REMAIN UNSIGNED — they are named on the agenda rather than carried in on this signature.

**Files** (repo-relative in full, because `G7` matches a ledger row to a guarded file by its exact repo-relative path and an abbreviated one silently does not match): `06-backend/apps/rating/pricing/percent_basis.py` (new) · `06-backend/apps/rating/pricing/models/percent_of_service.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/engine.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/pricing/contracts.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/pricing/stages/normalize.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/selectors.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/services.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/models.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/migrations/0043_cr130_percent_basis.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/api.py` · `06-backend/apps/rating/sample_data.py` · `06-backend/core/sample_fixture.py` · `06-backend/apps/billing/rating_seam.py` · `06-backend/apps/billing/gather.py`.
**Tests:** `06-backend/tests/test_cr130_percent_basis.py` (new) · `tests/test_us_rat_012_percent_of_service.py` · `tests/test_cr081_sewer_volume_basis.py` · `tests/test_cr043_line_wording.py` · `tests/golden/`.

### WHAT WILL BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURES

Read these four sentences aloud. They carry every number this change decides.

**1 · The one they asked for, and it is new.**
*"If a utility bills sewer as a share of the water CHARGE, and the water charge on the bill is
$100.00 and the share is 80%, the sewer line is **$80.00**. The $25.00 water standing charge on the
same bill is not counted — 80% of $125.00 would have been $100.00."*

**2 · The other way round, which the product already did, now with a ladder behind it.**
*"If the utility bills sewer as a share of the water USED, and the meter read 100 gallons and the
share is 80%, the sewer line is for **80 gallons**, priced at the utility's own sewer rate. At 50
cents a gallon that is **$40.00**. If the utility prices sewer in blocks instead — the first 30
gallons at $1.00, the next 30 at $2.00, everything above at $3.00 — those same 80 gallons bill
**$150.00** across three lines, and each line says it came from 80% of the water."*

**3 · Nothing already billed changes, and here is what was at stake.**
*"The reference sewer bill still charges **$36.00** — 90% of 8 thousand gallons at $5.00. The other
three signed sewer figures are still $54.00, $27.00 and $27.00. If that same schedule had been read
as a share of the water CHARGE instead, it would have billed **$35.55** — forty-five cents a month,
on a bill that adds up correctly either way. That is why every rate schedule already in the system
has been written down as 'share of the water used', by name, one by one, rather than left to take a
default."*

**4 · What the product refuses to guess.**
*"Where a schedule does not say which of the two it is, the bill is not produced for that account —
it goes to the run's exception list instead. The same happens if the water figure it needs is not on
the bill at all. A sewer charge of $0.00 would be a bill that quietly forgives it."*

### WHAT IS **NOT** COVERED BY THIS SIGN-OFF AND MUST RETURN TO THE AGENDA

* **The $80.00 is the Product Owner's own worked figure and is NOT a ❄️ B5-signed golden test.** It
  is asserted against the real engine here; it has no entry in the frozen corpus. If the charge
  basis is to carry a frozen figure, that is a separate HUMAN-GUIDE §6 signing.
* **WHICH dollars — `OQ-232`, OPEN.** A percentage of another service's charge may be taken on the
  PRINTED line amounts or on the unrounded figures behind them. The printed reading ships, which is
  the disposition the register already records with its reasoning. **$100.00 at 80% is $80.00 either
  way**, so the figure above does not decide it; the readings part company one cent at a time.
* **Taxability was raised by the PO and is NOT built here** — the reasoning is in the decision log
  of 2026-09-22 and in `CR-130-BRC07` §5, and it reopens ❄️ B4.2 if they still want it.
* **Three refusals have no customer sentence yet.** `rating.percent.basis_is_itself`,
  `rating.percent.basis_meters_nothing` and `rating.percent.rate_not_on_charge_basis` are raised by
  the backend and land in the eleven catalogues with wave B. Until then they reach a clerk as
  silence, and `G32` counts three more unresolved keys.

## `metering/0060` — A PREMISES NAMES ITS MASTER ACCOUNT (2026-09-22) · `BR-MET-1181` · HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**The file:** `06-backend/apps/metering/migrations/0060_br_met_1181_premises_master_account.py`
(🔒 migration ordering). Lane C1 of `CR-130-BRC07` part three. Closes `DEF-MET-6139`.

### WHAT IT DOES, IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURES

**One new column on a property: the account the owner is billed through.** Nothing else is
added, nothing is removed, and no existing row is changed by the migration itself.

**Why it was needed, measured on a copy of the beta before anything was changed.** A clerk
fills in the Add Premises form completely — the owner's name `Harriet Vane`, *person*, a
Social Security number, and the account type *residential* — presses Create, and the
property is saved. **No account is opened.** Master accounts stayed at **1 → 1**; the
address got none; the only explanation was a line nobody's screen prints. A company with a
Tax ID behaved exactly the same way.

**On that whole database, 0 of 79 properties had an owner account.** That matters because
the charge for an empty unit — **$30.50 a month** — and a move-out shortfall are both
billed to the owner, and there was nobody at any address to bill them to.

**The cause was one line of code, not a missing decision.** The code asked for an *owner
record* first and gave up before it ever looked at the name and the identifier the clerk
had just typed — and **no screen in the product can create an owner record**, so that
requirement could never be met. The Product Owner ruled on 2026-09-22 that a property
should point at the account directly: *"why you are point is at owner id - why not directly
at master accoutn Id - it will solev the problem"*.

**After the change, the same form on the same data:** the account opens, numbered from the
utility's own Settings series, and the property points at it. Nothing new is asked of the
clerk.

### THREE PLACES COULD ANSWER *WHO OWNS THIS ADDRESS*, SO THE ORDER IS WRITTEN DOWN

1. **the property's own answer** — wins whenever it has been given;
2. **the older owner-record link** — used for properties saved before this change, because
   **nothing is back-filled**;
3. **an account that merely names the property** — *never* used to answer this. Ordinary
   tenants' accounts name a property too, so using it would make a tenant the owner.

Every screen now says **which of the two answers it is showing**, for the same reason a map
pin says whether it is the flat's own location or the building's.

### WHAT IS PRESENTED FOR REVIEW, AND WHAT IS NOT

**PRESENTED:** the column and its nullability · the three-way order above · that the form
opens the account and that **nothing new is collected** · that an account which already
exists can be attached to a property, on the add form and on the edit form both · that a
non-owner account offered there is refused and says so · that nothing is back-filled.

**NOT PRESENTED, and it stays flagged:** whether a landlord's SECOND address should find
the account their first address already has, instead of asking for the identifier again.
That is `OQ-MET-12573`, open, and it is a real cost — eleven extra entries for a landlord
with twelve buildings. It is a question for the Product Owner because the obvious answer,
matching a party by the name somebody typed, is forbidden by a signed rule (`BR-MET-151`).

### WALKED, AND WHAT COULD NOT BE WALKED

Measured on real PostgreSQL 16 against a private clone of the beta, by
`10-scripts/br_met_1181_premises_master_account_readback.py`, which **writes nothing** — every
section runs inside a transaction that is aborted, and the last lines re-read the counts to
show the database is as it was found.

⚠ **The suite runs on in-memory SQLite and CANNOT prove the savepoint** (CLAUDE.md hard-won
law 14): SQLite has no aborted-transaction state, so the version without it passes every
test and destroys a real save. That is proved by the script above and by nothing in
`06-backend/tests/`.

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

**Rollback:** the migration is reversible (`migrate metering 0059` drops the column). No row
is back-filled, so dropping it loses only links written after this change — and every one of
those also wrote the older owner-record link where an owner record existed. Reverting the
code returns the form to saving the address and opening no account.

## `CR-131-BRC07` steps 2–7 — a route reports what it collected, and stores six buildings instead of 726 units (2026-09-22, lane R2, version 2.326.0)

is AI-authored under the PO ruling of 2026-08-09 and is **HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING**.

### WHAT WAS SHOWN TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, AND WHAT THEY RULED

Three things were put to them in plain sentences with a figure each, and they answered all three.
This is what was shown, verbatim on both sides:

**1 · "When a clerk opens RT-009 and asks what was read on it, should the answer be the 100
readings collected on that route, or the readings on the meters that are on it today — which is
0 the moment its eight properties move to another route?"**
**PO: "100".** Their reasoning, verbatim: *"you will build it in dynamic way not static. when you
query or search for 100 meter and its reading they are property of meters … if you hard code it -
you will not find it, if you use logical code you will find it"*.

**2 · "Must a reader's printed sheet be reproducible exactly as it was issued?"**
**PO: "not required, you dont have to reproduce it . option a".**

**3 · "Walk order — one number per property, or one per unit?"**
**PO: "a is okay"** — per property.

### THE COST THAT WAS STATED TO THEM BEFORE THEY ANSWERED, AND IS NOW BUILT

*On a utility whose oldest readings were taken before we started recording which route collected
them, those readings have no route: they will not appear when you filter by route, and their Route
column will be blank.* **On the demo data that is 0 of 516 readings.** It is in the release note
for 2.326.0 in those words, in `BR-MET-081`, and it is asserted by a test so it cannot be quietly
reversed.

### WHAT IS NOT YET REVIEWED AND STAYS FLAGGED

**The migration itself.** It creates one table, gives it row-level security, and copies each
route's list of properties across from the old per-unit list. On the seeded database it turned
**155 unit rows into 88 property rows**. It has not been read to the Product Owner and does not
need to be — it moves no figure they have signed — but it is a 🔒 migration-ordering file and the
rule is that it carries this row until a human has looked at it.

⚠ **ONE THING IN IT IS WORTH A HUMAN'S EYE AND IS NAMED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT IN THE FILE.** The
first draft of that copy step **wrote nothing and reported success.** A migration does not run with
row-level security switched off, so without naming each utility explicitly it could see no rows at
all — and the table would have been empty, every route would have lost its properties the moment
the new code read it, and no test anywhere would have gone red. It was caught only because the step
prints the two counts it wrote. It now names each utility explicitly and prints how many it named.

**Not presented, and it stays flagged:** whether a reading that has no recorded route should be
offered under a *"no route"* filter option rather than simply being absent. Nobody asked for one;
it is not a question this lane invented an answer to.
