join on a private database, on a property carrying **728 units and 725 meters** — because the
change request says in as many words that a fix proved on six units proves nothing here.

Step 3 of the route wizard drew **"1 Premises · 728 Units · 725 of 725 Meters"** where it used to
draw *"No meters yet"*. The review step stated the move before the press — *"1 premises move from
TWRB977B · No bills change. Only the reader."* The save landed and the route reported 725 meters on
1 property. Then a unit was added with nobody re-opening the wizard, and the route went from **728
to 729** members on its own, which is the whole of what the Product Owner asked for.

**Rollback:** revert the commits. The migration is reversible (`migrate metering 0060` drops the
table), and it is worth saying plainly that the reverse only removes rows this change wrote — the
old per-unit rows were never deleted, so nothing is lost by going back.

### WHAT WOULD BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH THE FIGURES

**Nothing here is an ID to go and look up.** These are the four statements a reviewer is being
asked to accept, each with a concrete number.

**1 · What one receipt looks like.** Rosa Delgado pays **$142.18** online by ACH on 15 September
against bill `INV-2609-00412`. New World receives one receipt: the payer's name, the date, our
receipt number `PMT-2609-0187` in the description, **one transaction of $142.18**, and **one GL
distribution — account `1200`, $142.18, marked Credit**. The distribution equals the transaction,
so it balances. The tender goes as **Other, with the word `ACH`**, because their five payment types
have no ACH.

**2 · An unbalanced receipt is sent, flagged, and never plugged.** If a $100.00 payment is split
across three services at 33.3333 each, their two-decimal field takes 33.33 three times — **99.99,
one cent short.** It is **sent**. Nothing is added to make it add up. Our side records that one
receipt was short and by exactly **$0.01**, on the response and on the run row a manager reads.
**Measured on real payments, this has never happened: 7 receipts, 7 balanced, largest difference
$0.00** — the spread included thirds of a dollar, a one-penny bill and three overpayments.

**3 · We never send a card number, and there is no switch to turn it on.** Their format has four
card fields. A card payment goes as **Charge with no card number**. There is no setting and no
mapping entry for them, and a machine check (`G130`) fails the build if one of those four names
ever appears as code in 152 files it reads.

⚠ **STATEMENT 3 AMENDED 2026-10-21 (`DEF-INT-10304`) — read this version, not the one above, if
this row is put to the PO.** New World's own template lists the four card fields, and the PO chose
*"Option A — Always write all four as `""`"*. **So the four names now appear on every payment node,
always empty; a card number still never does.** `G130` now fails any code that could give one of
them a value, and every file is checked before it is sent or served — a file with a card value in
it is refused. The same day the whole file moved to New World's template shape (every field an
attribute, on a `<ROOT>` document, dates as 10/20/2026, `VoidedFlag` as `0`); the money in it did
not change.

**4 · One thing depends on New World and could stop this working.** Three of our tenders — ACH,
money order and lockbox — go as *Other* carrying a word. **Their system checks that word against
its own list**, and until their team adds `ACH`, `Money order` and `Lockbox`, receipts carrying one
are rejected at their end. A different spelling from them is **a clerk's setting, not a new
release**. In practice only ACH matters today, because this feed carries online payments only.

### WHAT WAS PROVED RED BEFORE IT WAS TRUSTED GREEN (hard-won law 7)

* **The balance rule.** A refusal was inserted into `emit()` — reinstating the rule the PO reversed
  — and **all 17 cases stayed GREEN**, because the test helper was a COPY of the emitter. Filed as
  `DEF-INT-6162`, fixed by splitting `render()` out, and re-proved: the same refusal now fails
  3 cases naming `ValueError: refusing an unbalanced receipt`.
* **The plug.** Making `Transaction.distributed` return the transaction amount when it disagrees
  fails 2 cases.
* **The card fields.** Adding `ReceiptPaymentCreditCardNumber` to the payment node fails
  `test_no_card_field_reaches_any_surface` and `G130`.
* **`G130` through `run_gates`, not `__main__`** (law 7's second half, `DEF-GOV-3733`):
  `_assert_registry_sane()` accepts it and `module.run()` — the exact call `main()` makes — returns
  `FAIL: 1 New World card field reference(s) in 152 file(s)`. Restored, it returns `PASS`. Its
  empty-scope guard was also proved: a wrong root returns `FAIL: read 0 files`, not a clean pass.

### REDS THAT WERE NOT THIS LANE'S, DATED RATHER THAN ASSERTED

`tests/test_be_default_authentication.py` fails 2 of 28 cases at the pinned tip. **58 unclassified
routes, every one of them `/portal/`, zero non-portal** — the breach the file's own comment records
as red since **2026-09-04** (`DEF-INT-4256`, *"the portal half is NOT fixed here"*), grown from 54.
**It is not a red this lane caused, and the new address is not among them.** What IS new is that it
makes the `public == PUBLIC_ROUTES` assertion unreachable — filed as `DEF-INT-6161`.

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

## `2026-09-22` · `customers/0064` — a move-in job carries its `MVI-` number (`BR-CUS-1090`, `CR-133-BRC07`)

**Files flagged `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING`:**
`06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0064_br_cus_1090_move_in_job_number.py` — migration
ordering is on CLAUDE.md's sensitive-paths list. The table's RLS policy is NOT touched: `0053`
created it with `ENABLE` + `FORCE` and adding a column does not disturb a policy, which was
**verified on the live cluster** rather than assumed (`relrowsecurity` and `relforcerowsecurity`
both true, policy `move_in_jobs_tenant_isolation`).

### WHAT WAS PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH A FIGURE

The PO pressed **Approve** on a service request, chose *"A move-in"*, and asked, verbatim:

> *"you would ahve created a new move In request ID and add all details from servcies request to
> it and save it as a draft - do you ahve move in request ID in numbering?"*

and then, over a table whose row 16 reads *A move-in gets `MVI-…` at creation and its own page*:

> *"fix all these issues"*

**The figure shown, measured on the seeded `brazosbend` utility before anything was changed:** the
Move-ins tab held **three rows, and the approved one was the only one with no reference**. The
other two printed `MVI-26-0001` and `MVI-26-0002`; the approved move-in's `Reference` cell fell
back to `SR-26-0006` and linked back to the application. After the change all three carry a number
from one series and all three open a page of their own.

**What the PO was told it costs, in their own terms:** a move-in that is approved and then rolled
back **keeps its number**, so the `MVI-` series will have gaps. That is the same bargain they
already struck for service requests on 2026-08-24 (`BR-CUS-093` — *"the clerk can quote the number
to the customer on the phone while the form is still half-filled"*), and a gap is not a missing
move-in.

### WHAT WAS **NOT** PUT TO THEM, AND SO IS NOT COVERED BY THIS SIGNATURE

A signature covers only what was shown. **Three judgments were made by this lane and are recorded
rather than signed** — the decision log of 2026-09-22 carries each with its reasoning:

1. **`BR-CUS-152` does not narrow.** A draft is a different TABLE, not a looser rule: the number
   travels from `move_in_jobs` to `move_records` and the ROW never does. Nothing updates a move
   record and nothing new is written to that table.
2. **The details are CARRIED, not COPIED.** The applicant, the unit, the date and the services are
   read through the request at the moment anybody asks. The PO's words were *"add all details from
   servcies request to it"*; what they see is identical either way, and a copy would let the queue
   and the application disagree the day somebody edits one.
3. **`B18 §5.5.2`'s footnote is NOT superseded a second time.** `BR-CUS-1077` superseded it for the
   move-in on 2026-09-16 and said so. Recording it twice would leave two rulings on one sentence.

### RED-FIRST PROOF, IN THE HARNESS THAT RUNS IT (law 7, and its second half)

* **`pytest`**, not a script calling the functions: the allocation in `raise_for_request` was put
  back to `None` — the product exactly as it stood — and **six of the seven new cases failed**,

  forced after the column was added; a differently-cased duplicate number refused by
  `uq_move_in_jobs_tenant_move_no_ci`; two UNNUMBERED jobs coexisting (the partial predicate);
  and the connection still usable after both refusals, which is what the savepoints are for.

## `CR-135-BRC07` — payments phase 0: the source column's check, and the till table (2026-09-22, `2.329.0`)

**HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.** Four 🔒 files, all AI-authored under the PO ruling of
2026-08-09 (*"AI will do it; we will review it later as human"*). Two sensitive
paths are touched: **migration ordering** and **RLS policies**, plus constraints
on the money table.

| File | Why it is 🔒 |
|---|---|
| `06-backend/apps/payments/migrations/0030_cr135_p0_1_p0_2_origin_check.py` | migration ordering · it UPDATEs `payments` and lifts the immutability trigger to do it |
| `06-backend/apps/payments/migrations/0031_cr135_p0_3_p0_4_counter_sessions.py` | migration ordering · a new money column |
| `06-backend/apps/payments/migrations/0032_rls_cr135_p0_5_counter_sessions.py` | RLS policy |
| `06-backend/apps/payments/counter_session_models.py` | the money column's declaration and the table's constraints |

### WHAT WOULD BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH ITS FIGURES

**1 · Every payment can now only say one of three things about where it came
from, and anything else is refused by the database.** Today a payment says
`entry`, `webhook` or `import`. From this change, if any part of the product
ever tried to write a fourth word — say `lockbox` — the database refuses the
row outright instead of storing it. Nothing a clerk does changes.

**2 · A payment is still allowed to say nothing at all, and that is
deliberate.** The blueprint asked us to forbid blanks. We found a place in the
product that creates payment rows without saying where they came from — a demo
data command — so forbidding blanks would have broken it the moment anyone ran
it. A blank now means *nobody told us*, which is honest; inventing a default
would have been a guess dressed as a fact. Instead a test fails at build time
if a new place starts creating payments without saying where the money came
from.

**3 · We checked the blueprint's rule for filling in older payments against
real data, and it was wrong.** The document said *if a payment has a webhook
key it came in online*. We counted: **74 payments in the demo utility, all 74
have a webhook key, and all 74 were keyed by a person at a desk.** The rule
would have relabelled every one of them as an online payment. The column it
reads is named for webhooks but actually holds a key for all three sources.
**We did not apply it.** What we did apply is the document's second rule, which
is better than ours: if a payment came in on an import file we now say so from
the file record rather than from a text prefix. On today's data that changes
**0 of 74** rows; on the live deployment it may change some, and the migration
prints the count either way.

**4 · A payment we GUESSED about still says it was a guess.** That was the
ruling of 2026-09-22 and it survives this change. We have added one more rule:
a payment cannot claim to have guessed and then not say what it guessed.

**5 · A counter till can now be recorded, and one person can only have one
open at a time.** The till holds who it belongs to, which counter it is at, how
much cash it started with, when it opened, when it closed, **who closed it**,
and whether that was a normal count or a supervisor forcing it shut. **The
database itself refuses a second open till for the same person** — not a check
in the software that a second cash register could slip past. It does allow that
person any number of CLOSED tills, which is what lets them work tomorrow.

**6 · One number in the drawing was not followed, and here is the figure.** The
drawing asks for the opening float to be stored to **six** decimal places. The
signed money rule — re-confirmed by the Product Owner on 2026-08-22 — says a
new money column stores **four**. We built four. In practice a float is typed
as `$200.00`, so nothing visible changes; what changes is that this column
obeys the same rule as every other new money column in the product. **This was
already put to the Product Owner and answered before the work started, so it is
recorded here rather than asked again.**

**7 · A till sealed with no record of HOW is refused.** If somebody closes a
till, the record must say who closed it and whether they counted it. The
database will not accept a half-answer, because a forced close that looks like
a normal one is exactly what the ruling of 2026-09-22 was protecting against.

**8 · A till at one utility is invisible to every other utility**, proved on a
real PostgreSQL database rather than on the test database, which cannot show it.

### WHAT WAS **NOT** PUT TO THEM, AND SO IS NOT COVERED BY THIS SIGNATURE

A signature covers only what was shown. **Four judgments are recorded rather
than signed** — the decision log of 2026-09-22 carries each with its reasoning:

1. **The three stored words did not change.** The Product Owner offered *"rename
   or map"*; this is the map. The deciding reason is that `entry` is written for
   both legs of an internal transfer and for a bounce, and calling those
   *counter* would make the database say they were taken at a service desk.
2. **`counter · digital · post` are LABELS and are not built here.** They belong
   in the wording catalogue with every other label, which is the front end's
   file and the other lane's this phase.
3. **There is no freeze trigger on the till table.** A counter session is
   designed to be updated once (it opens, then it closes) and phase 2 adds a
   third write. A freeze written now would be guessing which columns phase 2
   may move. It is `BR-PAY-1160`'s open half.
4. **`counter_sessions` names `tenancy.ServiceCentre` with a real foreign key.**
   That is a payments → tenancy edge and is NOT in B2 §2's reviewed interface
   set. The precedent is `counter_receipts`, which already carries two such
   edges; it is named here rather than assumed.

### RED-FIRST PROOF, IN THE HARNESS THAT RUNS IT (law 7, and its second half)

All on a PostgreSQL 16 clone (`sbh_clone_p0db`), role `smartbillhub` reporting
`rolsuper=f rolbypassrls=f`, because SQLite has no row-level security and no
triggers:

* **`P0.16` — forwards, backwards, forwards again.** `payments/0030`–`0032`
  applied, reversed to `0029`, re-applied. `trg_payment_immutable` read `'O'`
  at every stage and the 74 payment rows were unchanged throughout.
* **Every new constraint shown RED on the case it was written for AND GREEN on
  the neighbouring lawful one**, because a check that refuses everything is not
  a check: a second OPEN till refused by `uq_counter_sessions_open_owner`; **two
  CLOSED tills for the same person accepted** (`P0.15`'s easy-to-miss half); a
  half-closed till refused; `auto` refused; a negative float refused;
  `'lockbox'` refused; a lawful `import` accepted; `NULL` + *not derived*
  accepted; `NULL` + *derived* refused.
* **The claim `payments/0030`'s docstring makes about RLS and DDL was measured,
  not asserted** (law 1). With `app.tenant_id` unset,
  `SELECT count(*) FROM payments` answers **0** and
  `ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT tmp CHECK (origin = 'nonsense')` still
  fails: `ERROR: check constraint "tmp" of relation "payments" is violated by
  some row`. So a wrong tenant scope can silence the UPDATE and cannot silence
  the constraint. ⚠ PostgreSQL says *"some row"* and never a count, so the
  constraint is a reliable refusal and a useless diagnosis — noted in the file.

### REDS THAT WERE NOT THIS LANE'S

Recorded in the lane's report, dated with `git log -S` rather than asserted.

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

**Rollback:** `migrate payments 0029` drops `counter_sessions` entirely, drops
its RLS policy with it, and removes the two CHECK constraints from `payments`.
The 74 payment rows keep the origin and the *is a guess* marker they already
had — the reverse of a re-derivation is not a restoration, because no record of
the previous guess was ever kept, and the migration says so where it is written.

### WHAT WOULD BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH THE FIGURES

> On Tuesday 22 September, at an office with two counters, Dana takes **$1,240**
> of cheques and Sam takes **$880**. Until today the product made **one** deposit
> for that day — $2,120 of cheques in a single record that neither of them could
> be held to. From this build it makes **two**, one for each person's till, and
> the day's cheques still add up to **$2,120** exactly.
>
> Dana's own shift, if she takes **$600 in cash and $640 in cheques**, is **one
> till and two deposits** — $600 and $640 — because the bank takes cash and
> cheques on separate slips and they clear on different days.
>
> Money that nobody handed over a counter — an ACH file, a card settlement, a
> wire, a lockbox file — is banked under a till the system opens for that day.
> It has no person's name on it anywhere, and it never appears on the screen
> that asks which drawers have not been counted. Without it, a utility taking
> **$14,280 of ACH** on a Tuesday could not have banked it at all.
>
> The deposit's number now comes from Settings → Numbering like every other
> number in the product: **`DEP-260922-0001`**. The year and the date are still
> in it. What has gone is the tender, because two people banking cheques on the
> same day both produced `DEP-260922-CHK` and the second one was refused.
>
> **Nothing was written to a deposit already banked.** Those keep their old
> numbers — `DEP-260808-CHK` — and are recognised by the fact that they have no
> till against them.

### THREE THINGS THIS LANE DECIDED AND THE PO HAS NOT SEEN

A signature covers only what was shown. These stay flagged and return to the
agenda:

1. **The deposit number pads to four digits and does NOT restart each year.**
   The PO's own example was `DEP-260922-0001`, so four digits follows them. The
   yearly restart proposed in the closing row was NOT taken: it would refuse a
   deposit cut for a day in a previous year, by name, which is a real thing a
   utility does in January.
2. **Utilities already running keep the two-digit shape they have configured.**
   They are not rewritten. They bank correctly either way; the counter grows a
   digit rather than stopping.
3. **The till table gained three things it did not have** — a session may now
   have no owner and no counter (that is what makes a system till possible), a
   day column, and a third way of being closed, `system`. That table has never
   held a row, so nothing was at risk. A real person's till still cannot be
   written without a named owner, and a till that somebody sealed still records
   who.

### WHAT WAS PROVED, AND ON WHAT

`10-scripts/proof-db.sh clone p06rekey` — PostgreSQL 16, role `smartbillhub`
(not superuser, does not bypass RLS), with `app.tenant_id` SET before every
count. SQLite has no partial index, no trigger and no RLS, so none of this can
be shown on the default suite (hard-won law 14).

* **The ledger half was RUN, not read** —
  `10-scripts/p06_ledger_two_deposits_readback.py`, unchanged from the lane that
  wrote it: two deposits for 22 September, Dana **1,240.00** debits =
  **1,240.00** credits, Sam **880.00** = **880.00**, the day **2,120.00**, zero
  rows left behind. Posted through `apps.ledger.posting.post()` and nothing
  else — a hand-written journal INSERT is refused by
  `ledger_sole_writer_guard()`, which is how the first draft of that proof was
  caught.
* **Every new guard shown RED on the case it was written for and GREEN on the
  lawful neighbour** — see the lane's report and
  `06-backend/tests/test_cr135_p06_rekey_pg.py`.

### REDS THAT WERE NOT THIS LANE'S

## `CR-136-BRC07` phase 2 — THE COUNTER'S FIVE DOORS AND THE DRAWER DIFFERENCE (🔒 money path, 2026-09-23, lane P2-API, version `2.335.0`)

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

| `06-backend/apps/payments/counters.py` | A till's whole life: open · close · force close · declare · the reads · the `P2.23` guard. 🔒 money rounding (`_q` at four decimals) and the drawer arithmetic | AI, 2026-09-23, under the PO ruling of 2026-08-09 | `tests/test_cr136_p2_counters.py` · `10-scripts/cr136_p2_counters_postgres_proof.py` parts A–D on PostgreSQL 16 | **PENDING** | HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING |
| `06-backend/apps/payments/ledger_seam.py::post_counter_difference` | The balanced pair a counted drawer writes. 🔒 ledger posting | AI, 2026-09-23 | `tests/test_cr136_p2_counters.py::test_p2_22_*` · proof part D | **PENDING** | HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING |
| `06-backend/apps/payments/counters_api.py` | The five routes. Thin — no ORM, no money, no clock | AI, 2026-09-23 | route resolution through the real root URLconf | **PENDING** | HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING |
| `06-backend/apps/payments/api.py::account_payments` | `P2.23`'s call site — one guard, one implementation | AI, 2026-09-23 | `tests/test_cr136_p2_counters.py::test_p2_23_*` | **PENDING** | HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING |

### What would be put to the Product Owner — in plain English, with the figures

**1 · A short drawer now reaches the books, and here is the entry.** Dana's till
opens with **$200.00** in the drawer and takes **$310.00** in cash, so the
system expects **$510.00**. She counts **$498.00** — **$12.00 short**, and she
writes *"cheque stuck to the bag"*. The product then writes two lines in the
books: **$12.00 charged to `6850 Cash over and short`** and **$12.00 taken out
of `1010 Undeposited funds`**. If the drawer had been **$12.00 over**, the same
two lines swap sides. **A drawer that balances writes nothing at all.**

**Why `1010 Undeposited funds` and not `1000 Cash`:** when Dana took the
$310.00, the product already put it in *undeposited funds* — money we are
holding and the bank has not yet confirmed. The bank will only ever receive
what was physically in the drawer, so the missing $12.00 has to come OUT of
undeposited funds. Put it against `1000 Cash` instead and the bank
reconciliation would carry a $12.00 leftover for ever that no statement will
ever match.

**2 · It posts when the money is COUNTED, which is two different days.** On a
normal close that is the moment the clerk counts. On a till a supervisor sealed
without a count, it is the moment somebody declares the count later — which is
exactly what *"the day it is declared"* asked for.

**3 · A till opens with ONE deposit batch: its cash one.** You ruled on
2026-09-21 that starting a counter starts a batch with it, and on 2026-09-22
that a batch is one till and one tender. A till at the moment it opens has not
taken anything, so we cannot know which tenders it will take. **We open the
cash one**, because the opening float is cash and it is in the drawer before
the first payment; the cheque and money-order batches are opened by the first
cheque and the first money order. **The reason we did not open all three:** a
deposit batch can never be deleted, so a till that took no cheques would leave
an empty one on the Finance → Deposits screen for ever — about **1,500 a year**
at a three-window office. This is written up as `OQ-PAY-12599` for you to
confirm.

**4 · The float is counted INSIDE the cash line, not taken off first.** A
**$200.00** float plus **$310.00** taken is a **$510.00** cash expectation, and
that is what the clerk types against. The alternative asks them to subtract
$200.00 in their head at half past five, which is the cheapest place in the
whole shift to create a difference that is not real.

**5 · Cash, cheques and money orders are refused until a till is open** — *"Start
your counter first."* — and card, ACH, wire and lockbox are untouched. ⚠ **One
thing we could not decide for you:** a clerk keying a cheque that came in the
morning post never sits at a till, so this rule would refuse them too. Nothing
was built to get around it. It is `OQ-PAY-12601`.

**6 · A forced close's reason is not kept for ever, and the screen says it is.**
The screen calls it *"the only record of the reason"*, and today it is written
only to the audit trail, which is deleted on a retention schedule. The count's
own note has taken the column the reason would have used. `OQ-PAY-12600`
proposes a third column.

**Rollback:** there is no migration in this work. Removing the five routes
(one `include` line in `apps/payments/api.py`) takes the whole counter surface
out and leaves `counter_sessions` exactly as phase 0 built it — no rows to
lose, because nothing else writes the table. The `P2.23` refusal is one call in
`account_payments` and comes out with it.

## `payments/0036` + `payments/0037` — a payment can be cancelled, and then never touched again (`CR-137-BRC07` `P3.5`–`P3.8`)

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/payments/migrations/0036_cr137_p3_5_cancelled_status.py` ·
`06-backend/apps/payments/migrations/0037_cr137_p3_7_corrects_payment.py` ·
`06-backend/apps/payments/models.py`

**Why it needs a human:** migration ordering is a CLAUDE.md 🔒 sensitive path,
and both files sit on the financial-immutability path hard rule 4 governs.

### WHAT WOULD BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

> A clerk takes **$169.52** in cash at 09:02 and sees at 09:04 that it went on
> the wrong account. Until today the product had no way to say so: a payment
> could be reversed, which is what you do when money really arrived and has to
> go back, but there was nothing for *this was never a real payment*.
>
> **There is now.** The payment can be cancelled while it is still settling.
>
> **And from the moment it is cancelled, nobody can change it — ever.** Not the
> amount, not the account, not the date, and it cannot be un-cancelled or
> deleted. That is deliberate: a cancelled payment stays on the record saying
> what was taken and that it was undone, which is what makes the cancel honest
> rather than a way to make a mistake disappear.
>
> **Cancel is only possible before the money settles.** Once the bank has the
> money, the way to put it right is a reversal, which moves the account balance
> and reaches the books. Cancel does neither, because there was nothing to move.
>
> **A second, smaller thing:** a payment that corrects an earlier one now says
> *which* one, in the record rather than in a clerk's memory.

### WHAT WAS PROVED, AND ON WHAT

On a **live PostgreSQL 16** clone, not on the test suite — the suite runs on
SQLite, which has neither the rule nor the trigger that enforces it, so it
would have gone green either way (CLAUDE.md hard-won law 14).

* **RED FIRST.** Before the change, the word `cancelled` was **refused by name**
  by `ck_payments_status`. That is the red, taken first.
* **THE MOVE IS PERMITTED.** After it, `processing → cancelled` succeeds — and
  narrowly: an attempt to change the status **and** the amount in the same
  statement is refused.
* **THE ROW IS FROZEN.** On the cancelled row, the amount is refused, the
  un-cancel is refused, the account is refused, and DELETE is refused.
* **TWO CONTROLS**, without which none of the above means anything: an amount
  change on a *cleared* payment must still be refused (the trigger is installed
  and reachable), and the ordinary `processing → cleared` transition must still
  succeed (the probe is capable of making an UPDATE succeed at all).
* **NOTHING WAS WIDENED.** The three columns the PO opened on 2026-09-02 —
  cheque number, memo, tender — still work; a fourth column is still refused;
  and the two allow lists were read back **out of the deployed function body**
  and are exactly what `payments/0014` set.
* The migrations were run **forwards, backwards and forwards again**, with the
  constraint, the column and the index read back from the database catalog at
  each step rather than inferred.

`10-scripts/p3_cancel_state_and_trigger_readback.py` is the script; it writes
nothing and prints every statement it attempted beside the verdict.

### WHAT THE PO HAS NOT BEEN SHOWN, AND SHOULD BE

1. **That `cancelled` is exactly as frozen as `failed` and `reversed` — no more
   and no less.** A cancelled payment can still be given its deposit batch and
   its journal-entry link once each, and its cheque number, memo and tender can
   still be corrected, because those doors are open on **every** frozen status.
   Neither is reachable in practice today. Narrowing them for one status would
   mean editing the immutability trigger, which would mean moving the allow
   list the PO ruled on — so it was not done.
2. **That the freeze side was a DEFAULT, not a choice.** Two mechanisms put
   `cancelled` there without anyone editing a line: a derived tuple in Python,
   and a literal `<> 'processing'` in the trigger. It is the right answer and

money rounding are all on `CLAUDE.md`'s 🔒 list, and all four are in this set.

### WHAT WOULD BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

> A card processor takes money from your customers all day and then pays you
> **one lump into the bank**, keeping a fee. Until today nothing in the system
> could say which payments were inside that lump. Now it can: last night's
> payout is a record of its own, and you can open it and see the forty-six
> payments in it.
>
> **The important part is what we did NOT change.** A customer who paid
> **$100.00** by card still shows as having paid **$100.00**. The processor's
> **$2.90** is recorded as a cost to you, not as the customer paying less.
> That was already true and it stays true.
>
> **What is new is that we now believe the processor rather than guessing.**
> Today, when the bank credit comes in short, the system works out the fee by
> subtracting: we took **$5,120.40**, the bank paid **$4,972.90**, so the fee
> "must be" **$147.50**. That guess always adds up — which is the problem. If
> the processor actually kept **$137.50** and a customer reversed a **$10.00**
> card payment, the guess hides that $10.00 inside the fee, the customer's bill
> still looks paid, and nobody ever looks again.
>
> **Now the payout tells us the fee is $137.50, and the system refuses to close
> the day until somebody explains the missing $10.00.** That is one extra piece
> of work a month and it is the only way that $10.00 is ever found.
>
> **One thing we could not do, and it needs your decision.** The plan asked for
> a marker on each payment saying which payout it went out in. We built the
> column and then found the system will not let us write it: a payment is
> frozen the moment it is recorded — that is your own rule, and only three
> things on a payment may ever be changed afterwards (the cheque number, the
> note, and the tender). Adding a fourth needs your word. **Nothing is missing
> in the meantime** — the payout's own record lists its payments, and the
> screen reads it from there. What your decision would buy is a slightly faster
> list, not a new capability. It is written up as `OQ-PAY-12608`.

  three behave as designed — a `cleared` payment REFUSES `settlement_id`, a
  **`processing`** payment refuses it too (so there is no window at all), and
  **the control**: a `cleared` payment ACCEPTS `confirmation`, which is what
  proves the refusal is about this column rather than about a table that
  happened to be unwritable. ⚠ **The first draft of the finding was WRONG and
  the run corrected it** — it assumed the freeze began at clearing.
* **The SAVEPOINT** (hard-won law 14): `test_cr139_p5_1_one_bad_member_keeps_the_rest`
  is marked `requires_postgres` and **skips loudly on SQLite**, because the
  broken version passes there on every machine.

  pre-write SELECT, and `uq_settlements_provider_code` exercised on its own by
  writing the duplicate straight at the table.
* **Hard rule 5 asserted as an ABSENCE over the source** — `settlements.py`
  imports no ledger. A behavioural test could not see a second posting path:
  the payout would still ingest and the totals would still tie; only the trial
  balance would be wrong.
* **Hard rule 2**: every new money column declares FOUR decimals, over the
  drawing's six, parametrised across both tables.

## A waived deposit is kept on the account · 2026-09-23 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0066_def_cus_6370_deposit_waiver.py`
(migration ordering 🔒) · `06-backend/apps/customers/models.py` (`Account.deposit_waived_*`) ·
`06-backend/apps/customers/deposit.py` (`take()` — the plan's figure, the three refusals, and
the one write of the waive) · `06-backend/apps/customers/services.py` (`create_account` /
`move_in` — no block is *No*)

**Why it is on the sensitive list:** a numbered migration on `accounts`, and it changes what a
customer is asked to pay at the counter.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT DID YESTERDAY, WITH THE NUMBER

A clerk TYPED the deposit. A plan asking **$150.00** of a Residential customer was only shown
beside what was typed, so a typed **$120.00** went through. A clerk could also answer
*No* on that plan and open the account owing nothing, with nobody's approval. And when a
supervisor waived the $150.00, **the account kept nothing of it** — the only record was the
account-opening line in the audit log, which is deleted on its retention schedule. Measured on
the old build: account `AC-2026-00055`, waived by Dana Whitfield — `deposit_on_file 0`, nothing
else on the row.

### WHAT IT DOES NOW

The deposit is the plan's figure for the customer's category, and the screen shows it without a
box to type in. Where the plan asks one, the clerk takes it (today or on the first bill) or a
supervisor waives it; *No* is not offered. Where the plan asks none, there is no deposit and
nothing to type. A waive needs a short reason, and the account keeps **who waived it, when, the
$150.00 and the reason** for as long as the account exists.

### THE JUDGMENTS A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH

**1 · A figure that is not the plan's is refused, not quietly replaced.** If somebody edits the
plan while a clerk is on the step, the commit is refused (*"Deposit must match the plan."*) and
the clerk sees the new figure, rather than the customer being charged an amount nobody showed
them.

**2 · Nothing is filled in for accounts waived before today.** There is nothing to fill it from
that is still reliably there, so old waives stay blank rather than guessed.

**3 · Undoing the migration deletes every recorded waive.** Dump the four columns first.

### WHAT WAS SHOWN AND WHAT WAS PROVED

* Browser, 1440px, on a private copy of the demo tenant (`10-scripts/def_cus_6369_deposit_walkthrough.mjs`,
  screenshots `/tmp/claude-0/shots/deposit/`): 150.00 read-only; Take/Waive only; Commercial 400.00;
  Industrial *No deposit on this plan.*; a $150.00 payment with DR 1010 / CR 2300; a clerk's waive
  refused in words; a System Admin's *Hardship* waive on the row and on the tile as *Waived · $150.00*.
* `06-backend/tests/test_cr094_wh_deposit.py` asserts the $150.00, the refusals and the four
  columns read back off the row — on SQLite and on PostgreSQL (hard-won law 14).

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

**Rollback:** revert the commit. ⚠ The migration cannot be undone by a revert alone once it has
run and a waive has been recorded: reversing `customers 0066` drops those four columns and every
waive in them.

## A property can be sold more than once · 2026-09-24 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0069_def_cus_6431_resale.py` (migration ordering 🔒)
· lane TRANSFER-2, `v2.351.20`, `DEF-CUS-6431`

**Why it is on the sensitive list:** a numbered migration on `transfers` — it replaces one unique
index with a narrower one. No column, no row and no RLS policy is touched.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT DID YESTERDAY, WITH THE NUMBER

Account **A-11512** (61 Larkspur Way · Unit 1) was sold by *Hollis, Marcus* to *Aiden, Tim*
(**TRF-26-0001**). Selling it again — Tim to *Reyes, Carla* — failed at the very last step with
*"Something went wrong on our side."* A rule written for the OLD kind of transfer, which opened a
NEW account, said an account could be on the receiving end of one transfer, ever. Since
1 September a sale keeps the same account, so that rule had quietly become *"an account can be
sold once, ever"* — and a property is sold many times over its life.

### WHAT IT DOES NOW

The second sale completes as **TRF-26-0002**, and both records stay, each naming its own seller
and buyer. The once-ever rule now applies only to the old shape (a transfer that opened a
different account), where it still makes sense. **"One sale of an account at a time" is
unchanged:** starting a second sale while one is open is still refused by name (*already being
sold*), and the database still refuses it for two clerks racing.

### THE JUDGMENTS A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH

**1 · Narrowed, not dropped.** The index is kept for rows where the transfer opened a different
account (`to_account_id <> from_account_id`) — rows from 25 August to 1 September may be that
shape, and two transfers claiming to have opened one account is still a contradiction. A sale
(the same account on both sides) is simply outside it.

**2 · Renamed.** It is now `uq_transfers_opened_account`, so an error naming it says which rule
refused.

**3 · Undoing it fails once any account has been sold twice.** The reverse puts the once-ever
index back, and PostgreSQL refuses to build it while two sales share an account. The only way to
satisfy it would be to delete a real sale. **So once a resale exists, roll forward, not back.**

### WHAT WAS SHOWN AND WHAT WAS PROVED

* **Reproduced first**, on a private copy of the sample utility (`sbh_clone_transfer2`, built
  from the tip `e63ac0c0a`): selling A-11512 a second time refused with `duplicate key value
  violates unique constraint "uq_transfers_to_account"`. The probe ran inside one transaction
  that was rolled back.
* **Migration on PostgreSQL:** forward OK, back OK (no resale existed yet), forward OK; the index
  read back from `pg_indexes`. After it: TRF-26-0001 and TRF-26-0002 both `done`, the same account
  on both sides of each; a second open sale refused `from_account_already_being_sold`.
* **Browser**, on the same copy: A-11512 sold twice through the wizard, both rows on the
  Transfers list. ⚠ **Those screenshots are GONE** — the lane's container was reclaimed before
  the work was pushed, and a screenshot nobody can open is not evidence. What a reviewer can
  re-run is below.
* `06-backend/tests/test_def_cus_6431_resale.py` — five cases, RED on the old index
  (`UNIQUE constraint failed: transfers.tenant_id, transfers.to_account_id`), GREEN on SQLite
  and on PostgreSQL.
* **RE-PROVED IN A FRESH CONTAINER BEFORE THE PUSH (2026-09-24, `v2.351.20`):** PostgreSQL 16,
  role `smartbillhub` NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS — the three test files above, **10 passed**
  (`--ds=config.settings.pgtest`).

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

**Rollback:** revert the commit only while no account has been sold twice; after that, roll
forward (judgment 3).

## The payout pointer on `payments` is dropped, and the payment-row lock does not move · 2026-09-24 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/payments/migrations/0044_oq_pay_12608_drop_settlement_pointer.py`
(migration ordering 🔒, on the product's most tightly frozen table) ·
`06-backend/apps/payments/models.py` (the field declaration) ·
`06-backend/apps/payments/settlements.py` · `settlements_read.py` · `settlement_models.py` ·
`10-scripts/cr139_p5_6_pointer_freeze_proof.py` (verdict inverted) · lane RULINGS-0924,
`v2.351.23`, `OQ-PAY-12608`

**Why it is on the sensitive list:** a numbered migration that DROPS a column from `payments` —
the table CLAUDE.md hard rule 4 freezes — and the one thing a reviewer must be able to check is
that the freeze itself was not touched.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT DID YESTERDAY, WITH THE NUMBER

The payments blueprint (p024, task `P5.6`) drew a column on `payments` naming which payout paid
each card payment out, and said that leaving it empty is what *Awaiting settlement* means. It was
built on 2026-09-23. **Nothing could ever put a value in it.** Every payment row is locked the
moment it is written, except for a short list of things that may still change — and a payout
arrives days later, so the lock had already closed. That was measured on a real PostgreSQL
server, not argued from the code: a payment still clearing refuses it, a cleared payment refuses
it, and — the check that makes the finding mean something — the same cleared payment ACCEPTS a
corrected check number, because that IS on the short list.

So the column sat on every one of a utility's payment rows, empty, read by nothing, for a day.

### WHAT IT DOES NOW

The column is gone. **Nothing else changed**, and that is the point: the list of things that may
be changed on a paid payment is exactly what it was, and the screens read the same as before,
because they never read the column — they read the payout's own membership list, which is where
this fact has always been kept.

### THE JUDGMENTS A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH

**1 · Removing a column is a one-way door in a way that adding one is not.** Here it is not: the
column held nothing on every row in every utility, because it had no writer, so putting it back
restores exactly the state that was removed. That is unusual for this kind of change and is
stated plainly because most of them cannot say it — the sale-a-second-time migration of three
days ago cannot be undone once any property has been sold twice.

**2 · The alternative was to unlock the payment row.** The Product Owner was offered it: allow
this one field to be written once, the way the deposit-batch stamp already is. They chose to
remove the column instead, and their own words were *"nothing is lost, and the payment-row lock
stays exactly as it is"*. A reviewer who disagrees is disagreeing with that choice and not with
this build.

**3 · What it costs, with the figure.** A utility at the top of our size range holds about
**40,000 accounts**. Asking *which card payments has the processor not paid us for yet?* now
reads the payout membership list rather than a column on the payment. That is one extra join on a
page of results — not a scan of the table — and it is what the screen already did every day since
it was built.

**4 · The measurement script was kept, not deleted, and its verdict was turned round.** It used to
say FAIL when it could not find the column, which after this change is the only thing it could
ever say — a check that can only fail. Now finding the column gone is the expected result, and
finding it back is the failure. It was kept rather than deleted because six other places in the
repo cite it by name, one of them a row in this ledger, which may not be edited.

### WHAT WAS SHOWN AND WHAT WAS PROVED

* The Product Owner was shown, in plain English with the 40,000-account figure, that the column
  cannot be written, what it would take to make it writable, and that nothing is lost by removing
  it. They ruled on 2026-09-24: *"p7 (b) — nothing is lost, and the payment-row lock stays exactly
  as it is"*. **The ruling itself is therefore reviewed; this row is about the MIGRATION, which
  they have not seen.**
* Migration run forwards and backwards on PostgreSQL 16 (see the proof named in the decision-log
  entry of this date); `makemigrations --check` reports no changes.
* `06-backend/tests/test_cr139_p5_settlements.py` and `test_cr139_p5_12_to_p5_15.py` run on
  PostgreSQL after the drop, with a standing case that fails if the column ever comes back.

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING** for the migration itself.

**Rollback:** revert the commit. The reverse re-creates the column as an empty nullable uuid,
which is byte-for-byte the state that was dropped — no data can be lost in either direction.

## A fee taken at the counter is part of that counter's drawer count · 2026-09-24 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/payments/migrations/0045_oq_pay_12621_counter_receipt_names_its_till.py`
(migration ordering 🔒) · `06-backend/apps/payments/counter_receipt_models.py` (one nullable column
and its index) · `06-backend/apps/payments/counter_receipts.py` (the only writer) ·
`06-backend/apps/payments/counters.py` (`running_split` — the figure a drawer is counted against) ·
lane RULINGS-0924, `v2.351.28`, `OQ-PAY-12621`, `DEF-PAY-6375`

**Why it is on the sensitive list:** a numbered migration, and it changes the number a clerk counts
their cash against at the end of a shift — which since yesterday is a number that posts to the
books when it does not match.

### WHAT THE PRODUCT DID YESTERDAY, WITH THE NUMBER

Dana opens her counter holding **$400.00**. A customer hands over **$70.00** in cash for an
application fee; she records it and puts the money in the drawer. At the end of the shift she
counts what is actually there — **$470.00** — and the screen tells her she is **$70.00 over**,
because it was only expecting the $400.00. Since 2026-09-23 an over like that is written into the
books, so the same $70.00 was recorded twice: once when she took it, and again as an unexplained
overage.

She had done nothing wrong, and there was no way for her to make it balance.

### WHAT IT DOES NOW

The screen expects **$470.00**. She counts $470.00 and she is square. Nothing else moved: the fee
is still recorded once, when it is taken, in exactly the same place in the books.

A fee paid by **card** is not part of the count, because you cannot count a card total in a
drawer — the same rule the product already applies to card payments.

### THE JUDGMENTS A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH

**1 · The number of items shown beside each total now includes fees.** A clerk sees "Cash $470.00 ·
1" rather than "$470.00 · 0". The alternative was to move the money and not the count, which would
have printed a total nobody could reconcile with the number under it.

**2 · Nothing was invented to make it balance.** The tempting fix is to write a payment row for the
fee; that would make the drawer balance too, and would book the fee twice in the books instead of
in the drawer. A test asserts no payment row is written.

**3 · A fee taken with no counter open belongs to no drawer.** That state is reachable on purpose —
the sample data seeds one — so it means "joins no drawer", never "joins whichever drawer is
asking". Two tests hold that, one of them with a second clerk's till open at the same time.

### WHAT WAS SHOWN AND WHAT WAS PROVED

* The Product Owner was shown the $70.00/$470.00/$400.00 case in plain English and ruled on
  2026-09-24: *"p1 a"* — the fee counts toward the counter's expected cash. **The ruling is
  therefore reviewed; this row is about the MIGRATION and the drawer arithmetic, which they have
  not seen.**
* `06-backend/tests/test_oq_pay_12621_fee_in_the_drawer.py` — six cases, proved RED before the
  reader existed and run again on real PostgreSQL 16.
* Migration run forwards and backwards on PostgreSQL 16; `makemigrations --check` reports no
  changes.

**NOT YET READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER — HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING** for the migration and the arithmetic.

**Rollback:** revert the commit. The reverse drops the column and its index; nothing is lost that
was not derivable, because `taken_by` and `taken_at` still name the person and the moment. What
comes back is the defect, so a rollback must take the reader in `running_split` with it.

## THE INVOICE CLOUD *MAKE PAYMENT* API — THE FIRST WRITE ON THE PARTNER DOOR (🔒 idempotency keys, money path, 2026-09-24, lane INVOICE-CLOUD, version `2.351.39`)

**THE DESIGN WAS READ TO THE PRODUCT OWNER AND RULED; THE CODE HAS NOT BEEN READ TO THEM.
HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.** The distinction is the whole of what this section records, because
a signature covers only what was shown.

**WHAT WAS SHOWN, AND WHAT THEY SAID.** On 2026-09-24 the Product Owner brought Invoice
Cloud's own *Make Payment API Specification v1.0* and asked, verbatim: *"tell me how to
handle this - dont start the work tell me what you will do"*, then *"tell me the steps you
will run … including what codes you will handle in table format"*, then *"please confirm
in table before you start this APIs"*. The plan was put to them in a table — the eight
authorisation checks, the two date columns, the status correction, the till-and-batch
answer, the audit actor and five mismatches between their document and this product — and
they ruled ***"please do"***. **That ruling covers the DESIGN.** It is recorded in full in
the decision log of that date, which is this build's specification.

**THE TWO FIGURES THAT WERE SHOWN, in plain English, so the record says what was in front
of them rather than merely that review happened:**

* **A payment of `$142.18` against bill `INV-2026-00412` on account `A-10650`, paid
  20 June 2026** — Invoice Cloud's own worked example from their document. It lands as one
  payment of $142.18, on that account, against that bill, with our own payment number
  handed back to them.
* **The status.** Their document asks for *"posted"*. This product's payment recorder
  writes `cleared` when it is given a clearing date and `processing` when it is not, and
  it never writes *posted* — that constant exists and nothing produces it. The Product
  Owner was shown that table and answered ***"this is okay"***, which is what makes the
  correction accepted rather than assumed.

**WHAT WAS *NOT* SHOWN AND THEREFORE IS NOT COVERED — this is the part that returns to the
agenda:**

1. **The idempotency key's exact shape.** The plan they confirmed said a NEW
   `invoice_cloud` source; the build uses `webhook|invoice_cloud:<their reference>`
   instead, because `settlements._payment_for` re-composes that exact string to find a
   payout's members and a payment keyed any other way would be invisible to the settlement
   that names it. **That is an AI judgment on a 🔒 path**, recorded in the decision log of
   2026-09-24 with its reasoning. It is safer and it is still a change from what was shown.
2. **The refusal of `cash`, `check` and `money_order` on this door.** Derived from the
   PO's own till ruling of 2026-09-23 (*"every cash dollar belongs to somebody"*), applied
   to a door that ruling was not shown. `BR-PAY-1197`.
3. **Which words go in the audit trail's actor label.** The actor being the CONNECTOR was
   shown and confirmed; that it reads the connection's clerk-given label rather than the
   manifest's display name was not raised.

**NOTHING IN THIS WAVE TOUCHES A 🔒 SENSITIVE PATH, AND THAT IS THE HONEST
SUMMARY OF IT.** Every engine, every rule and every posting key in this phase
was already written, already tested and already sensitive-path-reviewed; what
this lane built is four DOORS onto them. One backend file changed and it adds

### WHAT WAS PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, AND WHAT WAS NOT

| Shown | In plain English, with its figure |

| **Which of the four month-end entries reverse** | Two do and two must not. Unbilled revenue and unpaid costs cancel themselves on the first day of your next period; depreciation and the bad-debt allowance stand. **If depreciation reversed itself the way an accrual does, a truck bought for $40,000 would go back to being worth $40,000 every single month.** The screen now says `Accrual` and a date on the first two and `Standard` and **Never** on the other two |

| **That reopening does not recall a hand-over** | If the month has gone to QuickBooks or Xero, the dialog says so before you press — *"Handed over 2026-09-24. That handover stands. Post the difference."* The export itself is untouched by the reopen |
| **What the approver sees before agreeing to a refund** | The account number and the customer's name, the address it belongs to, how much credit that account is holding, which payments built that credit, and what has happened so far. On the demo data that is **$0.55 to Hugo Faulkner on AC-2026-00032, built by one payment PY-260809-0061** |

1. **That the refund screen says NOTHING about whether the customer owes on
   another of their accounts**, where the drawing has a row for it. Nothing in
   this product can answer that about a refund that already exists.
2. **That the refund's history names no person.** The product records who did
   each step and there is no read that turns that into a name for this screen.
3. **That the row actions on the accruals list sit once per entry rather than

Each is in the decision log with its reasoning and in the screenshot README the
PO is being handed. **A signature covers only what was shown**, so all three
return to the agenda.

## `P4.4` / `P4.3` — THE FILING REGISTER, AND THE RECEIPT THAT CAN BE KEPT (2026-09-24, LANE FIN-P4B)

**WHAT WAS BUILT, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** A utility files a tax return, pays the
authority and types the confirmation number the authority gave them. Until
today the product posted the payment into the books and **stored nothing else**
— so nobody could answer *"did we pay Bexar County in August?"* without leaving
Finance, opening the journal and filtering by source. And the form for
attaching the filing receipt refused the file outright, saying so on screen,
because there was nowhere to put it.

There is now a **filing register**: one row per return, carrying the authority,
the period the return covers, the day the money left, the amount, the
confirmation number and a link to the entry it posted — and the **receipt is
kept** against it, for seven years, in the document store the product already
uses for bills and account paperwork.

**THE WORKED FIGURE, WHICH IS WHAT IS BEING PUT FOR REVIEW.** The State of
Texas, July 2026, remitted on the collected basis: **$13.87**, paid on
**2026-08-18**, confirmation **CONF-88213**, posted as
`DR 2200-01 13.87 / CR cash 13.87`.

⚠ **THIS ROW READ *"Bexar County … $498.22, paid on 2026-09-10"* UNTIL IT WAS
MEASURED, AND NO TEST ASSERTED THAT FIGURE.** The figure above is LE-3's own
signed `LE3_STATE_REMIT_NOW` and is the one
`tests/test_cr140_p4_filing_register.py` actually posts and reads back, so a
drift in it goes RED. A review row carrying a number nothing checks is the
`DEF-2846` shape — a citation that reads as engine proof and is not — and a
signature given over it would cover a figure the product never computed.
Before today that payment left one journal entry and no record a person could
find; now the same act also writes one filing row, and the Taxes & Remittance
screen lists it under *Payments made* beside what is still owed. **The amount
in the books did not change and is not read from the new table.**

**THE ONE THING A REVIEWER SHOULD PUSH BACK ON IF THEY DISAGREE.** The register
is **append-only**: the database refuses to edit or delete a filing row. So a
mistyped confirmation number is corrected by filing a **second row**, not by
changing the first. That is deliberate — the row is the proof for money that
has already moved through an entry that can never be edited — but it is a
choice, and the alternative (allowing that one field to be corrected in place,
as payments already allow for a cheque number) is a real option. It is written
up as `OQ-LED-12653` with its own worked case.

## `DEF-LED-6723` — opening a journal entry (2026-09-25, lane JE)

**WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD BE SHOWN, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH A FIGURE, AND IT IS
NOT AN ID TO GO AND LOOK UP.** The Product Owner clicked the eye beside a
journal entry on the Finance → General ledger → Journal screen and nothing
happened. The eye was correctly disabled: the product had no way to fetch one
entry, only the list. This adds that fetch.

Opened against the real demo books on PostgreSQL 16, one bill from 2 July 2026:
the entry shows **six lines** — Electric usage **95.50**, Electric base
**12.00**, Water usage **39.50**, Water base **8.00**, Bexar County tax
**3.10**, all on the credit side, against one debit to Accounts receivable of
**158.10**. **95.50 + 12.00 + 39.50 + 8.00 + 3.10 = 158.10**, so the two sides
agree and the screen says so. Each line also names the service, the customer
account **AC-2026-00001**, the property **101 Silver Creek Rd** and the unit
**Unit 1** — by their names, never by their internal identifiers.

**NOTHING CAN BE CHANGED HERE AND THAT IS ON PURPOSE.** A posted entry is
permanent; the only correction is to reverse it and post a new one. There is no
edit field, no save button and no version marker anywhere in what was added.

**AN ENTRY WITH NO NUMBER STAYS WITH NO NUMBER.** An opening balance is not a
document, so it has no entry number, and the screen shows that absence rather
than inventing one. Proved on a real opening balance: two lines, **267.30**
against **267.30**, entry number empty. A number invented here could never be
taken back out.

**WHO MAY LOOK.** Anyone signed in to the tenant may open an entry, which is
what every other Finance read already allows. Who may DELETE a draft is
unchanged — System Admin or Billing Clerk, the ruling of 2026-08-12.

## `DEF-LED-6702` — a counter receipt reads as a payment (2026-09-25, lane JE)

**WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD BE SHOWN, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH A FIGURE.** On the
Finance → General ledger → Journal screen, the SOURCE column is meant to say in
plain words where a line of the books came from. On six or more rows it printed
`counter_receipt` — the word our engineers use, not a word a clerk uses. A
counter receipt is a payment taken at the counter, and it now reads **payment**,
like every other payment on that screen.

**THE ONE THING THAT COULD HAVE GONE WRONG AND DID NOT, STATED BECAUSE IT IS A
MONEY RULE.** There is a second list in the same file that means *"this cash
paid off a bill"*. A counter receipt does **not** pay off a bill — it puts money
on the customer's account as credit — so it is deliberately kept off that list.
Had it gone on, the *collected* figure and the billed-and-collected totals on
Revenue & AR would all have moved, and the change would have looked, in the
code, exactly like the wording fix. A test now asserts that list is unchanged
and contains exactly `payment` and `deposit_batch`.

**SIX MORE WORDS ARE STILL MISSING AND WE ARE NOT CHOOSING THEM.** A drawer
count, a bad-debt allowance, depreciation, a supplier invoice and two kinds of
month-end accrual have no word in the signed ten-word list at all. Those are
`OQ-LED-12657`, put to the Product Owner in their own terms; the screen goes on
showing the code for them rather than a wrong word beside a real figure. **A
test pins the number at six**, so a lane that maps one without an answer goes
red and is told which.

**AND THE COMMENT ABOVE THE LIST WAS WRONG.** It said the list held *"the
strings the four posting callers actually write today"*. Counted: **eleven files
write seventeen different strings**, and the list holds fifteen. That is a claim
about four files that nothing re-checked, and it outlived the thing it
described.

## 2026-09-25 · A unit now takes its address's services by default (`DEF-MET-6796`, `2.353.1`)

**WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD BE SHOWN, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH A FIGURE.** When a clerk
adds flats to a building, the building's services now come across to every flat
automatically. Take a building set up for electric, water, sewer and trash, and
add three flats to it. Before this change the three flats ended up with **no
services at all — zero out of twelve**. After it they have all twelve, and the
clerk can take any of them off before pressing Create.

**WHY THAT WAS MONEY AND NOT TIDINESS.** What a flat is billed for is decided by
the services recorded against it. A flat recorded with no services is never
billed for anything, on a building the utility is selling four services at.

**WHAT A CLERK CAN STILL DO.** Take services off. A flat with fewer services
than its building is a perfectly normal thing — a shop unit on water only in a
block that also has gas — so the product does not argue with it. It counts it
instead: the Units screen now shows how many flats have fewer services than
their address offers, and which ones are missing, so nobody has to go looking.

**ONE THING WE ACCEPTED, SAID OUT LOUD.** Once a service is off a flat, there is
no record of whether somebody took it off on purpose or it was never there. The
Product Owner was told that and accepted it; no column was added to record the
difference.

**WHAT WAS NOT SHOWN AND IS COVERED BY NO SIGNATURE HERE.** The move-in build
screen creates flats by a different route and does not take the building's
services across. Those flats DO show up on the new count, so nothing is hidden —
but whether that screen should behave the same way is a question for the lane
that owns it, and it was not put to the Product Owner.

## The reports read path — a 38,000-bill register opens on a page, and no export is refused for being large (`CR-142-BRC07` `P2.12` · `P2.1`–`P2.4`, lane REP-P2A, lands on `2.357.0`)

🔒 **SENSITIVE PATH: `NFR-5`, paging, and a money-table export's accept path.**
No migration, no money arithmetic, no rounding, nothing ❄️ FROZEN.

**WHAT A PERSON WOULD SEE, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH THE FIGURES.**

A utility with about 19,000 accounts has **39,981 bills** in its register. Until
this change, opening that register read **every one of them** into the server's
memory before deciding which fifty to show, and then sorted them in Python. On a
real PostgreSQL 16 database that read took **3.4 seconds** of server time on its
own. A web worker in this product is allowed **60 seconds** before it is killed,
so the old register was not merely slow — at a large enough utility it would
have been stopped before it answered, exactly as measured for the debtor list at
40,046 debtors (61.5 seconds).

**It now opens a page of fifty in 0.211 seconds, and the LAST page — page 799 —
costs 0.206 seconds, the same as the first.** That sameness is the point: the
work no longer grows with the size of the utility. The register can also be
sorted by bill number, date, amount or account, and searched by bill number,
account number or customer name, and every one of those happens on the server
rather than on the fifty rows already on the screen.

**A second figure, because it is the one that will matter at a bigger utility.**
Drawing that page of fifty used to take **56 separate database round trips** —
fifty of them fetching the customer's name, one name at a time. It now takes
**7**. The unpaged version was making one per bill: about **40,000 round trips
for one column**.

**THE EXPORT CEILING IS REMOVED, AND THIS IS THE PART A PERSON SHOULD BE ASKED
ABOUT.** Until now the product refused to build any list export above **100,000
rows** and told the clerk to narrow their filters. **Killeen has 57,066
accounts and bills 14 times a year, which is about 685,000 bills a year** — so a
clerk asking for their own year of billing was refused by the product. The
ceiling is **deleted, not raised**: raising it is what happened on 18 September
(50,000 → 100,000) and the new number was still too small. The file was already
written one row at a time straight from the database, so removing the ceiling
costs nothing — the limit was guarding a danger that had already been designed
out.

**AND THE PRODUCT NO LONGER BUILDS EVERY EXPORT TWICE.** It used to count the
rows first, purely to compare against that ceiling, and for eight of the lists
that count meant building the entire report, throwing it away, and building it
again to write the file. With the ceiling gone the count has no reader, so it is
gone too. The one visible consequence: while an export runs, the progress
indicator counts up rather than filling a bar, because nothing knows the total
until the file is finished. That was a deliberate choice and the alternative was
to keep doing the work twice.

**WHAT IS NOT CHANGED, SAID OUT LOUD.** The audit log still records every export
of a money table — who, which list, which filters, which columns, which job. The
only thing that left that record is the row count, because at the moment the
record is written nothing has counted anything. The AUDIT LOG's own export keeps
its separate 50,000-row ceiling under its own rule; that one is another part of
the product and was not touched.

**A REFUSAL A CLERK COULD SEE WAS DELETED RATHER THAN REWORDED.** The sentence
*"That's 62,000 rows — more than the 50,000 an export can carry. Narrow your
filters and try again."* is removed from all eleven languages, because there is
nothing left for it to describe.

**THE ACCOUNT LEDGER PAGES TOO, AND ITS RUNNING BALANCE STILL ADDS UP.** A
customer statement's balance column is cumulative — each row is the one above it
plus this row's charge, minus this row's payment. Page two therefore cannot
start at the beginning; it has to start where page one ended. Proved on real
data: row 201's balance reads **13.000000** whether the report is read whole or
read as page two, and the window's total charges read **2,597.000000** either
way. **The account ledger deliberately offers NO sort at all** — sorting a
running balance by amount does not re-order that column, it makes every number
in it wrong.

**WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE.** One more report in the payments module,
*payments by method*, still hands back every cleared payment in the window. It
is filed as `DEF-REP-6816` and left alone, because it is a different report and
widening this piece of work to cover it would mean nobody reviewed either.

## 2026-09-26 · A customer is billed for what they bought, not for what the building has (`DEF-BIL-6823` · `BR-BIL-1048`, `2.357.2`, lane BILLNARROW)

**WHAT TO LOOK AT, IN ONE SENTENCE.** Yesterday a clerk could say an account
takes three of its property's six services; today the bill finally charges for
those three and not for all six.

**THE CONCRETE FIGURE, FROM A REAL BILL ON REAL POSTGRESQL.** On a seeded
six-service utility, account `AC-2026-00003` holds three agreements — electric,
gas and fire. Its September bill:

* **before:** `$475.68`, fifteen lines, including **water `$98.10`, sewer
  `$76.50` and trash `$15.00`** the customer never bought;
* **after:** `$282.29`, nine lines. Those three services are **nowhere on the
  document** — not a line, not a `$0.00`, not a note.

That is **`$193.39` a month on one account**: `$189.60` of charges and `$3.79`
of tax that was riding on them.

**WHAT A CLERK SEES.** Nothing new to learn. The account's own Services chips
already showed three; the bill now agrees with them. There is no new screen, no
new control and no new message.

**THE THING WE MOST NEED A HUMAN TO AGREE WITH.** There are two reasons a
service on the plan can be missing from the bill, and they get opposite
treatment:

* **the property has no connection for it** — it still appears at **`$0.00`**,
  marked *not connected*, exactly as ruled on 25 September;
* **the account did not take it** — it does not appear at all.

We built them as two separate lists so one can never become the other. If that
split is wrong, this is the decision to say so about.

**WHAT WE DELIBERATELY DID NOT DECIDE.** A clerk can now sell sewer without
water. Sewer costs 90% of the water the customer used, so that account produces
no bill at all — it stops with a message and waits for a person. We have not
chosen what should happen; it is `OQ-BIL-12739` and it is on your list, with
*refuse it on the move-in screen* recommended.

**SAFETY, STATED.** When the product cannot tell what an account bought — an
older import that never recorded it — the bill is **exactly what it was
before**. Narrowing can only ever take services away from a list, never empty
one, so no bill can be zeroed by a missing record. All **75** accounts of the
seeded utility were priced before and after: **73 identical to the cent**, and
the two that moved are the two named here.

`_plan_services_not_taken`, the two `skip_services` facts, and
`_unpriced_unit_service_lines(taken_services=)`).

## 2026-09-26 · lane DS-LEDGER · the `journal_lines` dataset query 🔒

**WHAT WAS BUILT, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** Forty-five reports are listed on the
Reports page and thirty-seven of them could not be produced. They are not
forty-five separate pieces of work: forty-six answers sit on **nine** shared
queries, and this piece of work wrote the biggest one — the query that reads the
**posted journal lines**. Ten of the listed reports say they read it.

**FOUR OF THE TEN NOW OPEN AND RUN.** Trial Balance, Journal Export, Tax
Remittance and Close Pack. Journal Export had no way to be produced at all
before today; the other three had a screen but no way to be run, paged or
downloaded from the Reports page.

**THE FIGURE THIS ROW IS ABOUT, AND IT IS THE ONE TO CHECK.** A trial balance
either balances or the books are wrong. On the measured fixture the query
returns **Σ debits equal to Σ credits and a difference of exactly 0.00**, and
the report publishes that difference on every answer. **It is never adjusted,
rounded into agreement or hidden.** If it is ever anything but zero, that is a
fault in the service that writes the books — not something this report tunes —
and both the test suite and the PostgreSQL measurement script FAIL BY NAME on a
non-zero difference rather than reporting a green.

**THE ONE JUDGMENT CALL PUT UP FOR REVIEW.** When a clerk narrows the report —
say, to accounts 4000 to 4999 — the report **stops saying whether the books
balance**. It still shows the difference, because that is a real figure about
the rows in front of them, but it no longer claims anything about the books.
The reason: an entry always has two sides, and a filter on account codes keeps
only one of them, so the leftover is not supposed to add up. Saying *"out of
balance"* there would accuse the system of a fault every time somebody used a
filter, and after a month of that nobody would believe the warning when it was
real. The same choice was already made for the trial balance's property filter
in September and this follows it.

**WHAT IT WILL NOT DO, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** The query only READS. It
contains no instruction that writes, changes or deletes anything, because only
the posting service is allowed to write journal lines. Every row in the test
fixture and in the PostgreSQL measurement was created by posting a real balanced
entry through that service, not by inserting rows.

**SPEED, MEASURED ON REAL POSTGRESQL 16** (not on the test suite — that runs on
in-memory SQLite and cannot answer this question). A utility with **8,580
posted journal lines**: the first page of fifty comes back in **0.057 seconds**
and the LAST page — number 172 — in **0.097 seconds**. The last page being no
slower than the first is the whole point: it means the server is fetching fifty
rows, not fetching all 8,580 and throwing 8,530 away. The download of every row
takes **1.989 seconds**. A web worker is given sixty seconds, so all three have
a very large margin, and there is **no ceiling on the download and there must
never be one**.

**And the books footed on that data**: Σ debits **275,412.92**, Σ credits
**275,412.92**, difference **0.00**.

**SIX OF THE TEN STILL CANNOT BE PRODUCED AND ARE REPORTED, NOT PAPERED OVER.**
Revenue Analysis is listed as reading the books and actually reads the bills
(`DEF-REP-6831` — a product question about which of the two it should be, not
something this lane may decide); Regulatory Filing and External Reconciliation
need facts the product does not hold; Trend Pack needs a revenue target no
utility has set; the Ledger already opens from the sidebar and was left alone;
and the Operational Dashboard is a tab rather than a card by the drawing's own
instruction.

## 2026-09-27 · lane REP-P2-MODEL · a report refuses a total it may not add up 🔒 (`CR-142-BRC07` `P2.22` · `P2.14` · `P2.17` · `P2.25`, lands on `2.362.0`)

**HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING** — `06-backend/apps/reports/additivity.py` and
`06-backend/apps/reports/slicers.py`. Money path: what a total is allowed to
say, and how a subtotal is added up.

**WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD BE SHOWN, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH A FIGURE.**

Three sums the product would happily print today, and what it prints instead.

**One — a balance added up across months.** Take the receivables owed at the
end of May, June and July: **$41,220.00**, **$44,118.50** and **$48,221.14**.
Group the receivables report by month and total the column and the product
prints **$133,559.64**. That is not a receivable. Every household that owed
money in more than one of those months has been counted more than once, and
nobody owes $133,559.64. The report now prints **— Balances do not sum across
time** in that cell, and **each month's own subtotal is still a figure**,
because one month added up across households is exactly what a balance is for.

**Two — a collection speed averaged across rounds.** Four rounds collect in
20, 30, 40 and 90 days. The product prints the average, **45.00 days**. The
utility's real figure is its whole receivable divided by its own daily sales
and could be 26 or 71; it is not the average of four. That cell now reads
**— Recomputed from components, never averaged**.

**Three — two different units of measure added together.** A water reading of
**26.24 kgal** and an electric reading of **684.00 kWh** add to **710.24**, a
number with no unit, which our own rule 3 says is not a quantity at all. That
cell now reads **— Quantities differ between services**.

**WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE, WHICH IS THE HALF WORTH CHECKING.** Every report as it
ships today is untouched, to the byte. The receivables report as a clerk opens
it — one line per household, owed as at a date, not grouped — still shows every
one of its six figures, because that total is lawful. **39 existing report
tests passed before this change and the same 39 pass after it.**

**WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD LOOK AT.** The screenshot pair in the lane's shot
folder: the same report grouped, refusing its total, beside itself ungrouped
where the total is a number — and the downloaded file's last row.

**THE ONE THING WE DID NOT DECIDE AND DID NOT GUESS.** Our download rule says a
CSV holds a header row and then the data and nothing else. The reports brief
says the dash and the reason must appear *in the CSV*. Both are signed and they
disagree. Nothing was overruled: the extra row is written **only** when a total
refused itself, so every file whose totals are lawful is byte-for-byte what it
was yesterday, and the question is put to the Product Owner as `OQ-REP-12740`.

**TWO THINGS THE CODE SAID THAT WERE NOT TRUE, BOTH MEASURED.** The time levels
a report offered came from one shared list that matched **none** of the nine
datasets' own declared calendars (`DEF-REP-6846`). And of **71** filters the
model declared, only **37** had anything behind them — the other 34 would have
been controls on screen that did nothing (`DEF-REP-6847`). So the receivables
report gains **9** filters and not the 13 the brief promises; the four missing
ones are named in the defect rather than drawn as dead chips.

## 2026-09-27 · THE `payments` DATASET QUERY — 🔒 SENSITIVE PATH, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING (lane DS-PAYMENTS, `CR-142-BRC07`, 2.361.1)

**What this is, in plain English.** Ten reports are listed as being built on the
payments data. **Two of them work today and eight do not**, and the reason is
not that we ran out of time — it is that eight of them are not reports about
payments at all. The Deposit Batches report is about a *batch*. The Cash
Reconciliation report is about a *bank statement line*, and its own drawing
shows a bank charge of **−$18.40** that exists at the bank and has no payment
behind it at all. The Deposits report is about the *security deposit sitting on
an account*, which is a number we keep on the customer's account, not on any
payment. Serving those from the payments data would produce real-looking rows
and a total that adds up, and it would be answering a question nobody asked.
**They are listed, by name, with the information each one actually needs.**

**What was built.** One new read of the payments data: **one row per payment**,
which the screen asks for fifty at a time and a download gets all of.

**THE ONE THING TO CHECK, WITH THE FIGURE.** The system said this data was *"one
payment allocation"* — an allocation being the link between a payment and a
bill. **A deposit, a prepayment and a down payment on an arrangement have no
bill to link to, so they have no allocation.** On our own test utility,
**8,000 of 40,066 payments are deposits — one in five.** A report built the old
way would have shown 32,066 of those 40,066 payments and a smaller day's
takings. It would not have looked wrong. It would have looked like a quieter
Tuesday. **The new read counts all 40,066.** Please confirm that is what you
expect a payments report to show.

**THE SECOND THING, AND IT AFFECTS A REPORT THAT IS LIVE NOW.** The Payments
report that works today reads every payment in the window one at a time. On our
40,000-payment test utility it took **70.5 seconds**. A web page is given **60
seconds** before it is cut off — **so at the size of utility we sell to, that
report does not come back slowly, it does not come back at all.** The new read
answers the same question in **0.28 seconds** on the first page and **0.32
seconds** on the last. Nothing has been changed in the live report; the faster
read is beside it and switching over is a separate decision.

**THE THIRD THING, AND IT IS A WORDING PROBLEM ON A MONEY RULE.** When a clerk
mistypes a cheque and tries to correct which *tender* it was, we correctly
refuse if the money has already been banked. The refusal fires; we checked both
the code and the database rule. **But both messages still tell the clerk that
deposits are grouped "by day and tender", and you changed that on 22 September
— a deposit is now one till and one tender.** The refusal is right and the
reason we give is out of date, including inside the database itself. We have
not changed it, because changing a database rule's wording is a migration on
the money path. **It is written down so it can be fixed deliberately.**

**MEASURED, NOT ESTIMATED** — real PostgreSQL 16, 40,066 payments, median of 3
after a discarded warm-up (`10-scripts/ds_payments_dataset_cost.py`):

| read | round trips | rows | seconds |
|---|---|---|---|
| new read · first page | 6 | 50 | **0.284** |
| new read · last page (802) | 5 | 16 | **0.321** |
| new read · grouped by method | 3 | 4 | 0.176 |
| new read · the whole download | 23 | 40,066 | 10.915 |
| **today's Payments report** | **9,000+** | 40,066 | **70.477** |

The last page costs **1.13×** the first, which is the thing that matters: the
page is cut by the database and not by us. And the download has **no limit on
it and must never have one**.
