## NEW ROW 2026-09-27 · `CR-142-BRC07` PHASE 4 `P4.1` / `P4.2` / `P4.3` — REPORTS CAN NOW SEND THEMSELVES, AND ONE NEW TABLE DECIDES TO WHOM

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
**NEW** `06-backend/apps/reports/migrations/0004_cr142_p4_report_schedules.py` 🔒 (**migration ordering**) · **NEW** `06-backend/apps/reports/migrations/0005_cr142_p4_schedules_rls.py` 🔒 (**RLS policy** — the ordinary B2 §3 template, both clauses) · **NEW** `06-backend/apps/reports/schedules.py` (the sweep — it runs OUT OF REQUEST, which is where tenant context is lost) · **NEW** `06-backend/apps/reports/schedules_api.py` · `06-backend/apps/reports/models.py` (**NEW** `ReportSchedule`) · `06-backend/apps/reports/apps.py` (the beat entry is installed here).

**WHAT IT IS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURES.**

**(1) A report can now run on its own and arrive without anybody remembering.** Somebody opens a report, presses *Schedule it*, and answers three questions: how often, what file, and who gets it. Four choices for how often — every day, every week, every month, or **monthly when the books close**. Worked, so the date is agreed rather than assumed: a utility whose books close on **the third business day** schedules the AR ageing report on **25 September**; September's books close on **5 October 2026**, and the file is made at six in the morning that day. **The Friday-to-Monday case the phase is measured by**: a daily schedule set at nine on Friday morning makes its next file at **six on Saturday morning**, and carries on every morning after, with nobody signed in.

**(2) ⚠ THE ONE THAT NEEDS A HUMAN EYE — WHOSE *CYCLE CLOSE* IS IT?** The screen says *monthly, on cycle close*. There are two dates in this product that could mean, and **one of them is a question the PO already declined**. We used the **accounting period's** close — the date computed from the utility's own financial year settings, which is already on screen elsewhere and already agreed. The other reading would be *when a billing cycle is finished*, and on **23 August** the PO answered that with *"dont build it"*; the product refuses it by name to this day. **So the question is only about the WORD:** our product calls that date a *period* close and the drawing calls it a *cycle* close. Should the four choices read *Monthly, on period close* instead? It is `OQ-REP-12741` and **nothing is waiting on it** — the schedules work either way.

**(3) A report is sent to this utility's own staff and to nobody else.** There is **no box to type an email address into** — the screen offers a list of the utility's own people and refuses anything else, and so does the server. That is the rule agreed on 8 August (`BR-REP-020`): sending a report outside the utility means a utility's data leaves the utility, and it arrives later with a step that asks first. **Proved both ways**: a real person at a second utility was offered to the server and was **refused by name**, and an email address was refused too.

**(4) A schedule that fires twice makes one file.** Two beat ticks reaching the same due moment fold into the same job rather than producing two files with two sets of figures. ⚠ **AND WE FOUND THAT THE LOCK WAS NOT ACTUALLY SWITCHED ON FOR THIS KIND OF WORK.** The database has held the right constraint for months, but the existing Export button passes it nothing to lock on — correctly, because a clerk who presses Export twice wants two files. The scheduler passes it the schedule AND the moment it was due, so October cannot fold into September. **The clerk's Export button is untouched.**

**(5) A schedule whose report has broken stays on the list, marked *failing*.** It is not silently switched off and not retried every minute. A utility with no financial year set up at all gets a schedule that says *failing* from the first day rather than one that quietly never runs — **we do not invent a date for it**, because a made-up first-of-the-month would deliver a finance pack on a day nobody chose.

**(6) WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT.** No email actually leaves the building yet (`P4.10`, not built). No page for one schedule on its own (`4·2`, not built). No tenant-settable retention (`P4.6`, not built). No PDF — **there is no PDF renderer anywhere in this product**, so the format chooser offers CSV only rather than offering a button that makes nothing.

**WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK ABOUT THE 🔒 FILES, IN ONE SENTENCE EACH.** `0005` — that **neither** half of the rule mentions an ownerless row: unlike the two tables `0002` covers, there is no such thing as a schedule we ship, and a schedule of ours addressed to people we chose would be exactly the wrong thing to be possible. `schedules.py` — that the sweep enters one utility's context before it reads a single schedule row, and that the job body opens no second one (a nested one leaves no utility set at all and the job then reports failure over work it did correctly).

**PROOF, AND WHAT IT CANNOT COVER.** `06-backend/tests/test_cr142_p4_schedules.py` — the four cadences each against a hand-worked date (including **31 January → 28 February**, never 3 March), the refusal instead of a substituted date, a three-day outage producing **one** file rather than three, the fold-in asserted on the **job id** rather than on a row count, and both recipient refusals. ⚠ **THE TENANT-ISOLATION HALF IS NOT PROVED BY THAT SUITE AND CANNOT BE:** `config/settings/test.py` hardcodes in-memory SQLite, **which has no row-level security of any kind**, so every assertion about the policy would pass there by vacuum. **Until it is run on real PostgreSQL the policy on `report_schedules` is unproven**, and this lane did not get to that run — it is named here rather than left for somebody to assume.

**ROLLBACK:** revert the commit and run `migrate reports 0003`. The two migrations reverse cleanly; no existing table is altered and no existing row is touched. The Scheduled tab disappears, the tab strip returns to two words, and every report goes on being run by hand exactly as it is today.

## 2026-09-27 · `P2.20` — a machine that reads two reports, and nothing else

**Lane REP-P2-TAIL · `CR-142-BRC07` Phase 2 · 🔒 RLS + a credential path.**
HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING. AI-authored under the PO ruling of 2026-08-09 (*"AI will
do it; we will review it later as human"*).

### What was built, in plain English

A utility's Power BI can now read a report over the same web address a clerk's
screen uses. It signs in with a **token that belongs to the tool, not to a
person** — so when the clerk who set it up leaves, the board pack keeps working,
and when the tool is retired, one switch stops it without touching anybody's
account.

An **administrator** creates one, gives it a name like *Power BI · board pack*,
and **names the reports it may read**. Granted *Revenue Analysis* and *Trial
Balance*, it reads those two and gets a refusal on everything else. It shows up
in the *Started by* column on the report history under its own name, so a run
nobody recognises can be traced to the tool that made it.

### The figures, and what each one is

* **A token is 256 bits** and is shown **once**, when it is created. We store a
  one-way fingerprint of it, so nobody here — support included — can read a
  customer's token back out.
* **60 requests a minute per token**, settable per deployment. That is a limit
  on one tool, not on a utility: a bigger utility gets a bigger number or a
  second token, and neither needs a database change.
* **An empty list of reports grants nothing.** A half-finished setup is a token
  that opens nothing, never one that opens everything.
* **Revoking does not delete.** The row stays, with the date it was stopped, so
  *"why did the board pack break on the 12th"* has an answer a year later.

### The one decision that was put to a proof and lost

The first version worked out **which utility a token belonged to from the token
itself**. A two-tenant test on the real database refused it in one line —
`brazosbend's token resolves to brazosbend — resolved to nothing` — because the
database's own isolation rule hides every row from a request that has not yet
said which utility it is for. Making that version work would have meant reading
the credential **outside** the isolation rule, which is the exact door this
table exists to keep shut.

So it was rebuilt the other way round: **the web address says which utility, and
the token only says who.** A token belonging to utility B, presented on utility
A's address, is not found and rejected — **it is not visible at all**. That is
the database refusing, not our code remembering to check.

⚠ **This could not have been caught by our normal tests.** They run on a
lightweight database that has no isolation rules at all, so the broken version
passed everything, green, on every machine.

### What a reviewer should check, in one sentence each

1. Neither half of the isolation rule mentions *"no utility"* — unlike the
   report catalogue, where that is deliberate, a credential with no utility
   would be usable by all of them.
2. `FORCE` is on, so the rule applies even to the account that owns the table.
3. Creating and revoking a token is **administrators only**, and a token cannot
   create another token.

### What was NOT decided, and is one line if the PO wants it

The PO wrote *"Administrators only … M. Okonkwo creates it and hands Dana the
token + clerk"*, and Dana is a billing clerk. This ships as **an administrator
issues one and any staff member may hold and use it**. Whether a clerk may also
CREATE one was not assumed, because this is a credential.

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/reports/migrations/0004_p2_20_service_accounts.py` (the table
and its isolation rule, in one migration) ·
`06-backend/apps/reports/service_accounts.py` (the token and the named list) ·
`06-backend/apps/reports/service_account_auth.py` (how a token is checked) ·
`06-backend/apps/reports/models.py` (`ReportServiceAccount`) ·
`06-backend/apps/reports/api.py` (issue, revoke, and the per-report check).

**Proof:** `10-scripts/rep_p2_20_service_account_rls_proof.py` — ALL PASS on
PostgreSQL 16, 2026-09-27, two utilities, under a database role the isolation
rules genuinely apply to (it refuses to run as one they do not).

**Rollback:** revert the commit and reverse migration `reports.0004`. Nothing
else in the product reads this table, no screen shows it, and no existing
request path changes — a browser request carries no bearer token and takes the
same route it took yesterday.

## `rate_schedules` — the rate read, and why one report on it is refused

**Lane DS-SMALL · 2026-09-27 · CR-142-BRC07 · HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING**

**What this is, in plain English.** The Reports module can now list a utility's
rate schedules — each version of each schedule, when it took effect, when it
stopped, what its base charge is and who moved it. It is a reading screen's
data. It changes no price and it works nothing out.

**The one thing worth a human's attention, with its figure.** The compliance
report the design calls *Rate Change History* is **not being built on this**, and
that is a decision rather than an omission. The drawing puts **one component on
each line** — *Usage tier 1, 0.0142 → 0.0154, +8.5%* — and one rate schedule
version holds **many** components. A residential schedule with four usage tiers
that all move on 1 October is **four lines on the drawing and one line here**,
and there is only one price column, with nowhere to say which of the four it is.
Building it anyway would put one of four prices under a heading that says *the*
price, to four decimals, on a report an auditor reads. So it is refused by name
and the refusal says what a rate-change report would actually need.

**A second thing, and it is already ruled — no question is being re-asked.** The
drawing says this report should read from the audit log. The rating code has
said since it was written that a rate history read out of the audit log **loses
the "who changed it" column silently**, because the audit log is deleted on a
schedule and no kind of row is exempt from that (ruled 23 September). So the
name comes from the rate schedule's own record of who submitted, approved or
corrected it, and the audit log is not read at all.

**Nothing rounds anything.** A rate is stored to four decimals and is handed on
exactly as stored; the screen decides how to show it. That is deliberate: a
rounding done in this file would be a price change nobody signed.

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/rating/rate_schedules_dataset.py` (the whole read).

**Proof:** `10-scripts/ds_small_datasets_cost.py` on PostgreSQL 16, and
`06-backend/tests/test_rep_small_datasets.py`.

**Rollback:** delete the file. Nothing imports it yet — the Reports module's own
registration is a separate lane's commit — so removing it changes no screen, no
endpoint and no stored row.

## 2026-09-27 · lane DS-ACCOUNTS — three report reads, and five of eight reports refused rather than answered wrongly 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**In plain English, with the figures, and nothing here is an ID to go and look
up.**

We were asked to build the machinery behind **eight reports**: five on the
Customers side and three on the Compliance side. **Three of them now produce a
report. Five do not, and each one says why in its own words rather than showing
something that merely looks right.**

**THE THREE THAT WORK.**

*Account Census* — one row for every account, with the customer, the address,
the services, the status and the balance. A page of fifty comes back and the
four figures across the top are counted over the **whole** book and never over
the page, so they still say 1,947 when you are looking at fifty.

*Audit Trail* — one row for every recorded act, with who, what, before and
after. Three of its four tiles are real numbers; the fourth is the problem
below.

*Bill Delivery* — every bill that went out, on every channel, with what
happened to it. This one needed a whole new kind of report data that did not
exist; see below.

**THE FIVE THAT DO NOT, AND WHY — ONE SENTENCE EACH.**

*Account Activity* asks how many accounts opened, closed and transferred in a
month. That is a count of **things that happened**, and the data we were pointed
at is a list of **accounts that exist**. One account can move in and out twice
in a year; counting accounts would say one.

*Data Quality* lists the problems in a utility's records — *four accounts have
no address*, *sixty-one properties have no map point*. Each row is a **check**,
not an account. There is no account whose row reads *properties with no map
point, 61*, and the list of checks itself has never been written down anywhere
in this product.

*Plans & Discounts* asks what each account is signed up to. One account can be
on level pay **and** a payment plan **and** assistance at once — that is three
rows, with three instalments and three remaining balances, and an account-shaped
row has room for one of each. The drawing's own figures prove it: 184 + 84 + 50
comes to the 318 on the tile only because those are sign-ups, not people.

*Migration Assurance* compares what the old system held against what we loaded.
**The old system's figures are not in our database at all.** We keep how many
rows an import file had and when the cut-over was; we keep no money figure from
the old side, so *Opening balance 44,118.02* has nothing to compare against.

*Access Review* lists your staff, their roles and when each last signed in. We
were pointed at the audit trail for it — **and somebody who has never signed in
has never done anything, so they are not in the audit trail.** The tile that
says *never signed in: 1* is the whole point of that report, and reading it from
the trail would make it say **0** over a real dormant login. Everything it needs
is already on the staff records themselves.

**THE TENTH KIND OF REPORT DATA — WHAT WE DID AND WHY.**

*Bill Delivery* was pointed at the audit trail and its own drawing says it comes
from **notifications**. The trail could not have served one column of it: **no
record is written when an email bounces** — a bounce is the mail provider
telling us something, not an act anybody performed. So we built the tenth kind
rather than bending the ninth, and every column it draws was already stored:
the channel, the address, when it was sent, what happened and why.

**ONE THING WE CANNOT DO AND WANT YOUR DECISION ON.**

The Audit Trail draws four tiles and one of them is **Money events**. We cannot
produce it honestly: the trail records a clerk correcting a cheque number and a
clerk changing a setting in **exactly the same shape**, with nothing saying
which moved money. We could guess from the name of each act — that would count
a bill being printed and miss a deposit being waived, and it would print the
guess on a compliance report as a fact. **So the tile shows a dash with a stated
reason, and the other three tiles are real.** The question — build the list of
money acts, keep the dash, or take the tile off — is in the register and is for
you.

**FOUR THINGS WE CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, EACH WITH ITS FIGURE.**

1. **The status words.** A utility can call its account statuses anything it
   likes, in its own language. Every count here is worked out from what a status
   **does** (bills / bills base only / closed), never from the word. Our test
   fixture names them in French on purpose, so a count written against the
   English word measures **0 active accounts over three live ones** and the test
   goes red.
2. **Bounced post and email.** There are **three** spellings of a bounce in this
   product — an old one kept lawful on purpose, and a hard and a soft one added
   on 17 September. A tile counting one of them reports **0** here. The file
   refuses to load at all if a tenth delivery outcome is ever added without
   being counted.
3. **Letters still in the building.** A letter to a bad address is written,
   marked held and never posted. It is **not** in the sent figure, so the
   delivery percentage is struck against what actually left — six of eight in
   our fixture, not eight of eight.
4. **The address.** No report here keeps its own copy of an address. The census
   walks to the property; the delivery report shows **the address that was
   actually on the envelope**, because a letter returned *no such address* whose
   address has since been corrected must not render against the corrected one
   and read as a live fault at a good address.

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/customers/accounts_dataset.py` (the whole read) ·
`06-backend/apps/audit/audit_log_dataset.py` (the whole read) ·
`06-backend/apps/notifications/notifications_dataset.py` (the whole read).
**Nothing is registered and no screen changed** — `apps/reports/datasets.py` and
`queries.py` belong to another lane this session, so what needs registering is

## 2026-09-27 · lane DS-ACCOUNTS — AMENDMENT: the census now shows an account as it WAS, and the earlier row said that was impossible (`DEF-REP-6889`, `2.371.0`)

**In plain English.** The row above says the Account Census cannot show what an
account's class and status **were** on a past date, only what they are today,
and it gives a reason. **That reason is wrong and the census now does it
properly.**

**What happened.** The build brief says, as a statement of fact, that the
customers module keeps no history of these values. We checked that the way the
brief checked it — looking in the same file — found the same nothing, and took
it as confirmed. **The history is kept; it is in a different file.** It was
built the day before ours, on 26 September.

**Why that mattered.** A census for June would have shown every account's class
and status as they read **today**. An account that moved from Residential to
Commercial in September would have appeared as Commercial in June's figures —
and it would have come with a confident explanation of why that could not be
helped. **A wrong number with an excuse attached is worse than a bare wrong
number, because the excuse stops the next person looking.**

**What is built now, in four parts.**

1. The census reads the history for a whole page in **one** question to the
   database. The existing reader answers for one account at a time, which would
   be fifty questions for a page of fifty and forty thousand for a download.
2. Every row says which basis it is on — *as it was* or *as it reads today* —
   so a report covering a period that straddles the day history started is
   readable rather than misleading.
3. The counts across the top and the class and status filters follow the **same
   date as the rows**. A filter on today's value would have served a row under a
   *Residential* chip whose own class column said *Commercial*; a count on
   today's value would not have added up to the rows beneath it. Neither is an
   error anyone would have spotted.
4. Where there is no history for a date, the report says **how many** rows fell
   back — *12 of the 50 served* — rather than a warning that would be true of
   every report forever.

**And the old value, for dates before the history began, is gone.** It survives
only in the audit trail, which is deleted on schedule with no exceptions. The
report does not claim otherwise and neither does this row.

**What we checked so it does not spread:** we grepped the whole repository for
the brief's sentence. The only two places it appeared were our own file, and
both are fixed.

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:** `06-backend/apps/customers/accounts_dataset.py`
(the as-at section, `_as_was_for`, `_behaviour_q`, the class/status filters, the
row's `attribute_basis`).

**Proof:** `tests/test_rep_accounts_dataset.py::test_as_was_wins_where_a_history_period_covers_the_date`
— the same account reads *Résidentiel · Ouvert* in June and *Commercial · Soldé*
today, and June's active count is 3 where today's is 2 — and
`::test_a_class_filter_on_an_as_at_read_matches_what_the_row_shows` — the
as-was chip returns 1 row and today's returns 0.

**Rollback:** the earlier row's rollback still applies — delete the file.
Nothing imports it yet.

## 2026-09-27 · lane MET-IDX — the work-order RAISE DATE gets an index (`DEF-MET-6881`, `metering/0062`, `2.371.1`) 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**In plain English, with the figure.** Our work-order reports open sorted by the
date the job was raised. The database had no index on that date, so every time
a supervisor opened one of those reports the database read **all 40,025 work
orders** of a 40,000-account utility and sorted them from scratch — and on the
later pages it ran out of memory to sort in and wrote **4,288 kB of scratch data
to disk** to finish. This change adds one index on that date. Measured on a real
PostgreSQL 16.13 with 40,025 work orders in one utility, median of 7 timings
after a discarded warm-up:

| what was timed | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| the page of rows, first page | **0.0655s** | **0.0034s** | 19× faster |
| the page of rows, last page (801) | **0.0953s** | **0.0259s** | 3.7× faster |
| the whole screen call, first page | 0.156s | 0.131s | 1.19× |
| the whole screen call, last page | 0.876s | 0.694s | 1.26× |

**Both rows are true and the second is the honest one.** The index fixes the
fetching of the rows. The rest of what that screen costs is the six summary
tiles at the top, which add up every one of the 40,025 orders on purpose so the
totals match the whole report and not the page you are looking at. No index
makes that cheaper. So the screen gets faster, not instant, and anybody
measuring it later and finding a tenth of a second has not found a missing
index.

**What it costs.** The index measured **2,320 kB** beside a **13 MB** table —
17% — and it is the fifth index on this table. It is paid for when a work order
is raised, a few hundred times a day at that size, and it is earned back on
every dispatcher's screen and every report run.

**What was put to a proof and did not hold.** The defect report says the
disk-spilling sort happens *"on every page including page 1"*. On this server
page 1 sorted **in memory** (38 kB) because only the top 50 rows had to be kept;
only the deep pages spilled. Page 1 was still reading all 40,025 rows, so the
fix is the same, but the report's wording is corrected in the migration's own
docstring so a later reader does not check page 1, see no spill, and conclude
the problem is gone.

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/metering/migrations/0062_def_met_6881_work_orders_raised.py`
(migration ordering is a 🔒 sensitive path) and the five-line index declaration
in `06-backend/apps/metering/connections.py` (`WorkOrder.Meta.indexes`).

**What a reviewer should check, in one sentence each.**
1. The index leads with the tenant column, like the four already on this table,
   or row-level security makes it useless.
2. It declares no direction, so one index serves both the newest-first default
   and the oldest-first toggle — both were measured and neither sorts.
3. It ends in the row id, because two orders raised in the same second would
   otherwise be able to swap pages and show one twice.
4. It adds no limit of any kind on anything (`NFR-5`), and the same index serves
   a larger utility better, not worse.

**Proof:** `06-backend/tests/test_def_met_6881_work_order_raise_index.py` — seven
cases, four of which were shown to fail first against the tree without the index
and are quoted in that file's own header. The sibling suite
`06-backend/tests/test_rep_small_datasets.py` passes 25 of 25 with this change
in. The migration was applied forward, reversed back to `0061`, and applied
forward again against a real PostgreSQL 16.13 database; the index is present
after each forward and absent after the reverse.

**Rollback:** `manage.py migrate metering 0061` and remove the five-line
declaration from `WorkOrder.Meta.indexes`. Nothing reads the index by name
except the test above.

## 2026-09-27 · Reports · a scheduled report now tells the people it names, with a link (`CR-142-BRC07` `P4.10`, `2.376.0`, lane REP-P4-REST)

**What was shown to the Product Owner, in plain English with a figure.**

Until today, a schedule did everything except the last step. Dana sets the AR
ageing report to run on the first of the month and picks herself. On 1 October
at 06:00 it runs, the file lands on the History tab — **and nobody is told.**
The list of people a schedule names was stored, checked, and then never read
again by anything.

From this build, that same schedule writes **one message** for Dana. Its words
are: *"Hi Dana, AR Ageing ran on 1 October 2026 and its file is ready. Open it
here: ‹a link to the run›. The file is kept until 4 October. After that the run
stays in your history and you can run it again from there."*

**Three things about it that were decided here and are worth a minute of
anyone's time:**

1. **It carries a LINK and never the file.** A spreadsheet of the utility's
   customers, their addresses and their balances, sitting on an email, can be
   forwarded by anybody who receives it. The link only opens for somebody who
   can already sign in to that utility. **It cannot be edited out** — the system
   refuses to save a version of this message that has no link in it.
2. **A report that FAILS tells nobody.** The schedule stays in the list marked
   *Failing* so a person looks, and no email goes out claiming a file is ready.
   An email saying *your report is ready* about a run that errored is worse than
   silence, because the person stops looking.
3. **It can be switched off**, like every other message — *Scheduled report
   ready — email* is a row on Settings → Notifications. Switched off, no message
   is written at all.

**And what is NOT true yet, stated rather than implied:** nothing is sent.
Email delivery ships with all email in a later release. What exists today is the
message, queued and ready.

**The one thing we are asking for.** The four sentences above are **our words,
not agreed ones**. No signed document says what this message should say.
`OQ-REP-12757` is the question, written in plain English with the message quoted
in full. A utility can edit the wording on Settings whichever way it is
answered; what is being asked is what the DEFAULT should say.

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/notifications/report_events.py` (the writer) ·
`06-backend/apps/reports/delivery.py` (the reconcile and the link) ·
`06-backend/apps/reports/notifications_seam.py` (the boundary) ·
`06-backend/apps/notifications/catalogs.py` (`email_scheduled_report`) ·
`06-backend/apps/notifications/seed_templates.py` (`SCHEDULED_REPORT_BODY`) ·

**Proof:**

## 2026-09-27 · `P6.11` — THE FIRST THREE JOINING READS, and ONE DRAWN HEADER THIS LANE DID NOT MATCH (lane REP-P6-JOIN, `2.377.0`)

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/identity/access_review.py` ·
`06-backend/apps/metering/read_import_log.py` ·
`06-backend/apps/customers/account_activity.py` ·
`07-frontend/src/features/reports/ReportViewerPage.tsx` (the cell renderer).

**None of these is a 🔒 sensitive path** — no RLS policy, no rating math, no
idempotency key, no ledger posting, no money rounding, no migration, no webhook
key. They are read models and a renderer, and nothing here is flagged
`HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING`. This row exists for the **three product-visible
decisions** inside them, each stated in plain English with its figure, because
a reviewer cannot be expected to find them in 1,700 lines.

### 1 · A DRAWN COLUMN HEADER IS NOT MATCHED, AND THAT IS THE ONE TO LOOK AT

The Access Review drawing (p066) heads a column **LAST SIGN-IN**. We ship
**LAST ACTIVE**.

**The worked case.** A billing clerk signs in on 25 September 2025 and not
again. On 25 September 2026 a compliance officer opens the report. The only
table holding a literal sign-in is `sessions`, and a session is capped at
twelve hours (`BR-IDN-026`) — so `MAX(sessions.created_at)` for that person is
**nothing**, and a column headed *Last sign-in* would print **Never** beside a
real returning user. On the one report whose purpose is to find the account
nobody uses, that is the report manufacturing the failure it exists to catch.
`tenant_memberships.last_active_at` is durable and its own column comment
already reads *"null renders 'Never'"*.

**Ruled by the coordinator on 2026-09-27**, verbatim: *"Serve `last_active_at`
and label it what it is… If the PO wants the drawn wording back, that is a copy
change and a small one."* **If the Product Owner wants LAST SIGN-IN back, it is
eleven catalogue strings and nothing else** — the served value does not move,
because there is no other value to serve.

### 2 · A BOOLEAN AND A TIMESTAMP NOW RENDER AS WORDS AND DATES, PRODUCT-WIDE

`APPROVES MONEY` is the first **boolean** any report has served and `LAST
ACTIVE` the first **timestamp**. Until this commit they reached the screen as
the literal `true` / `false` and as
`2026-09-27T12:32:27.923853+00:00`. **Both were photographed, not caught by any
test** (hard-won law 6). `ReportCell` now renders a boolean as a catalogue word
and an ISO *instant* through `DateCell` in the tenant's own format.

⚠ **IT IS DECIDED BY TYPE, SO IT APPLIES TO ALL 46 REPORTS.** That is the point
to check: a later report serving a boolean gets the same treatment without
anyone remembering, and no seventh hand-typed column map was added (`P0.7`
deleted six).

### 3 · WHAT THIS LANE DELIBERATELY DID **NOT** CHANGE, AND WHY

A plain **calendar date** — `2026-09-27` — still renders as stored, on every
one of the 46 reports. Routing those through `DateCell` too would change how
every report prints a date, product-wide, on one lane's authority. **It is
reported rather than done**, so it can be decided for all 46 at once.

**Also not done, and this one changed under the lane:** `BR-REP-023` restricts
who may RUN Access Review, and **`P5.9` landed in `c79edc4c8` while this wave
was being re-derived** — `apps/reports/role_gate.py` now enforces it
server-side. This read model still adds no authorisation check of its own:
wrong layer, and a second check is how two answers to *who may see this* come
to exist. ⚠ **The constant that recorded this said the rule was UNENFORCED and
was amended rather than deleted or left** — a stale claim on a security rule is
the worst kind, and it is the one thing here that no test in this module could
have caught, because it is a claim about another module's state.

### 4 · THE FIGURES, MEASURED RATHER THAN ESTIMATED

Real PostgreSQL 16, `10-scripts/p6_join_cost.py`, median of 3 after a discarded
warm-up, on a tenant holding **40,007 memberships · 4,024 import batches over
80,201 file rows · 40,077 lifecycle events**:

| | first page | last page | export | statements |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R36 Access Review | 0.252s | 0.370s (page 801) | 8.622s · 40,007 rows | **2**, at per=50 AND per=200 |
| R32 Read Import Log | 0.954s | 0.955s (page 81) | 1.263s · 4,024 rows | **2**, at per=50 AND per=200 |
| R23 Account Activity | 0.138s | 0.167s (page 802) | 6.304s · 40,077 rows | **7**, at per=50 AND per=200 |

A web worker is given **60 seconds** (`docker-entrypoint.sh`). The flat
statement count across two page sizes is the check that matters: it is what
says the label reads are batched per page rather than one per row.

**Tenant isolation:** `10-scripts/p6_join_rls_proof.py` — six tables, ENABLE and
FORCE on all six, run as a role that is neither SUPERUSER nor BYPASSRLS, with
the neighbour's rows planted and **proved visible from the neighbour's own
context first**, so the probe cannot be measuring an empty table.

**Rollback:** revert the commit. There is no migration and no data to lose. The
one ordering that matters: do not remove `queries.KEY_STREAMS` while leaving a
per-key viewer behind — that combination leaves three exports reaching the
DATASET's generator and writing a valid-looking file of the wrong report's rows.

## 2026-09-27 · Reports · a utility can say how long its downloads are kept (`CR-142-BRC07` `P4.6` + `P5.12`, `2.379.0`, lane REP-P5-SETTINGS)

**What was shown to the Product Owner, in plain English with a figure.**

Until today, every utility on this product kept its generated files for exactly
**three days**, and no screen anywhere said so or could change it. The rule we
signed on 8 August says *"generated files are retained 3 days by default,
**tenant-configurable**"* — and only the first half of that sentence was ever
built. The second half is built now.

Settings → Configure → Reference data has a new **Reports** section. It has two
cards today:

* **File retention** — the number of days. Three to start with, which is where
  every utility already is, so nothing changes for anybody until somebody moves
  it. The smallest allowed is **one day**; there is no largest, because we do
  not put ceilings in this product.
* **Default format** — what a download is when nobody asks for anything else.
  **CSV is the only answer we can give today**, because there is no PDF maker
  anywhere in this product, so the control shows one option and says so rather
  than pretending there is a choice to make.

**The one consequence worth a minute of anyone's time, because it surprises
people.** Retention is worked out from when a report RAN, and it is not written
down on the run. So if Dana changes it from three days to one on a Wednesday
afternoon, **yesterday's file stops being downloadable the moment she presses
Save.** Nothing is deleted by that save and no report re-runs; the older runs
simply show as expired and can be run again from the history. **This is not
written on the screen** — our own rule puts explanations at zero words — so it
lives in the code and in this row, and the form says only *"Files are kept for
3 days."*

**And a line on the Reports history screen had quietly become false.** Under the
table it said *"Files are kept for 3 days"* — typed into all eleven languages,
over a number a utility can now change. It now states that utility's own number,
and **for a System Admin it carries a link straight to the control**, one click
away. A Billing Clerk sees the sentence and no link, because the form behind it
is not theirs to open; nothing explains why, for the same reason as above.

**What is NOT built, stated rather than implied.** The drawing puts **four**
cards in that section. Two of them — *Report groups* and *Delivery* — are not
here. Report groups needs a list screen behind it that does not exist yet.
Delivery is drawn as a list of where a schedule sends its file, and today those
people are named on each schedule rather than in one place; making a single list
of them is a decision about how the product should work, not a missing piece of
code, and it is written up in `CR-142-BRC07` §14.5 for whoever takes it.
**Neither is on screen as a "coming soon" card** — a promise with nobody's name
on it is worse than an absence.

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/tenancy/migrations/0053_p4_6_reports_settings.py` (one jsonb
column on `tenant_settings`, defaulted from the registry by dotted path exactly
as `0004` does for the other five families).

**Proof:** `tests/test_cr142_p4_6_reports_settings.py`. The one case a reviewer
should read is
`::test_a_short_window_sweeps_only_its_own_tenants_files` — every utility's
generated files live in ONE directory on the server, and the moment retention
became a per-utility number, a sweep run at one utility's one-day setting could
have deleted another utility's two-day-old file. That case plants both files,
sweeps at one day for one utility, and asserts **the neighbour's file is still
there**. And `::test_screen_5_1_states_this_utilitys_own_number` asserts the
sentence on the history screen carries the served figure rather than a three
typed into a catalogue.

**Rollback:** `migrate tenancy 0052` and revert the commit. The column goes and
with it every utility's override; everybody returns to three days, which is
where they are today. Nothing is deleted by the migration going backwards — no
file, no run, no schedule — and no other table references the column.

## The bill now charges the base charge code the rate schedule names · 2026-09-27 · 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**Files flagged `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING`:** `06-backend/apps/rating/selectors.py`
(`pricing_inputs_for_version`, `base_charge_from_charge_code`,
`_named_code_cannot_answer`) · `06-backend/apps/billing/gather.py`
(`_base_charge_code_for`, `_tariff_config_for`). Both are 🔒 sensitive paths:
rating math on a money path, across a module boundary.

### WHAT A UTILITY COULD NOT DO YESTERDAY, WITH THE NUMBER

A water utility has three charge codes ticked as the water base charge — say a
standard one at **$8.00 a month**, a second at **$19.75** and a third at
**$34.00** — and all three are available to every kind of customer. On the first
step of the rate schedule somebody picked the **$19.75** one, which is the whole
reason that box is on the screen.

**Every bill on that schedule refused**, with these words on the run screen:

> 3 base charge codes for water. Scope them on Charge codes.

The refusal itself is right in general: where nobody has said which code owns
the base, charging one of three would mean the order of a list decides what a
customer pays. **But somebody HAD said.** The choice was saved, the schedule's
own screen showed it, the ruled pricing chain honoured it — and the part of the
product that actually produces bills was never told. It asked *"which charge
code is water's base?"*, got three answers, and stopped.

**The effect on a real customer: a move-out final bill could not be produced at
all.** Nothing could be issued, and nothing said why the choice on the screen
was not being used.

### WHAT IT DOES NOW

The bill charges **$19.75** — the code that was picked. Not $8.00 (the first in
the list) and not $34.00 (the last); those two figures are in the test on
purpose, because they are what a bill would show if the product went back to
guessing.

### THE JUDGMENT A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH, AND IT IS ABOUT THE FAILURE DIRECTION

Once the product honours the choice, it has to decide what to do when the chosen
code **cannot answer** — somebody retired it, or took the base tick off it, or
narrowed it to commercial customers only, after the schedule was pointed at it.

There were two options and we took the second:

* **fall back to whichever other code calls itself the base.** A bill is always
  produced. It is a perfectly ordinary-looking bill for a figure the rate
  schedule's own screen does not show, and nobody can see it is wrong.
* **refuse that one account, naming the code.** Chosen. The clerk reads
  *"BASE-W-COM cannot price water here. Change it on the rate schedule."*,
  every other account in the run still bills, and the repair is on the screen
  where the choice was made.

This is the same answer the ruled pricing chain already gives, and it is the
answer the product already gives when somebody tries to ACTIVATE a schedule
pointing at a code like that — so what changed is only that a code broken
*afterwards* now fails the same way as one broken *beforehand*.

### WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED, AND THE FIGURE THAT PROTECTS IT

* **A schedule that names nothing behaves exactly as it did.** Three base codes
  and nobody choosing still refuses, in the same six words. That case is a test
  of its own and it passed before this change and after it.
* **No bill moves on any tenant today.** Every rate schedule version in the
  product stores that choice EMPTY, so the new question is asked with an empty
  answer and the old route answers, unchanged.
* **A utility that has not adopted charge-code base charges at all** — no code
  ticked as a base — still bills from its plan, exactly as before.

### WHAT A REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE ASSUME WRONGLY

That this makes the product more forgiving. It does not. It makes it charge the
figure a person chose, and it REFUSES in one new case that used to be met with
either a misleading sentence or a quietly wrong figure.

### ONE THING A REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE HAVE TO TAKE ON TRUST

**The rate schedule's own screen already behaves the way the bill now does.**
`07-frontend/src/features/rating/baseCharge.ts` resolves the named code first
and, where the named code is not in the catalogue, draws NOTHING rather than the
inferred code — its own words: *"falling back here would draw one code on screen
while the bill uses another, with neither visibly wrong."* Until today the
screen kept that promise and the bill did not. So this change does not invent a
posture; it makes the bill keep the promise the screen was already making.

### HOW IT WAS PROVED

**Every case was run RED first, on the branch tip, through `pytest` — the
harness that runs it — and each red is quoted on the case it belongs to.** The
three that reproduce the reported failure:

    apps.billing.gather.GatherProblem: 3 base charge codes for water. Scope them on Charge codes.
    KeyError: 'base_charge_code'
    AssertionError: assert 'BASE-W-COM' in '2 base charge codes for water. Scope them on Charge codes.'

The first is the Product Owner's own sentence, word for word.

⚠ **AND TWO OF THE NINE CASES WERE A CHECK THAT COULD NOT FAIL UNTIL THEY WERE
FIXED, WHICH IS WORTH A REVIEWER'S MINUTE.** The two that prove a retired or
un-ticked code refuses PASSED on the tip — green over a live path that was
quietly billing `$8.00` — because with the ruled `R3,R4` chain served, which is
the shipped default, the CHAIN refuses first and the test never sees what the
billing path does. They now state the chain off, and they are red on the tip:

    Failed: DID NOT RAISE GatherProblem

After the fix: **9 passed**, in `06-backend/tests/test_def_rat_5782_the_bill_
honours_the_named_base_code.py`.

**Files:** `06-backend/apps/rating/selectors.py` ·
`06-backend/apps/billing/gather.py` · the test file above. Shipped as
**`2.380.1`**, commit `81f007055`.

**Rollback:** revert that commit. There is no migration, no data is written and
nothing is stored differently; the column the binding lives in
(`tariff_versions.base_charge_code`) has existed since `rating/0037` on
2026-09-19 and is untouched here. Reverting returns every affected bill to the
refusal it produced yesterday — which is why the rollback is safe and also why
it is not a fix.

**Printed clerk-visible before and after:**
`scratchpad/po-shots/base-code-billing/what-the-clerk-sees.md`.

**And it was run on real PostgreSQL 16 as well as on the SQLite suite**, which
is CLAUDE.md hard-won law 14 — the default suite runs on SQLite and cannot see a
class of database behaviour at all. Red first, then green, on both:

| | red (branch tip) | green (after) |
|---|---|---|
| SQLite suite | 3 failed, 6 passed + 2 more red on the live path | **9 passed** |
| PostgreSQL 16 | 3 failed, 6 passed (26m39s) | **9 passed** (1m26s) |

**The neighbouring suites:** the golden ENGINE suite is **23 passed, 1 xfailed**,
and `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` reports **33 PASS, 0 FAIL** — both unchanged
by this work. `G64` reports the engine-verified figure unmoved at **14 of 61**:
this change adds no golden test and removes none, so no signed billing figure
moved and none needed to.

### WHAT WAS FOUND BESIDE IT, AND IT IS THE MOST URGENT THING IN THIS ROW

Running the base-resolution neighbourhood turned up **28 tests that have been
red on this branch for days and that nobody has read** — `DEF-RAT-6980`. They
are NOT this lane's: every one of them reproduces identically with
`apps/rating/selectors.py` and `apps/billing/gather.py` restored to their
pre-change content, and 17 of them are still red with `apps/rating/services.py`
restored to before this morning's commit too.

Eighteen of them are one cause: `rate_plans.account_type_id` became
`account_type_ids` on 2026-09-23 and three test fixtures still post the old
name, so the plan writer refuses them by name. Nine more serve no percentage
from the rate-change impact endpoint. One says the seeded price list totals
`$799.95` where it now totals `$829.95` — **a $30.00 difference in the shipped
sample data that nobody has explained**.

**None of this blocks the fix above**, and that is exactly why it is written
down here: a lane running one file sees green, because the file beside it that
fails 17 out of 17 is in no suite that gates a merge.

**AMENDED 2026-09-27, AFTER WALKING THE SCREEN IN A BROWSER.** Three further
things were found by looking at it and are worth putting to the PO in the same
plain words:

**5 · The screen was walked at 1440 and at 1280 and three faults were found that
every automated check had passed over.** Two were ours and are fixed: the bottom
panel's last two columns were touching, so the heading read *DifferenceResult*
and a row read *$0.00Foots*; and the *Service mix* panel was an empty box for a
month with no revenue, which a reader cannot tell apart from a panel that failed
to load — it now says *No revenue in this period.* The third was the layout at
1280: the panels sat two-across and every money figure wrapped onto its own
line, so they now sit one-across below 1440.

**6 · ONE FIGURE ON THIS SCREEN WILL BE WRONG UNTIL ANOTHER TEAM FIXES A REPORT,
AND WE HAVE LEFT IT VISIBLE ON PURPOSE.** Under *Outstanding* the screen reads
*0.00% against the comparison*, and it will read that for ever. The reason is
not this screen: **AR Ageing gives the same answer for every date you ask it
for.** Asked as at 30 September 2026, 30 September 2025 and 31 January 2024 it
returns the identical five figures — $7,678.46 in 31–60 days, $693.60 in 61–90,
$8,372.06 in total, across 26 accounts, all three times. So comparing this
month's receivable with last year's compares a number with itself.

**We could have hidden that by not drawing the comparison on that one tile, and
we decided not to.** Hiding it would put a defect in another team's report
behind our wording, and that tile would then be quietly different from the three
beside it for a reason nobody could find. It is written down as `DEF-PAY-6940`
and it is theirs to fix; the moment they do, this tile starts telling the truth
with nothing changed here.

## 2026-09-27 · Reports · a scheduled file may now leave the product, by a link that dies in four hours (`CR-142-BRC07` `P4.14`, `reports/0009`, `2.383.0`, lane REP-P4-LAST) 🔒 HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING

**WHAT WAS BUILT, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** A utility's administrator can now set up a
place for a scheduled report to be delivered to, and point a schedule at it. The
one kind of place that works today is **a web address we hand out** — a machine
such as Power BI fetches that address and gets the file. Nobody has to be signed
in to use it, which is the whole point and also the whole risk, so this row is
about exactly what that address lets somebody do.

**WHAT THE ADDRESS LETS SOMEBODY DO, AND FOR HOW LONG.** It gets them **one
file** — the report that one scheduled run produced — belonging to **one
utility**, for **four hours**, and they can only read it. They cannot list
anything, change anything, or reach a second file. Anyone who has the address
can fetch that one file, which is why it dies after four hours and why it is
only ever handed to a destination an administrator set up.

**THE FOUR HOURS ARE THE PRODUCT OWNER'S OWN NUMBER, NOT THIS LANE'S.** They
ruled it on **30 August 2026**, in these words: *"dont expire it in minutes -
exprise it in 3 or 4 hours"*. It was ruled then about the links that let a
customer open a bill we posted them. The same figure is used here rather than a
new one being chosen, and the code **reads it from the place that ruling lives**
instead of writing `4 hours` down a second time — so if it is ever re-signed,
both move together and there is no second copy to disagree.

**THE ONE THING A REVIEWER SHOULD PUSH BACK ON IF THEY DISAGREE:** whether four
hours is right for a *machine collecting a file overnight* as well as for a
*person opening their bill*. A nightly collector that is down for five hours
will find the link dead and will wait for the next night's. That is deliberate —
a longer life is a longer window for a leaked address — but it is the one
judgment in this row that a person might reasonably settle differently, and it
was not put to the PO as a fresh question because the figure was already ruled.

**WHAT WAS NOT BUILT, AND WHY IT IS A QUESTION RATHER THAN A GAP.** The Product
Owner's ruling names two ways a file could go out: this web address, **and
SFTP** — dropping the file straight into a folder the utility owns. The SFTP
half is **refused, by name**, and is open as **`OQ-REP-12767`**.

The reason is worth a reviewer's minute, because it is not *we ran out of time*.
When a program connects to somebody's folder over SFTP it has to decide whether
it is really talking to their machine. The convenient answer — *trust whatever
answers* — means that if somebody manages to impersonate the utility's server,
**the file goes to them, the transfer succeeds, and our own log records it as
delivered**. There is no error, nothing to notice, and nothing to find
afterwards. The file in question is a report like the debtor list: **412 names,
addresses and balances.** The safe answer is that the utility tells us a
fingerprint for their server when they set the folder up — but that is a fact
only they have, and it changes what they are asked to type. **That is a decision
for a person, not for us**, so nothing was chosen and the option is not offered
at all rather than being offered and failing later.

**THE SENSITIVE PART, FOR THE 🔒 REVIEW.** `reports/0009` creates two tables and
puts their row-level-security policies **in the same migration**, so neither
table exists for even one deploy without a policy on it.

**What a reviewer should check, in one sentence:** that neither policy on either
table mentions `IS NULL`, and that `FORCE` is on for both — because a row with
no utility on it would be a destination *every* utility's files could be sent
to, and without `FORCE` the table's owner ignores the policy entirely.

**THE FIGURES A REVIEWER CAN CHECK.** Six different forgeries of the address are
each tried and each refused, in `tests/test_cr142_p4_14_signed_delivery.py`:
changing which file it names, changing which utility it names, extending its own
expiry by a day, using it four hours and one second after it was made, altering
its signature by one character, and presenting a signature from a different part
of the product. The successful case is **one** test and the refusals are **six**,
deliberately — a checker that let everything through would pass the successful
case just as well as a correct one does.

**WHAT WAS NOT PROVED, COUNTED RATHER THAN PASSED OVER.** The browser walk and
the two-utility database proof were **not completed by this lane**. The machine
was running twenty other test processes at a load average of 45; the seeded
database those proofs need was still being built after an hour, and a single
type-check of the front end took over thirty-five minutes. What *was* proved is
listed above and in `CR-142-BRC07` §16.6. **This row states the gap rather than
leaving a reader to assume the proofs happened.**

## 2026-09-27 · Portal · a landlord sees their own account at a property and nobody else's (`CR-142-BRC07` `P4.15`, `CWP-078`, `2.383.0`, lane REP-P4-LAST)

**WHAT WAS BUILT, WITH THE PRODUCT OWNER'S OWN WORKED EXAMPLE.** At **1408 Elm
Street** there are five accounts: four flats and the owner's account for the
building's shared supply. In the customer portal the **owner now sees one row —
their own `$69.60` of common-area charges** — and does not see Unit 3's
`$100.00`, or any of the other three. A tenant signing in sees their own flat
and does **not** see the owner's `$69.60`. This is the PO's ruling of
**4 September 2026**, option **(a)**, and the Reports brief states it again as
law: *"Staff see it as drawn. In the customer portal a landlord sees their own
master account only."* **Staff are unaffected** — they still see the whole
property, as they already did.

**THE ONE DESIGN POINT A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH.** The obvious way to build this
is to run the staff report and then drop the rows that are not yours. That was
**not** done, and the difference matters: it would mean all five accounts'
balances are fetched and sit in memory, with only the last step keeping four of
them off the screen. **The screen never asks what is at the property.** It asks
which of *your* accounts are there, starting from the list of accounts your
sign-in already holds. There is no wider question being asked and then narrowed.

**A SECOND FACT WE DECIDED NOT TO SHOW, AND IT IS A JUDGMENT.** The staff report
has a fourth figure at the top: **how many flats in the building were billed this
month** — `4` at 1408 Elm Street. That is a fact about other people rather than
money belonging to the reader, so it is **not sent to the portal at all**. A
landlord almost certainly knows how many flats they own, so this costs them
nothing; the reason for leaving it out is that it would be the only place in the
portal where a figure counted people the reader has been ruled out of seeing.
**A reviewer who thinks a landlord should see it can have it back** — it is one
figure, and nothing else depends on the choice.

**AND THE SCREEN SAYS NOTHING ABOUT ANY OF THIS.** There is no line explaining
whose balances are shown or why a neighbour's is absent. That is deliberate and
is the standing rule about on-screen wording: the reasons a product works a
certain way belong in the code and the records, never on the page. A test checks
that the page contains none of the words a well-meaning explanation would use.

**THE FIGURES A REVIEWER CAN CHECK.** The four amounts in the tests are the
ruling's own: Unit 3 charged **196.00**, paid **96.00**, closing **100.00**; the
owner's common areas **69.60**. Both directions are checked — the owner must not
see the tenant's `100.00`, and the tenant must not see the owner's `69.60` — and
each check looks at **the whole page and the whole server answer**, not at one
column, because a figure that leaks usually leaks through a total or a heading
rather than through the column somebody thought about.

**ONE THING A REVIEWER WOULD OTHERWISE HAVE TO TAKE ON TRUST.** The check that
matters was **shown to fail first**. The tenant's row was added to the owner's
data, exactly as a leaking server would send it, and the test failed naming the
figure: *expected '1408 Elm StreetAccounts1Charged$69.60…' not to contain
'$100.00'*. It was then put back and passes.

**WHAT WAS NOT PROVED.** The same two proofs named in the row above — the
browser walk at phone and desktop width, and the two-utility database check —
were not completed, for the same reason. The screen's own tests run and pass;
what is missing is the photograph and the database-level isolation run.

## 2026-09-27 · RAT-REDS-9 · THE WATER BASE CHARGE IN THE RATE-CHANGE TEST (`DEF-RAT-7140`)

**NOTHING SIGNED MOVED, AND THIS ROW EXISTS SO A REVIEWER CAN CHECK THAT FOR
THEMSELVES** rather than take it on trust. No file on the 🔒 list was edited:
`apps/rating/selectors.py`, `engine.py` and `apps/billing/gather.py` are
untouched, and the only change is to one test file's fixture.

**WHAT WAS WRONG, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH THE FIGURE.** We have a signed example
of a water rate rise: an eleven-thousand-gallon household pays **$59.00** a
month today and **$62.54** after a six-percent filing — **$3.54** more a month,
and the filing goes through because six percent is under our ten-percent bar.
The **$59.00** is the water used and nothing else; that utility charges **no**
monthly standing charge, and its rate plan says so by writing the standing
charge down as **$0.00**.

The test that guards that example was building a pretend utility two different
ways at once. Its rate plan said the standing charge is **$0.00**, and the same
utility's charge-code list said **$8.00** — the figure from our sample workbook.
The product noticed and refused to price anybody, which is **correct**: a bill
worked out from whichever of two disagreeing figures the software happened to
read first is a bug we have already paid for once. But the effect was that the
rate-change screen could show **no figures at all** — the percentage, the
average change, the yearly revenue and the approval answer all came back blank.

**WHAT WE CHANGED.** The pretend utility now says **$0.00** in both places. It
writes the standing charge down as zero on the charge-code list too, the same
way a real utility would type it on that screen. **The $8.00 sample figure is
unchanged and is still $8.00 everywhere else.** A standing charge of zero is
already something we let a utility have — rubbish collection and sewer are both
seeded at zero on the PO's own instruction from 27 August.

**THE FIGURES A REVIEWER CAN CHECK.** With the fixture saying zero once instead
of two things at once, the signed example comes back exactly: **$59.00 → $62.54**,
**+$3.54** a month, **+6.00%**, and the filing needs no second approval. Before
the change **8 of 15** checks in that file failed; after it **15 of 15** pass.

**WHAT IS BEING PUT TO A REVIEWER, AND IT IS ONE QUESTION.** Is it right that a
test standing behind a signed money example may state that utility's standing
charge as **$0.00** on the charge-code list, when our sample workbook's water
standing charge is **$8.00**? We decided yes — the $8.00 describes our sample
utility, not every utility, and the signed example is explicitly about one that
charges nothing. **If that is wrong, the thing to change is the signed example,
not the test**, and that is a finance re-sign rather than an edit.

**WHAT WAS NOT PROVED.** Nothing was clicked in a browser. This is a test-only
change and the rate-change screen was not opened; what is proved is the server
figures, twice measured, on the same commit.

## 2026-09-28 · The statement screen — three faults, and one decision a reviewer should see

**Lane REP-STMT-SCREEN.** `DEF-REP-7072`, `DEF-REP-7053`, `DEF-REP-7052`.
Files touched are listed in the lane report; nothing on the sensitive-path list
was edited — no RLS policy, no rating maths, no ledger posting, no money
rounding, no migration. Every figure below was measured on the running product
against real PostgreSQL 16, not inferred.

**WHAT WAS WRONG, in plain words.** A clerk opening one customer's statement and
then pressing **Edit** watched the table go from seven columns to one. The one
column left was *Reference*. Nothing was broken in either piece of the screen:
the editor was offering the columns the underlying data source lists, and the
report was accepting the columns that same data source lists — and a statement
is built by its own code, which produces seven columns of which only *Reference*
appears on that list. Two correct halves that share a single word.

**WHAT WE CHANGED, and the choice a reviewer may want to question.** Three
repairs were possible and we took the one that makes the fault unreachable
rather than the one that hides it: a report that is built by its own code now
states which columns it produces, and both the editor and the report read that
one statement. The two we did not take are recorded with their reasons in the
decision log of the same date; the short version is that one of them would have
removed the feature and the other would have silently thrown away what the clerk
asked for.

**THE FIGURES A REVIEWER CAN CHECK.** Opening the statement for account
`AC-2026-00032` over the whole of the books: **seven columns before pressing
Edit and seven after**, where it was seven and then **one**. The editor's own
count reads **7 of 7**, where it read **7 of 5**. The four tiles read Opening
`$0.00`, Charges `$470.59`, Payments `$470.59`, Closing `$0.00`, unchanged.

**THE SECOND FAULT — a download that existed and could not be reached.** The
statement could already produce a file, and no button anywhere offered it. The
button is now drawn, and it was proved by pressing it and fetching what came
back: the server accepted the request, the file came down as
**583 bytes of real CSV**, named
`brazosbend_statement_20000101-20991231_posting_20260927T2306.csv`, with every
money figure written to **two decimal places**.

**THE THIRD FAULT — no statement said whose money it was.** The page head now
reads **`AC-2026-00032 · Hugo Faulkner`**. The account's internal database
number is not on the screen anywhere; it stays in the address bar, which is
where the product already keeps that kind of thing. A browser check confirms the
number does not appear in the page's text.

**WHAT IS BEING PUT TO A REVIEWER, AND IT IS ONE QUESTION.** On a statement for
a UNIT rather than an account, the file that downloads carries two extra
columns — who was living there and which account the line was posted to — and
on an ordinary account statement **those two columns are present and empty**. We
decided that is right: one report produces one kind of file, and a reader
comparing two downloads six months apart should be able to tell an empty column
from one that was never offered. The product already does exactly this in three
other reports. **If that is wrong, the alternative is two different files for
one report**, and that is a bigger decision than this fix.

**WHAT WAS NOT PROVED.** The unit statement was not walked in a browser — no
seeded unit in the sample utility carries ledger lines — so the unit head and
the unit file's two extra columns are proved by test and by the server's own
answer, and not by clicking. The customer and premises statements do not exist
yet and are another lane's work; what this lane owes them is a single place to
register their own head, and that place is named in the lane report.

## 2026-09-28 · The Units screen's gap block becomes a filter — `2.387.0`, lane `MET-GAPFILTER`

**WHAT A CLERK CAN DO NOW THAT THEY COULD NOT DO YESTERDAY.** The Units screen
used to carry a second table above the list, headed *Missing services*, showing
the units that hold fewer services than their address offers. The Product Owner
asked why it was built that way rather than as a filter, and ruled: *"the Units
'Missing services' block — filter or leave it. - filter"*. They were then shown
a seven-line plan and answered *"this is correct"*.

So the block is gone, and on the units list there is now a **Missing services**
button on the same row as the search. Press it and the ordinary list narrows to
exactly those units. On our sample utility that is **43 units out of 131**, and
because it is an ordinary filter you can now do four things the block could not:
search within it — *Missing services* and *Main* together gives **25** — combine
it with the four filters that were already there, page it with the list instead
of a second set of page controls, and **tick those units and assign a plan to
them together**. That last one is the reason the change was asked for: a missing
service is a thing to fix, and the block was the one place in the product where
those exact units could not be acted on together.

**THE NUMBER IS ON SCREEN WHETHER OR NOT THE FILTER IS SWITCHED ON.** The button
reads **`Missing services 43 units`** with nothing engaged. That is deliberate
and it is the point of the whole change rather than a detail: the defect that
created the block exists because nobody could see the shortfall at all, and a
filter nobody switches on is just as invisible. Walked in a browser at both the
widths staff actually work at.

**WHAT IT COSTS, MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED.** On a real PostgreSQL database we
grew the utility to **40,000 units** — the top of the size we sell to — and
timed the screen's read. With the filter off it takes **1.20 seconds**; with it
on, **1.02**; the number beside the button costs **0.17**. The whole page is
**1.4 seconds** where a web request is allowed sixty, and it is the same 1.4
seconds on a utility twenty times smaller. Nothing here gets slower as a utility
grows, which is the thing we have been caught by before.

**THE ONE QUESTION FOR THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** They asked for two
new columns: *Offered here* and *Missing*. *Missing* is new and is shown. But
*Offered here* turns out to be the same list as the **Services** column the
screen already draws — both are what the address offers. So we have built it and
left it switched off, reachable from the columns button, rather than draw the
same thing twice on a row that already carries ten columns. **The question: the
Services column already shows what the address offers, so Offered here is the
same list under a second name — is one column enough?** Nothing is lost either
way; it is one tick in the columns list.

**WHAT ELSE WE FOUND AND DID NOT FIX.** With any filter applied, the row of
controls at the top of the Units screen spills onto a second line. It does that
today with the filters that were already there, so it is not caused by this
change; it is written down as a defect rather than fixed in passing, because the
fix belongs to the shared filter bar and would change every list in the product.

**WHAT WAS NOT PROVED.** Nothing on this screen was left unproved: the filter,
the count, the search combination, the paging and the bulk bar were all clicked
in a browser at 1440 and 1280, and the read was timed at 40,000 units. What is
NOT covered by any signature is the *Offered here* question above — it is asked
here, not decided.

## 2026-09-28 · A STALE FIGURE ON A PLAN NO LONGER STOPS A BILL — `apps/billing/gather.py`, `apps/rating/seams.py` 🔒

**Lane BIL-PLANBASE · version `2.387.1` · closes `DEF-BIL-7170` (critical) and
`DEF-CWP-7001` · branch `claude/kind-goldberg-k0acqg`**

**THE RULING IS THE SIGNATURE FOR THE RULE. THIS ROW IS WHAT IS BEING SIGNED FOR
THE IMPLEMENTATION**, and a signature covers only what was shown, so what was
built is written out below in plain sentences with the figures a person can redo.

### What was wrong, in one paragraph

A plan carries a base charge figure and so does the charge code bound to it. The
billing engine read BOTH, and when they disagreed it refused to produce the bill
at all, saying *"Two base charges for water. Clear 11.50 on the plan."* Under the
Product Owner's ruling of 28 September that is the wrong answer: the amount comes
from the charge code, and a number left behind on the plan by an old migration
may not stop a customer's bill. Any utility whose data carried a different figure
had **every bill for that service stopped**, and was told to go and clear a value
on a screen the product itself says does not set the price.

### The three cases, each proved on a real PostgreSQL 16 database

The demo utility Brazos Bend, account `AC-2026-00001`, September 2026. Water's
charge code says **$8.00 a month**.

| What the data says | What the bill did before | What it does now |
|---|---|---|
| the plan says **$8.00**, the code says **$8.00** | water base **$8.00** | water base **$8.00** — unchanged |
| the plan says **$11.50**, the code says **$8.00** | **no bill at all** — *"Two base charges for water. Clear 11.50 on the plan."* | water base **$8.00**; the plan's $11.50 is not read |
| nobody has declared a base charge code for water | the bill charged the plan's **$8.00** | **no bill** — *"No base charge for water. Declare one on Charge codes."* |

**The third row is the only bill this change stops that used to be produced, and
it is stopped on purpose.** The ruling says the plan's figure is never a source
and never a fallback, *not even when the charge code is silent*. A utility in
that state is told so in six words and pointed at the one screen that can fix it
— never at the plan, which would have them type a number nothing reads.

**What did NOT change, and was checked rather than assumed.** Where a utility has
picked a charge code on its rate schedule and that code cannot price this
customer, the bill still stops and still names the code: *"BASE-W-COM cannot
price water here. Change it on the rate schedule."* Where two codes both claim to
be water's base and nobody has chosen, it still stops: *"2 base charge codes for
water. Scope them on Charge codes."* And a base charge deliberately set to zero
still bills **$0.00**, exactly as ruled on 19 August.

### The demo utility's own bill

The demo data used to write **$8.00** onto the plan for *every* service while its
charge codes said water **$12.00**, sewer **$8.00** and trash **$9.00** — so two
of the three disagreed and the customer portal's *stop or restart* screen could
show **no standing charge at all**. It stops writing that figure. **The screen
shows a number again, and it is `$29.00` a month** — water `$12.00` + sewer
`$8.00` + trash `$9.00`, measured on the demo utility's own account at
1408 Elm St before and after: **`—` before, `$29.00` after**. Six tests that had
been failing for twelve days pass.

### What is NOT being asked for here

Whether the plan should stop **showing** a base charge is a separate question and
was deliberately not touched. The Product Owner ruled on what the engine may
**read**. The column is still stored, still served and still on the screen.

### One thing found and left alone, on purpose

A second place in the engine still compares that retired figure — but only on a
configuration no installation runs, and it fails by refusing rather than by
charging the wrong amount. It is written down as `DEF-BIL-7310` rather than
changed, because a money fix nobody can run a reproduction against is exactly how
the fault above shipped in the first place.

### The frozen billing figures did not move, and that was run rather than claimed

The document check reports **33 of 33 passing**; it recomputes the signed figures
from the documents and loads none of the product's own code, so it can never go
red when the engine changes. The engine check is the one that protects a
customer's bill, and it is the smaller number: **14 of the 61 signed billing
figures are engine-verified**, and all 14 pass — 23 passed, 1 expected-fail.

## 2026-09-28 · The load balancer's health check, and who may call the API (`CR-144-BRC07`, version `2.388.0`)

**Status: HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.** Nothing below has been shown to the Product
Owner yet. It is written the way it would be read aloud.

### What a person can now do that they could not before

Nothing, on any screen. Every change here is about the machine the product runs
on, and a clerk sees no difference. That is worth saying plainly so nobody looks
for a screen to click.

### The health check — and the number that makes it necessary

The load balancer that will sit in front of the product asks each copy of the
app, every fifteen seconds, *"are you alive?"* — and it asks using the copy's own
private network address, something like `10.0.1.23`, rather than the public name
`api-smart360.bynry.com`.

The app only answers to names it has been told about. So, measured before
anything was built: **it answered `400` — "I do not know that name" — to the
load balancer's own question.** With the HTTPS redirect switched on it answered
`301` instead, which is also not "yes". **Either answer means the load balancer
decides the copy is dead and replaces it, for ever.** Nothing would ever have
served a customer.

The fix is that the health question is now answered **before** the app checks the
name it was asked by. The answer is `200` and the words `{"status":"ok"}`, and it
is the first thing the app does with any request.

**It deliberately does not check the database.** If it did, a slow database would
make every copy of the app look dead, every copy would be replaced, and a slow
product would become no product — the monitoring would cause the outage it was
meant to report.

### Migrations stop running in every copy of the app

Until today, every copy of the app ran the database upgrade at start-up. With one
copy that is fine. With two it is a race: both start the same upgrade, one loses,
it stops with an error, and the machine restarts it straight back into the same
race. And while the upgrade runs, nothing answers the health check — so the load
balancer kills the copy **partway through the upgrade it is waiting for**.

The upgrade now runs **once**, as its own job, before the new version is released.
The checks that are about a copy's own safety stayed where they were — including
the one that refuses to start at all if the database is not enforcing the rule
that keeps one utility's data away from another's.

### Who may call the API

The app will be at `api-smart360.bynry.com` and the screens at `app.bynry.com`.
Two different names, so the browser now asks permission before every call. **The
permission is granted to exactly one address per environment, never to "anyone".**
Granted to anyone, it would not even work: a browser refuses the combination of
"anyone" and "send the sign-in cookie", and the sign-in cookie is the whole point.

**And there is a second lock, which is the one worth reading.** Because both names
end in `bynry.com`, a browser treats them as the same place and will attach a
signed-in user's cookie to a form sent from **any** page ending in `bynry.com`.
Permission-to-read does not stop that form being sent; it only hides the reply.
So a page at, say, `evil.bynry.com` could have made a signed-in clerk's browser
perform a real action. **The app now refuses any action-taking call that arrives
from an address other than our own screens**, before it does anything at all.

Calls that carry no address at all — a script, a payment provider's notification,
a partner's system — are still allowed through, deliberately. They cannot be the
attack, because the attack needs a browser and a browser always sends an address.

### The sign-in cookie is now marked `Secure`

One setting, read in all three places the product issues a sign-in cookie, and it
is **on by default**. Local development over plain `http://` turns it off for
itself. **Neither cookie changed its name** — renaming a live sign-in cookie signs
every signed-in person out at once.

### What is being asked for

Confirmation of two judgments, not of the mechanics:

1. **A call carrying no origin address is let through.** This is what keeps
   partner systems and payment notifications working. The alternative is to
   refuse them, which would break those integrations and defend nothing.
2. **The health check reports "the app is running", not "the app is ready".** It
   will answer `200` while the database is unreachable. That is deliberate — see
   above — but it means a database outage will not show up as unhealthy copies,
   and has to be noticed by monitoring instead.

### Files flagged `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING` (sensitive paths — middleware order)
