## 2026-09-28 · `CR-145-BRC08` — the six session and lockout settings (backend)

**Version `2.389.0`.** Lane SESS-BACKEND. Status: **HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING.**

### What changed, in one sentence

Six numbers that were the same for every utility — how long staff stay signed
in, how long they may sit idle, whether "Keep me signed in" is offered and for
how long, and how many wrong passwords lock an account and for how long — are
now each utility's own choice, inside limits the PO agreed on 2026-09-28
("Im okay with these limit").

### The one thing a utility will actually notice

**Two of the old inactivity choices are gone: 4 hours and 8 hours.** The
choices are now 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes. Any utility sitting on 4 or 8 hours
is moved to **60 minutes** when this ships, and **their staff will be signed
out up to seven hours earlier than they were the day before**. That is the
only visible change in the whole of this work; everything else starts at the
number it already had, so nobody else notices anything.

The move writes a record for each utility it touches, saying what the setting
was and what it became, and it **prints the count while it runs** — on the
database this was proved against, **no utility was on either value, so the
count printed was 0**. The real figure comes from the production database at
deployment and will be in the deployment record.

### The bug this fixes, which is worth more than the settings

"Keep me signed in" has never worked the way it reads. The server kept the
session alive for thirty days correctly — and the browser threw away the only
way to name it the moment it closed. So a person who ticked the box was signed
out anyway, every time they shut their laptop. All three places this product
hands out a sign-in cookie had the same fault. They now say how long the
cookie should live: **the utility's own number when the box is ticked, and
until the browser closes when it is not**.

### Two things that are deliberately NOT settings

1. **The customer portal gets none of its own.** Its fixed 12-hour limit now
   follows whatever the utility chose for its staff. The PO ruled this on
   2026-09-28 — *"one setting is less for an admin to get wrong"*.
2. **The temporary-password lifetime (7 days) and the password rules stay
   fixed.** They sit in the same block of code and on the same screen as the
   six that moved, which is exactly why they are named out loud in the code:
   so nobody widens this change to them later and calls it the same ruling.

### Who may change them — unchanged

Only the System Admin saves. The Executive may look. The Billing Clerk cannot
see the screen at all. That is the same as it was before this change, and
there are three tests holding it there.

### What is being asked for

Confirmation of three judgments, not of the mechanics:

1. **The utilities on 4 or 8 hours are moved without being asked.** They get a
   record of it and nothing else — no notice, no opt-out. The alternative is
   leaving a utility on a number its own settings screen no longer offers, so
   the next person who opens that screen and saves anything at all gets a
   refusal they did not cause.
2. **One fact about a utility is readable without signing in: whether the
   "Keep me signed in" box is offered.** The sign-in screen is drawn before
   anybody has a session, so there is no other way for it to know. It tells a
   stranger nothing else — not the lockout numbers, not the timeouts — and a
   utility nobody has heard of gets the same answer as a real one, so it
   cannot be used to find out which utilities exist.
3. **Dead session rows are deleted nightly, and nothing has ever deleted one
   before.** Only sessions that have expired or that somebody signed out of. A
   session somebody is using is never touched, and a session merely sitting
   idle is not touched either.

### Files flagged `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING` (sensitive path — migration ordering)

`06-backend/apps/identity/migrations/0006_cr145_session_settings.py` — adds the
five columns, each starting at the value that utility already had.
`06-backend/apps/identity/migrations/0007_cr145_withdraw_long_timeouts.py` —
the one that moves utilities off 4 and 8 hours, writes their records and prints
the count. It does not reverse: putting a utility back on a number the product
no longer offers would leave its screen showing a value missing from its own
list.

### Proof

`06-backend/tests/test_cr145_session_settings.py` — 31 cases, every one of them
changing a setting and then measuring what a person at the browser gets:
lockout set to 3 locks on the third wrong password, a 5-minute lock still
refuses at 4 minutes 59 and lets them in at 5 minutes 1, a 4-hour limit ends
the session at 4 hours 1 minute, a 15-minute idle setting signs them out at 15
minutes 1 second, and a 1-day renewal stops renewing after a day.

`06-backend/tests/test_cr145_migration_pg.py` — 8 cases on **real PostgreSQL**,
because the move and the tenant separation cannot be proved on the database the
ordinary test run uses. Four utilities are set up on 4 hours, 8 hours, 30
minutes and 60 minutes, and only the first two move. The separation is proved
as a role the database's own row security genuinely applies to, with each
utility's row planted and shown visible from its own side before either
absence is believed.

Every new case was shown failing first, through the same test runner that runs
them, against the code as it was before this change.

⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-09-28 EVENING, BY THE BACKEND LANE THAT FIRST RAN THEM
(`DEF-IDN-7503`, `DEF-IDN-7504`).** The sentence above was not true when it was
written: the files had not been run. On their first run, **27 of 108 cases
across the eight CR-145/identity test files were red**. Most were the tests'
own mistakes and were corrected; two were real, and they change what is shown
here:

* **The five new settings could not be saved from the screen at all.** The
  save accepted them, answered "saved", and threw them away. Fixed; the
  refusals above (3 to 10 tries, 4 to 12 hours, 1 to 30 days, 5 to 60 minutes)
  now actually refuse, and each is tested through the real save.
* **On a real deployment the move off 4 and 8 hours would have moved nobody
  and printed "0 utilities moved".** The migration looked for the rows before
  telling the database which utility it was working for, and the database's
  row security — which binds even the account that runs migrations — answered
  "none". The tests passed only because they ran as an all-powerful database
  account. A second migration now does the move one utility at a time:

`06-backend/apps/identity/migrations/0008_cr145_withdraw_long_timeouts_per_tenant.py`
— **flagged `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING` (migration ordering).** It moves each
utility still on 240 or 480 minutes to 60, writes the same record, and prints
its own count. `0007` is left untouched, because migrations here are never
edited once they are on the main line. **The number the PO is given is the two
printed counts added together**; on a real deployment `0007`'s will read 0 and
`0008`'s carries the answer. Proved on PostgreSQL 16 as a role row security
genuinely applies to: before the fix, a utility on 480 minutes stayed on 480
and the count read 0; after it, the utility is on 60, the count reads 1, and
one record names that utility.

## `customers/0074` — one table answered "something went wrong" where it should have answered "nothing here" (`DEF-GOV-7821`, 2026-09-29)

`06-backend/apps/customers/migrations/0074_rls_def_gov_7821_attribute_history_deny_on_unset.py`
— **flagged `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING`** (row security AND migration ordering, both
🔒 paths). AI-authored under the ruling of 2026-08-09, *"AI will do it; we will
review it later as human"*. Not RATIFIED without sign-off.

### What to put to the Product Owner, in plain English

**One of our tables was set up to protect itself the wrong way round, and it
would have told a stranger something it should have kept quiet about.**

Every table that holds a utility's data is guarded by a rule saying *only show
a row to the utility it belongs to*. On `account_attribute_history` — the table
recording what class, type and status each customer account had, and when —
that rule was written so that if the system had not yet been told **which**
utility is asking, the database **raised an error** instead of simply showing
nothing.

**Why that matters even though no customer data crossed between utilities.** An
error is an answer. A page that fails with "something went wrong" tells whoever
is asking that they touched something real; a page that shows an empty list
tells them nothing at all. Our rule is the second one — a row belonging to
another utility should be *invisible*, not *forbidden*. **No data leaked. What
leaked was the fact that there was something there to ask about.**

### The concrete figures

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Asking with no utility set | **`ERROR: invalid input syntax for type uuid: ""`** | **0 rows, no error** |
| Asking as the row's own utility | admits it | admits it, unchanged |
| Asking as a different utility | refuses it | refuses it, unchanged |
| Tables in this product with the wrong form | **1 of 305** | **0 of 305** |
| The check that finds this | 1 failed | **7 passed, 1 skipped** |

**It took 1.4 seconds to prove and the fix is six lines of database
instruction.** Nothing about what the product does changes; the only difference
is that one screen which would have shown an error now shows an empty list.

### Why nobody caught it for three days

Three things had to line up, and they did:

1. **The written template we copy from was wrong.** Our database design
   document shows the exact instruction to use for each new table, and that
   example still carried the old faulty wording — while a later page of the
   *same document* said the corrected wording was required. Whoever wrote this
   table followed the template exactly, as they were supposed to. **The
   template is corrected in the same change**, or the next table repeats it.
2. **A one-off repair in September fixed every table that existed at the time**
   and could not fix one created afterwards. This table was created on
   26 September, after it ran.
3. **The check that would have caught it had never run on a developer's
   machine** — it could not find a suitable Python, so it reported "skipped",
   which reads like "nothing to check" (`DEF-GOV-7813`, fixed the same day).
   And the only stored proof we had was taken using an all-powerful database
   account, which is exempt from these rules entirely — **so those earlier
   passes had never actually tested a single refusal.**

### What is being asked for

Confirmation that **showing an empty list rather than an error, when the system
does not know which utility is asking, is what we want** — and that this is a
correction to an existing rule rather than a new one. The corrected wording is
already used by every other table; this brings the last one into line.

### Proved, and how

On real PostgreSQL 16 as `sbh_gate_iso` — deliberately an ordinary database
account that the rules DO apply to, not an all-powerful one. Measured before
and after, side by side, including the old wording failing on the same input
that the new wording handles. The wider suite this belongs to reports **307
passed** under that account.
## `CR-145-BRC08` CLOSED — the six settings, walked in a browser (2026-09-29, version `2.393.6`)

**Files this row covers:** `07-frontend/src/features/identity/SettingsSecurityTab.tsx` (the last
two hand-typed option lists deleted) · `07-frontend/src/api/endpoints.ts` (`SecurityPolicyLimits`
grows the two password entries) · `10-scripts/cr145_t10_six_settings_walkthrough.mjs` (new).
**None of them is a 🔒 sensitive path** — no row-security policy, no rating maths, no ledger
posting, no money rounding, no migration. The migration half of this change request is covered by
its own row of 2026-09-28 and is not re-opened here.

### What is being put to the Product Owner, in plain English with the figures

**All six settings were set to one value, then to another, and the product was watched to see
whether it actually behaved differently. Seventeen checks; every one passed.** Setting a field and
reading it back was deliberately not accepted as proof, because a saved value that governs nothing
is exactly what this change request exists to prevent.

* **Sign out after being idle.** Set to **15 minutes**. A signed-in browser was left completely
  alone for **16 minutes and 20 seconds** by the clock, then a screen was opened: *"Session
  expired — sign in again to continue."* Set to **60 minutes**, a session left alone for
  **20 minutes** was not signed out.
* **The hard limit after signing in.** Set to **4 hours**, a fresh sign-in was stamped to end
  4 hours later; five hours on, the clerk was signed out although they had just been active. Set
  to **12 hours**, the same five hours changed nothing.
* **Whether *"Keep me signed in"* is offered.** Switched off, the tick box disappears from the
  sign-in screen. Switched on, it is back.
* **How long it remembers a browser.** Set to **1 day**, the browser was told to keep the sign-in
  for **1.000 days**; set to **30 days**, for **30.000 days**. A remembered browser two days old
  was let straight back in at 30 days and sent back to sign in at 1 day.
* **How many wrong passwords lock an account.** At **5 allowed**, three wrong passwords locked
  nothing and the right one signed in. At **3 allowed**, the *same three wrong passwords* locked
  the account and the right password was then refused too.
* **How long the lock lasts.** Set to **5 minutes**: still locked after 1 minute, and the right
  password accepted after **5 minutes and 30 seconds** of real waiting. Set to **60 minutes**, the
  same six minutes left it locked.

**Two of the six cannot be waited out by anybody — a twelve-hour session and a thirty-day
remembered browser — and that is stated rather than papered over.** For those two the session
row's clock was moved backwards in the database instead, which is arithmetically the same as time
passing and changes no code and no setting; the walk prints `SUBSTITUTED:` wherever it does this.
The two shortest windows were waited out for real.

**How many utilities the release will move off the four- and eight-hour timeouts: on this demo
database, one.** That figure is demo-only and is labelled so. **The production figure is the sum
of the two lines the upgrade prints while it runs** — on a real deployment the first reads 0 and
the second carries the number; on this machine it came out the other way round, because the
database account here is unrestricted and a real one is not. **Add the two lines; the sum is the
answer either way.**

**What is NOT claimed, and it is the part a signature must not cover:**

* The sign-in screen still prints *"After 5 failed attempts sign-in pauses for 15 minutes"* for
  every utility, including one that has chosen three tries and a sixty-minute lock. Written down,
  not fixed here — the sign-in screen has nobody signed in and cannot read that utility's
  settings, and whether a stranger may be told them is an unanswered question.
* Five older sentences on the Security screen run past our own six-word cap for a plain fact.
  They pre-date this change (checked in the code at the commit before its first) and are written
  down rather than rewritten inside it.
* The customer portal follows the staff setting and has none of its own, which is the ruling. That
  was read in the code, not walked in a browser.

### The test that goes RED if any of this drifts

`07-frontend/src/features/identity/SettingsSecurityTab.test.tsx` now renders the screen against a
**second, different server** — one offering a 14-character minimum, a 16, and a one-year password
expiry, none of which is written anywhere in the front end — and requires the dropdowns to follow
it. A test that only asserted 8, 10 and 12 would pass just as happily with the deleted literals
put back, and would therefore prove nothing about this change. It was shown failing first, through
`vitest`, on `expected … to contain 'value="14"'`.

**Human review: PENDING.** Nothing here moves a signed figure; every limit is the one the PO
signed on 2026-09-28 (*"Im okay with these limit"*), and the two password lists are the values the
server already enforced, now merely published to the screen.

## 2026-09-29 · NEW REQUEST'S FOUR STEPS — THE SERVER HALF (lane REQ03-SERVER, `2.398.0`)

Two 🔒 sensitive paths are touched: a MIGRATION (`customers/0075`) and MONEY
ROUNDING (a fee table's total). Both are AI-authored under the PO ruling of
2026-08-09 and both are flagged `HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING` in the files themselves.

### What this would put to the PO, in plain sentences with the figures

**1 · A fee table's total is now worked out by the server, and it is not what
you get by adding up the column.** Put two fees on a request — a $45.00
connection fee and a $60.00 expedite — and then waive the expedite. The table
still shows both lines, $45.00 and $60.00, because a waived line is a thing
that happened and not a thing that vanishes. **The amount owed is $45.00.**
Adding up the column on screen gives $105.00, which is the number nobody owes.
So the total comes from the server and the screen prints it. Nothing about
what is charged changed; what changed is who does the arithmetic.

**2 · A check is now spelled `check` everywhere a service request stores it.**
It was stored as `cheque`. Payments has always said `check`, and a translation
sat between the two. Requests already in the database are corrected when the
upgrade runs; anything still sending the old word keeps working and gets the
new one stored. **Nothing about a payment already taken changes** — no amount,
no receipt, no ledger entry. The word is the only thing that moves.

**3 · The review step can show what the customer will be told, and two of its
three lines say they will not be sent.** For a request with an email address:
*Request received* is queued the moment you submit; *Documents needed* and
*Fee due* are listed and say they are not going, because **this product has no
wording written for either of them**. A line that is not sent still gets a row,
because a row that is missing and a row that is withheld look the same on a
screen. Writing those two letters is separate work and is not in this change.

### What a signature here would NOT cover

* Whether `Fee due` and `Documents needed` SHOULD be sent, and what they should
  say. The drawing shows the fee line going out on submit; the product cannot,
  and the card says so rather than promising it.
* The service centre still cannot say in American English that its counter
  takes checks — the portal's own list refuses the word (`DEF-TEN-7861`). That
  is written down and not fixed here; the code is another module's.
* `Charged per` on a fee row is whatever the screen sent, and blank when it
  sends nothing (`DEF-CUS-7862`). The price beside it does come from the price
  list. Written down, not fixed: there is nowhere on a charge code to state a
  charged-per, and picking one would be inventing a rule.

### The tests that go RED if any of it drifts

`06-backend/tests/test_req03_four_steps_server.py` — 28 cases, and **23 of them
were shown failing first**, through `pytest`, by undoing each of the four
mechanisms in turn and running the file against the broken code. The two
figures above are asserted by value: `$45.00` against a column of `$105.00`,
and `check` read back off the stored row after both spellings are sent in.
`06-backend/tests/test_req03_told_card_rls_pg.py` — 3 cases on real
PostgreSQL under the non-superuser probe role, because the default suite runs
on SQLite where a tenant-isolation assertion passes by vacuum. The tenant
filter was removed and the file re-run to prove the isolation case can fail.

**Human review: PENDING.** No signed figure moves. B4/B5 are untouched: this
adds no rate, no rounding rule and no new money column — the total is the same
`quantize` to two places every other figure on this screen already uses.

## 2026-09-29 · NEW REQUEST IN FOUR STEPS — STEPS 1 AND 2 (lane SCREEN-A, `2.395.0`)

**What was built.** The New Request form now has four steps instead of six —
*Applicant · Property · Service · Review*. This lane built the first two from
the drawings the PO approved on 2026-09-29
(`05-prototype/new-request-four-steps-2026-09-29/`). Nothing a clerk could ask
for before has been dropped: all 42 questions the six steps carried still have
a place.

**Put plainly, what a clerk sees change on step 1.** Everything about the
applicant is on one screen now — the eleven questions, the co-applicant, and
the documents they brought in. The customer category and the sub-category moved
here from the old step 2, because they describe the person applying. The
co-applicant's three boxes appear when the box is ticked and are typeable
straight away; they also say whose they are, which they did not before — all
three read the same words as the applicant's own boxes.

**On step 2.** *Billing address* is now *Mailing address*, which is also the
word the database uses. When *Same as the service address* is ticked, the
screen **prints that address** — `Mark 234, Unit 12` over `Ottumwa, Iowa 12365`
— instead of showing five empty grey boxes. Clear the tick and the five boxes
open, ready to type.

**One button was removed and one capability was kept, which is the thing to
check.** *Add another document* has gone, as the PO asked. *Attach a file* now
does both jobs: with a file in the box it attaches it, with nothing in the box
it records that the document is still expected — the only way to make the row
that reads *Nothing attached*. A test asserts the second route still works, so
losing it would go red.

### THE ONE THING THIS SIGNATURE WOULD COVER THAT IS A REVERSAL

**City, State and ZIP on step 2 can no longer be typed into.** They are filled
from the premises record and are read-only, which is what the approved drawing
shows and what the rule about where an address lives requires. **This reverses
what the PO asked for on 22 September** — *"correct address will be on presmies
but first time you will ahve to take the details to match it"* — which made
them typeable while no premises had been found.

**The worked case, so nobody has to imagine it:** a clerk takes a new
connection for a plot at the edge of town that is not in the premises register
yet. They can type the street — *Lot 14, Willow Bend* — and that is kept word
for word. **They can no longer type *Ottumwa*, *Iowa* or *52501*.** Those three
boxes sit empty until somebody adds the plot to the premises register.

The columns are untouched, so nothing already recorded is lost and a request
created by any other route can still carry them. **If that is not what was
wanted, it is one line to put back.**

### What is NOT claimed

* Steps 3 and 4 are another lane's and are not built here. They still hold
  the old Service, Fees, and Check panels, re-numbered — the table arrays the
  drawings show are that lane's work.
* The step count itself, `CAPTURE_STEPS`, is shared with that lane and was
  moved here by agreement. It is four.
* The screens were walked in a browser at 1440, 1280 and 420 and photographed
  beside the drawings. Every difference found is written down in
  `05-prototype/new-request-four-steps-2026-09-29/DIVERGENCES-steps-1-and-2.md`
  — ten of them, each with its reason.
* The *found a premises* state on step 2 could not be reached on the demo
  database (nothing matched the search), so that half is proved by a test with
  a faked matching row rather than by a photograph. Said out loud rather than
  left as a gap.

**Human review: PENDING.** No signed money figure moves. The one reversal is
named above, in its own section, with the worked case.

### WHAT WOULD BE PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH THE FIGURES

**No ID to go and look up.** Four statements, each with a number.

**1 · A rate schedule could hold four prices for the same day, and it can no longer.**
The design has said since day one that two versions of one rate schedule must
never both be in force on one date, and the database was supposed to refuse it.
**It never did** — one missing PostgreSQL extension meant the rule was written
down and never switched on, and a note saying it was "left for the human review"
sat in the code for six weeks while nothing counted it. **Ottumwa Water Works
has four versions of one sewer schedule in force on 29 October 2026.** The
database now refuses a fifth, and refuses any new overlap anywhere.

**2 · Correcting a price still works, and that took a deliberate choice.**
When a clerk fixes a typo in a live rate — the board approved `$3.20` and
somebody typed `$32.00` — the product keeps BOTH rows on purpose: the wrong one
for the record and the right one for the bills. **The rule as originally written
down would have refused every one of those corrections**, on all five kinds of
priced thing. The constraint is written so a correction is still allowed, and
there is a test whose only job is to fail if anyone changes that.

**3 · Nothing was repaired on real data, and this is the part to read twice.**
The repair ran on a COPY of the demo database, which holds **4 rate-schedule
versions in 1 utility and no overlaps at all**. So it is proved to run, and it
is proved to find and fix a problem we planted on purpose — and **it proves
nothing about Ottumwa or any other live utility.** The same one-line command
has to be run against the real database, and its answer is the only thing that
says how much there is to fix.

**4 · Where the repair cannot tell which price is right, it stops rather than
guess.** If two versions start on the SAME day and neither is marked as a
correction, there is no way to tell which one the utility meant, and picking
one would put a price on a customer's bill on the strength of a coin toss. The
upgrade stops, prints the utility, the schedule and both rows, and waits for a
person. **That is the intended behaviour, not a failure** — and on a real
database it means somebody must look before the upgrade can finish.

### THE ONE THING THAT NEEDS A DECISION AND IS NOT DECIDED HERE

When two prices ARE in force on one day, the nightly bill run silently charges
the newer one and a one-time or move-out final bill refuses to produce a bill at
all. **Same utility, same day, two answers.** On a `$18.40` / `$21.60` pair, the
household billed by the nightly run pays `$21.60` and is told nothing; the
household closing their account that morning gets no bill. Neither behaviour was
changed here — it is a money judgment and it is written up in
`12-governance/02-decision-log.md` under `DEF-RAT-8004` with the worked figure,
for the PO.

### WHAT WAS PUT TO THE PRODUCT OWNER, AND WHAT THEY RULED

**No ID to go and look up.** They were shown three options for what a corrected
rate row should record, and chose (a), verbatim:

> *"i will take this and use superseded_by in filter - so that it is always
> unique and even if we see in audit it is clear"*

**IN PLAIN ENGLISH, WITH THE FIGURES.** When a clerk fixes a typo in a live
rate — the board approved `$3.20`, somebody typed `$32.00` — the product keeps
both rows: the wrong one for the record, the right one for the bills. The wrong
one had **no end date**, so the schedule's own history table showed it as
`02/01/2026 →`, which on that screen means *still running*, on a row that had
not priced one bill since the day it was corrected. It now reads
`02/01/2026 – 03/01/2026`.

**THE TWO CASES SHOWN, BOTH TESTED.** A version priced from **1 February** and
corrected on **1 March** now ends **1 March** — *in use a month, then
replaced*. The same version corrected on **15 January**, before it had started
pricing at all, ends **1 February** — *replaced the day it would have started*.
That second one is not a nicety: without it the end date lands **17 days before
the start**, the product refuses that shape by name, and **the whole correction
fails, so the clerk cannot fix their typo at all.**

**WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE, AND IT IS THE MONEY HALF.** No bill is re-priced by
this and no bill changes which rate it was worked out from. A corrected row
stops pricing the moment it is corrected — that has been true since
`DEF-RAT-5715` and it is the mark on the row, not its dates, that does it.
Both places in the product that decide which version prices a date drop the
corrected row before they even look at a date.

### THE ONE CLAUSE THIS ROW DOES **NOT** COVER, BECAUSE IT WAS NEVER SHOWN

⚠ **A version that a LATER RATE CHANGE already closed keeps the end date it
already has.** The question was put and answered for the ordinary case — the
version in force now, whose window is open — and a signature covers only what
was shown. **The worked figure a reviewer should weigh:** a version running
**2026-02-01 → 2026-03-31**, superseded by a rate change on 2026-04-01 and
corrected on 2026-06-01, keeps **2026-03-31**. Writing the correction date over
it would make the register claim it priced two months it never priced, and it
would move a date somebody typed and a bill was reproduced against — which is
the rule `rating/0046` already states for this same column. **This returns to
the agenda**; it is not covered by the ruling above.

### THE SECOND THING THAT RETURNS TO THE AGENDA

⚠ **NOTHING IS BACKFILLED, DELIBERATELY.** Every rate row corrected before
today keeps its open end date, so a live tenant will show both shapes side by
side. Whether the old ones should be given an end date too is a separate
decision, and the figure it needs is **0 corrected rows with no end date across
all 8 databases reachable from this container, out of 41 rate-schedule versions
and 0 superseded rows in total — and this container holds no production data.**
The one-line command is `10-scripts/rat_schedule_overlap_census.py
--corrected-open`, and its answer against the REAL estate is the only thing
that says whether a backfill is a migration or a project.

### HOW IT WAS PROVED

**RED FIRST, IN THE HARNESS THAT RUNS IT** (hard-won law 7). Against
`caab7e774` in a clean worktree, **2 of 8 cases failed and 6 passed** — the six
describe behaviour that was already right and are in the file so a later
"simplification" cannot take it away. The two reds, verbatim:

    FAILED …::test_br_rat_1044__corrected_after_it_started_ends_on_the_correction_date
    FAILED …::test_br_rat_1044__corrected_before_it_started_ends_on_its_own_start_date

⚠ **THE POSTGRESQL HALF EXISTS BECAUSE THE SUITE CANNOT SHOW IT** (hard-won law
14). `config/settings/test.py` hardcodes in-memory SQLite, which has no
exclusion constraint, so a version of this change that produced a pair
`ex_tariff_versions_no_overlap` refuses would pass the whole suite green. And
under `django_db` a DEFERRED constraint is **never checked at all** — the trap
the sibling `test_def_rat_8000_no_overlap_pg.py` fell into on its first draft —
so every case calls `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE` at the point where the
answer is due.

## 2026-09-30 · A READ BATCH KEEPS THE RECEIPT OF ITS OWN POST (`DEF-MET-8106`, `2.411.2`)

**Files, HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING:**
`06-backend/apps/metering/migrations/0064_def_met_8106_read_post_receipt.py`
(migration ordering is a 🔒 sensitive path) and the one-line field it adds,
`ReadImportBatch.post_receipt` in `06-backend/apps/metering/models.py`.

**What the Product Owner ruled, and what was shown.** On 2026-09-30 the PO was
told, in plain English, that posting 480 meter readings took about 42 seconds
locally and about 60 on a production-like server, that the server stops
waiting at 60 seconds after the readings are already saved, and that the clerk
then sees *Internal Server Error*; the PO said go on all four fixes (decision
log, *"READS UPLOAD 500 ON 480 READINGS"*). Fix (A) posts a file of more than
200 readings in the background. **The column is how the receipt survives
that:** the request that started the post answers at once, so the figures a
clerk reads afterwards — *480 posted, 2 held and why* — have to be kept
somewhere the screen can ask for them when the progress bar reaches the end.
**The PO was not shown the column itself**; it is a consequence of the ruled
fix and is reviewed here, not ratified.

**What a reviewer should check, in one sentence each.**
1. It is one nullable JSON column added to `read_import_batches`, with no
   default, no backfill and no index: every batch that exists today reads NULL,
   which the receipt endpoint answers with a 404 rather than an empty receipt.
2. It is written once, inside the post's own transaction, by the same function
   that builds the synchronous answer — so a background post and an ordinary
   post print one receipt.
3. It carries no money figure and nothing bills from it.

**Proof:** `06-backend/tests/test_def_met_8106_read_post_job.py` — 11 cases,
9 of which failed on the branch base `e04a500af` (quoted in the file's
header); the endpoint case walks a 202, a 404 before the job runs and the
receipt after it. Applied forward on a PostgreSQL 16.13 database with
`manage.py migrate metering`, reversed to `0063` (column gone) and applied
forward again (column back); the progress half was watched from a third
connection while a real 300-reading background post ran
(`10-scripts/def_met_8106_read_post_cost.py --progress-proof 300`: eleven
intermediate readings of the gauge, 25 → 275, while the job said `running`).

**Rollback:** `manage.py migrate metering 0063` drops the column. The only
reader is `GET /read-batches/{id}/post-receipt`; without it a background post's
screen falls back to the batch's own counts.

## 2026-09-30 · A CATCH-UP STRETCH NOBODY READ: THE READING FIRST, THEN THE METER'S OWN ESTIMATE (`DEF-BIL-8324`, PO option A, 🔒 rating math — back-bill)

| File (repo-relative) | What it is | Authored | Machine evidence | Human review | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `06-backend/apps/billing/backbill.py` (`_fill_never_read_stretches`, **NEW**; `prepare_back_bill` takes `keyed_reads`; the cut-sub-period estimate no longer refuses a sub-period that measured nothing) · `06-backend/apps/metering/selectors.py` (`back_bill_segment_estimate`, **NEW**, read-only; `measured_from` on every read row) · `06-backend/apps/billing/contracts.py` (`ServiceReading.measured_from`) · `runs.py` · `one_time.py` · `penalty.py` (typed readings reach the catch-up and penalty preview) · `06-backend/tests/test_def_bil_8324_catch_up_never_read_stretch.py` (**NEW**, 7 cases) · `tests/test_us_bil_013_backbill.py` tc10 (rewritten to the ruling) | A catch-up is walked meter by meter over its whole window. (1) A read taken after a month nobody read measured that month too, so it is **shared by days** across every month it measured and each share is marked estimated — never billed whole in its own month while the empty month is estimated again, which would bill the same water twice. A reading the clerk types on step 2 is such a read, so it is used first. (2) What no read measured is priced on **the meter's own estimate from its history** (metering's BR-MET-026 average, OQ-191's option C), marked estimated. (3) Only when neither exists does it refuse, naming metering's reason. | AI, 2026-09-30, one-time bill lane (PO ruling *"A for catch-up estimate"*) | Red first on the original code, 7 of 7 (no such seam, no `measured_from`). Green on the default suite. ⚠ **The back-bill ENGINE suites cannot prove this**: their fixture refuses `R3: connection size 'W-58'` before any code under test runs (`DEF-BIL-8326`, filed); the new tests drive the pass directly with real reading objects and run metering's estimate on real reads, and the J70 walk (E4, P5) drives the whole path on the real seed on PostgreSQL. | **PENDING** — the RULE is the PO's; the day-sharing of a covering read is our reading of *"used first"* and has not been shown | HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING |

**In plain English, with the figure.** A catch-up for July to September where
the water meter was last read on 30 June at 460.0 kgal, and the clerk types
470.0 for 30 September: that one reading measured 10 kgal over 92 days, so July
carries 10 × 31/92, August 10 × 31/92 and September 10 × 30/92 — 10 kgal in
all, each month marked estimated. Had nothing been typed, each month would be
the meter's own daily average from its last three real reads times the days in
the month. The PO ruled the fallback; **how a covering reading is shared is a
judgment and returns to the agenda.** ⚠ **SETTLED 2026-09-30 BY THE COORDINATOR UNDER AN EXISTING RULING, NOT RE-ASKED (law 13):** the PO ruled on 2026-08-12, verbatim *"Split by days"*, that usage spanning two prices inside a back-billed period is shared by calendar days (B4.3's proration) — a reading covering several months of a catch-up is the same arithmetic, so it is shared by days. Worked: 10 kgal over 92 days, July's 31 days = 3.37 kgal. **Rollback:** revert the six files; a
never-read stretch refuses again. Nothing is posted by a preview; bills already
issued keep their lines (immutable).

instalment as its own line. Its total stays its own charges and the amount due does
not change, because the $45 is already inside the balance carried forward from
earlier bills. ⚠ Whether a plan account should be asked only for new charges plus
the instalment is NOT decided and is the question to put. *Apply to this bill* was
already built; a new two-month test shows the $120.00 reduces the debt once
($200 − $120 = $80 carried into both September and October).

## 2026-09-30 · B27 — EACH CHECK BATCH OF 500 READS ITS DATA ONCE; A RESULT IS STAMPED WITH WHEN ITS FACTS WERE READ (`DEF-BIL-8491`, `DEF-BIL-8490`, `2.416.0`)

**What changed, in one paragraph.** The bulk Check asked the database about 429
questions per account, two thirds of them identical for every account. It now
opens one memo per batch of 500 (`06-backend/core/batch_reads.py`, bound to one
tenant and closed with the batch), asks each owning module to answer the
batch's own rows in one query set (`06-backend/apps/billing/batch_seams.py`),
and serves every per-account read from that. Separately, every saved result is
stamped with the time the batch READ its facts, not the time it was saved, so
the staleness sweep catches a payment, reading, meter or plan change made after
the read (`DEF-BIL-8491`); and reading lookups use a range on the partition key
(`DEF-BIL-8490`).

   and the memo is discarded in a `finally` when the batch ends.

**In plain English, with figures — not shown to the PO; returns to the agenda:**
1. **Sewer on a catch-up is 40% of THAT month's water.** Maria Alvarez, Unit E,
   July–September: August's water was 15.09 kgal and September's 14.60 kgal, so
   sewer is $30.18 and $29.21. The bill charged $59.39 for each month (the two
   months added together, twice). The bill goes from **$710.06 to $649.49**. The
   penalty bill for Unit F goes from **$1,268.62 to $1,167.85**. Both figures were
   re-priced by hand from the seed's rates before the fix was trusted.
2. **A catch-up shows and stores its months.** Review shows July, August and
   September as three groups with their own subtotals; each stored line carries its
   month; every water line names its meter (12 of 16 did not).
3. **A first bill's footer adds up.** Subtotal $198.84 + Tax $3.98 + One-time
   charges $195.00 (deposit $150.00, connection $45.00) = $397.82. The stored
   `invoices.subtotal` still holds the taxable subtotal ($198.84), as every bill's
   does — changing that column would move every cycle bill with an untaxed line.
4. **A catch-up saves into Meter Reads only what no reading measured.** On Unit E
   every estimate was a share of a real reading, so nothing is saved (saving it would
   make the next true-up subtract the same water twice). A stretch with no reading at
   all is saved as an estimated reading on its own last day.
5. **An interim meter can be estimated.** Hannah Ortiz, W-10460, no September
   reading: the clerk presses *Estimate*, the meter is billed on Meter Reads' own
   estimate (6.0 kgal) and issue saves it as an estimated reading.

**Not proved:** WE-10 (❄️ GT-26) is not engine-verified and the back-bill suite
(`test_us_bil_013_backbill.py`, `test_us_bil_014_penalty.py`) is red on this branch
before this change on its fixture (`DEF-BIL-8326`, 23 tests refusing at gather), so
the per-group call is proved by the new tests and by J74 on PostgreSQL, not by those
suites. **Rollback:** revert the lane's commits; no migration.

**THE IDEMPOTENCY PROOF, in plain English with the figures (PostgreSQL 16, `test_def_bil_8710_send_resume_pg.py`):**
a six-bill run is sent in batches of three; the first batch runs in a SEPARATE Python process with its own
database connection and is **SIGKILLed with one bill issued and the second half-way through its own
transaction**. The batch record is left `running` (a kill writes nothing). A fresh worker takes the second
batch (three bills); the Send screen's poll then hands the Send back by itself (`resumed: true`), reading
**4 of 6** — counted from the bills, never 0 — and the Send finishes. Afterwards, from the database: **6 of 6
issued, each with exactly one journal entry and one `invoice.issued` audit row; every invoice number the one its
draft carried and none used twice in the utility; the release completed once (one `bill_run.released` row,
`released_at` stamped once).**

**What the Product Owner ruled, and what was shown:** nothing new was put to the PO. The batch size (500) and
the cap formula (half the billing workers, never fewer than 1, a platform setting) are the Check's rulings of
2026-09-30, carried to the Send; the judgments taken are in the decision log (*"SEND AT SCALE"*).

**What was NOT shown and returns to the agenda, in plain words:**
1. *"A 40,000-bill Send is now cut into 81 pieces of 500. With 8 billing workers a utility sends 4 pieces at a
   time; with 2 workers, 1. Its cap is a separate setting from the Check's, with the same default."*
2. *"If the machine sending your bills stops, the Send screen notices within about 20 seconds of a fresh
   machine being up and carries on from the bills already sent; it never sends a bill twice."*

**Rollback:** revert the lane's commits. Migration 0037 reverses cleanly (`DROP INDEX`); a Send in flight when
the code is reverted is finished by the old single-task body, which selects the remaining drafts.
